The admissible nonclinical bench is synthetic end-to-end autonomous controller workflow with independent clocks, permission service, dummy load and immutable event packaging. The observable endpoint is independent event-trace completeness [fraction]. Its strongest plausible benchmark is simple append-only signed audit records plus independent bench instrumentation and manual forensic reconstruction. The central mistaken-mechanism alternative is unlogged local actions, timestamp editing, selective case deletion, invalid replay assumptions or cryptographic integrity mistaken for physical truth. Five official family flagships / 正式中英文研究題名 F031 | Causal Identification of Acupuncture-Induced Bioelectric Changes at the Limit / 針灸刺激與生物電變化因果辨識極限 F032 | Placebo and Signal Confounding Separation in Acupuncture at the Limit / 針灸安慰效應與訊號混雜分離極限 F033 | Counterfactual Validation of Acupuncture AI Models at the Limit / 針灸 AI 模型反事實驗證極限 F034 | Multivariable Causal Network Reconstruction in Acupuncture at the Limit / 針灸多變因因果網絡重建極限 F035 | Causal Safety Assurance for Autonomous Acupuncture at the Limit / 針灸自主控制因果安全保證極限 The family integration and five distinct causal objects F031 — Causal identification of electrical responses Three-coupling: controlled surrogate stimulus × independent bioelectric voltage witness × intervention-versus-artifact identification. The admissible nonclinical bench is isolated saline or conductive-gel phantom, coded electrical pulses, independently powered differential voltmeter, optical placement reference and fully disconnected clinical pathways. The observable endpoint is externally measured stimulus-attributable voltage contrast [mV]. Its strongest plausible benchmark is randomized source-on/source-off differences and a circuit-equivalent linear regression with equal calibration budget. The central mistaken-mechanism alternative is shared-ground pickup, electrode polarization, timestamp drift and heating driven by the source circuit rather than a separate biological mechanism. This programme does not combine five incomparable endpoints into one achievement score. Instead, it retains their exact intervention semantics, physical unit ledger, blinded validation budget and stop boundary. A causal conclusion is to be withdrawn or restricted for loss of electrical isolation, undefined intervention dose, uncalibrated voltage reference, nonpositive overlap or any proposal to apply the bench result to a person. A named acupoint or meridian supplies a historically meaningful question; neither is a separately established physical electric-field entity. The admissible nonclinical bench is synthetic deidentified event tables and nonliving signal phantoms with simulated expectancy labels; no induced placebo response or new human intervention. The observable endpoint is unexplained confounding-adjusted response contrast [mV]. Its strongest plausible benchmark is predeclared context-only model, calibrated blinded source-off condition and negative-control analysis. The central mistaken-mechanism alternative is expectation-label leakage, channel gain drift, attention-dependent missingness, assessor knowledge and correlated electrode changes. This programme does not combine five incomparable endpoints into one achievement score. Instead, it retains their exact intervention semantics, physical unit ledger, blinded validation budget and stop boundary. A causal conclusion is to be withdrawn or restricted for unverifiable placebo labels, unmeasured common cause admitted as proof, data privacy violation, source-off negative control failure or clinical extrapolation. The role of attention and ritual is a source of inquiry in traditional practice, not evidence that simulated expectation causes patient benefit. The admissible nonclinical bench is versioned synthetic structural-causal simulator with withheld perturbation seeds and an isolated inert stimulus source. The observable endpoint is absolute effect-estimation error on sealed synthetic truth [mV]. Its strongest plausible benchmark is simple outcome-regression, stabilized inverse-propensity weighting and zero-effect or randomized-source oracle cases. The central mistaken-mechanism alternative is positivity violations, propensity overfitting, post-treatment feature leakage and a simulator favoring the candidate algorithm. This programme does not combine five incomparable endpoints into one achievement score. Instead, it retains their exact intervention semantics, physical unit ledger, blinded validation budget and stop boundary. A causal conclusion is to be withdrawn or restricted for zero intervention overlap, undefined potential outcomes, unbounded importance weights, hidden test-label access or use as clinical decision policy. An unspoken alternative future echoes the question of what language omits; counterfactual quantities remain analytical constructs rather than Daoist cosmology. The admissible nonclinical bench is electrically isolated multichannel phantom and seeded synthetic directed acyclic graph with controlled common-source perturbations. The observable endpoint is false-directed-edge fraction on known synthetic interventions [1]. Its strongest plausible benchmark is sparse lagged regression, fixed known circuit diagram and deliberately acausal correlation network. Instead, it retains their exact intervention semantics, physical unit ledger, blinded validation budget and stop boundary. The observable endpoint is measured unwanted electrical output after veto [mJ]. Its strongest plausible benchmark is fixed-rule fail-closed watchdog and a supervised safe-state controller under matched intervention and latency budgets. evidence_items.summary: Agentic systems extend artificial intelligence (AI) models, including large language models and other foundation models, with capabilities such as planning, tool use, persistent memory, external API access, code execution, and collaboration with other agents. These capabilities enable increasingly autonomous operation, but they also create security, privacy, and safety risks that are not adequately captured by model-level analysis alone. The 1st Workshop on Security, Privacy, and Safety of Agentic AI Systems (AGENT-SEC 2026), held in conjunction with the 2026 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS '26), provides a forum for researchers and practitioners to explore and investigate these system-level risks and the corresponding defenses, evaluation methods, and governance mechanisms. The workshop covers attacks on agentic workflows, privacy risks arising from tools and memory, safety and alignment of autonomous agents, secure distributed and federated agents, governance and accountability, real-world applications, and security assurance and benchmarking.
evidence_items.title: AGENT-SEC '26: 1st Workshop on Security, Privacy, and Safety of Agentic AI Systems

organizations: KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm, Sweden
evidence_items.summary: Vulnerability evaluations of LLM-guarded platforms typically stop at the guardrail boundary: an attacker bypasses the guardrail, exfiltrates a record, and the assessment ends. We report a case study of the platform, a deployed research-data analysis system that fronts a Kubernetes-based RPC infrastructure with an LLM guardrail agent, where a credential-disclosure side effect of a large-scale adversarial probing campaign against the guardrail became the first link in a six-stage lateral movement chain. Starting from a reflected environment variable leaked during guardrail evaluation of submitted analysis code, we recovered an over-privileged workspace token, achieved remote code execution on a Kubernetes pod through an exposed worker daemon, used the daemon’s own logged token to bridge a network-level firewall trusted only inside the host’s institutional cloud, and from there reached private S3 storage, a Weaviate vector database holding both research data and roughly twenty third-party LLM provider API keys, and seven unauthenticated locally hosted inference models. We map each step to the platform’s own threat model, show that the guardrail’s narrow scope (dataset-analysis only) was contradicted by the token’s actual scope (315 enumerated service descriptors, including physical laboratory equipment, several of which we verified were directly accessible), and argue that guardrail-only evaluations systematically under-report blast radius. We discuss the architectural anti-patterns responsible – reflected secrets, daemon token logging, and firewall trust scoped to network origin rather than identity – and give concrete mitigations for LLM-fronted infrastructure of this kind.
evidence_items.title: From Guardrail Leak to Agentic Infrastructure Compromise: Lateral Movement Across an LLM-Orchestrated Kubernetes Platform

evidence_items.summary: The rapid integration of large language models (LLMs) into mobile applications has introduced a new class of privacy and security risks that existing analysis techniques are poorly equipped to address. Unlike conventional third-party service integrations, LLM integrations are bidirectional: sensitive user data flows into model endpoints as part of carefully constructed prompts, and model-generated text flows out into app logic, UI surfaces, notifications, and downstream APIs. Both directions introduce distinct risks, including data leakage, unsafe reuse of model outputs, and input-safety weaknesses, that have not been systematically studied at scale. We present Janus, a static analysis of end-to-end LLM interaction pipelines in Android apps. It recovers request construction semantics, identifies response-entry points and their downstream propagation, and employs a multi-agent reasoning layer to classify privacy- and security-relevant findings. We evaluate Janus on a curated micro-benchmark suite and use it to conduct the first systematic characterization of privacy and security risks in LLM-integrated Android apps. We find that such risks are prevalent in practice, with recurring categories such as client-side secret exposure (e.g., embedded API keys and system prompts), sensitive-data outsourcing to third-party LLM services without corresponding disclosure, secondary leakage of LLM responses to downstream components, and prompt/input-safety weaknesses such as prompt-injection-prone handling. We also present representative case studies that illustrate how these risks manifest in deployed apps and what concrete harm they may enable. In line with our ethical process, we responsibly disclosed critical findings to affected developers.
evidence_items.title: Janus: Characterizing Bidirectional Privacy and Security Risks in LLM-Integrated Android Apps

organizations: University of St. Gallen, St. Gallen, Switzerland
evidence_items.summary: Banks and compliance teams are exploring large language models (LLMs) as fraud analysts. Money laundering, however, is a structural crime. A single laundering transaction looks ordinary, and the evidence lies in how funds move across accounts. An LLM can only support anti-money-laundering (AML) work if it uses this structure rather than surface features. We test whether current LLMs do. We evaluate Claude, GPT-4.1, Phi-4, and Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite on 6,302 transactions from the IBM AML dataset. The benchmark keeps all 370 labeled laundering instances whole across eight typologies. We vary the context from a single transaction, to transaction history, to history with typology definitions and chain-of-thought reasoning. Only two of the four models beat chance, and only with the richest context. Their recall follows how often an account repeats within a laundering instance, not the shape of the instance. They detect hub-based typologies such as fan-in far better than bipartite or cycle typologies. The four models also rarely agree on which transactions are suspicious. These results suggest that current LLMs use repeated account activity as a proxy for fraud, and that they are not yet ready to serve as standalone AML detectors.
evidence_items.title: Do Large Language Models Understand Financial Fraud?

evidence_items.summary: Open-source package ecosystems such as PyPI and npm remain persistent targets for malicious campaigns. These campaigns have outgrown signature-based triage, so recent work has turned to large language models (LLMs) that scan package content and return a verdict, which lets the analysis consume attacker-controlled text. In 2026, the Hades campaign on PyPI carried a prompt injection written to hijack the scanner’s instructions and coerce a clean verdict. Indirect prompt injection is well studied, but its reach into automated package-security analysis remains unmeasured. We therefore ask a broader question. How reliable are LLM-based package scanners when the package itself is written to manipulate the analysis? We present PkgScanArena, a benchmark that pairs a vetted dataset of 2,000 malicious and 1,000 benign npm and PyPI packages with a taxonomy of 11 techniques and 3 injection channels across three attacker goals, namely evasion, denial, and sabotage. An AST-guided pipeline injects these prompts into real packages, and we evaluate 25 open-weight and proprietary model configurations together with two deployed scanners. Our benchmark inverts the expected threat. Evasion proves largely unattainable, at or below 0.6% for nine of ten cloud models. Exposure instead shifts to the opposite direction: benign accuracy degrades for all but two of the 25 backends, sabotage reaches 31.1%, and denial reaches 19.6% on the most safety-aligned model. The two deployed scanners inherit both weaknesses. The exposure lies not in coercing a scanner to miss malicious code, but in coercing it to condemn benign code.
evidence_items.title: PkgScanArena: Benchmarking LLM-Based Package Scanners against Indirect Prompt Injection

evidence_items.summary: To address the scale and spread of digital misinformation, researchers have developed automated techniques to aid in the fact-checking process. Unfortunately, these systems are rarely designed for real-world deployment settings and struggle with the unique challenges of realistic verification: claims may lack ground truth, evidence is sparse and evolving, and decisions must be made within hours. In this paper, we present and evaluate a new system for automated fact-checking, RealTiCheck, that integrates large language models (LLMs) with web search to gather, collate, and employ online evidence to fact-check recent potential misinformation claims. We evaluate RealTiCheck on state-of-the-art benchmark datasets, with our system outperforming comparable prior work (Macro-F1 score of 0.81). We then explore how RealTiCheck can be used in practice by hiring seven professional fact-checkers to fact-check 174 novel and recent (less than 24 hours old) claims. We evaluate how well our system triages and adjudicates claims compared to professional fact-checkers' verdicts. We conclude by discussing design recommendations for future real-time fact-checking systems.
evidence_items.title: Designing an Automated Fact-Checking Pipeline for Recent Claims

evidence_items.summary: Financial documents combine narrative disclosures, accounting metrics, corporate structures, management commentary, and time-dependent facts, making them difficult to represent using conventional chunk-based retrieval-augmented generation systems. This paper presents an auditable, schema-driven methodology for constructing temporal financial knowledge graphs from page-delimited documents parsed using a general purpose document intelligence service. Overlapping document windows undergo phased large language model extraction of structural entities, quantitative observations, and domain-specific relationships. Candidate graph elements are validated against predefined schemas and consolidated through scope-aware exact, normalized, fuzzy, embedding-based, and LLM-assisted entity resolution. Temporal merge constraints, deterministic edge deduplication, conflict-aware property management, and fine-grained provenance preserve issuer identity, reporting-period validity, and traceability to source evidence. The contributions of this work comprise the proposed methodology for financial knowledge graph construction, the creation of an evidence-grounded temporal knowledge graph from heterogeneous financial documents, and an intrinsic framework for evaluating the quality of the resulting graph. The evaluation framework assesses seven weighted dimensions, two hard validation gates, and structural diagnostics. By separating graph-quality assessment from downstream retrieval and answer generation, the framework supports systematic diagnosis and iterative refinement of the constructed graph. The resulting knowledge graph is subsequently used as the retrieval substrate for GraphRAG-based financial question answering, with FinanceBench serving as a downstream evaluation benchmark. This work establishes knowledge graph construction and quality evaluation as explicit, measurable, and auditable components of financial document intelligence.
evidence_items.title: Auditable Financial Knowledge Graphs: Schema-Driven Construction and Intrinsic Quality Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Financial disclosures carry much of their quantitative content in charts rather than in text, and vision-language models read those charts poorly. On FinChart-Bench, a benchmark of real financial charts, its authors report that models built specifically for charts trail general-purpose models of comparable size. We ask what chart-to-table supervision, a core objective of those specialised models, contributes when a general VLM is fine-tuned on financial charts. Our corpus pairs 2,926 charts with gold tables: 249 real financial charts whose tables were drafted by a language model and verified against the image by human annotators, and 2,677 rendered charts whose tables come from the generating code. From these tables we generate arithmetic question–answer supervision programmatically, so every derived answer is exact with respect to its table and no teacher model produces the supervision. We train on that supervision together with the chart-to-table pairs themselves. A 4B model fine-tuned on the resulting mixture averages 0.793 ± 0.005 across three seeds on FinChart-Bench, above every open-weight model in the benchmark’s published evaluation, including one six times its size, although those figures come from a different harness; under ours, the strongest re-run baseline, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, averages 0.689. A controlled ablation separates the two ingredients. Removing the chart-to-table samples, with all other supervision held fixed, leaves chart reasoning unchanged (+ 0.003 ± 0.004) but reduces chart-to-table extraction by 0.182 ± 0.056, to below the untrained backbone. Under joint fine-tuning, extraction supervision is therefore protective: it preserves a capability that question-answering training otherwise erodes. The same pattern holds on the 848 document pages of FinCriticalED, where removing it nearly triples the number of values the model invents. On these general documents, however, our model is less faithful than its backbone. We release the corpus, a 50-chart extraction benchmark withheld from training, and the adapter.
evidence_items.title: From Curriculum to Rehearsal Learning: Towards Small Financial Chart VLMs

evidence_items.summary: Feature engineering in tabular fraud detection is critical yet challenging to automate due to extreme class imbalance, which heavily penalizes spurious features. While Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate candidate features from dataset schemas, schema-level plausibility correlates poorly with actual predictive value. We propose an LLM-based Automated Feature Engineering (AutoFE) framework that assesses candidates strictly on executed empirical behavior. Every candidate is executed on a data split to extract a structured profile of empirical metrics, including deterministic data-integrity checks and output value distributions. A role-separated multi-agent panel, comprising a Critic, Proposer, and Adjudicator, evaluates this evidence to rigorously retain, repair, or discard features. Because the optimal interpretation of raw diagnostics is unknown a priori, a single evaluation pass is insufficient. To bridge this gap, a validation-gated meta-learning stage optimizes the system iteratively across multiple execution passes. By analyzing the realized downstream utility of previously accepted features, this stage dynamically refines the natural-language skills used to read diagnostic tools, updates system memory regarding feature-family behavior, and recalibrates acceptance thresholds for subsequent passes. Evaluated on three severely imbalanced fraud benchmarks (CCF, TabFormer, BAF v2), our framework achieves the strongest PR-AUC among the evaluated LLM-based methods while retaining compact feature sets. By consolidating the evaluation process, moving from iterative, trial-and-error prompting to a single, comprehensive diagnostic profile, the method reduces per-pass evaluation costs by 42% while significantly lifting predictive performance, including a PR-AUC increase from 0.878 to 0.949 on the CCF dataset.
evidence_items.title: Don’t Trust, Verify: Adaptive Multi-Agent Feature Engineering for Financial Fraud Detection

evidence_items.summary: Gradient boosted decision trees (GBDTs) are widely used for tabular data in finance, healthcare, and risk assessment. As GBDT training and inference are increasingly outsourced, clients need to verify that models are trained as claimed and predictions are consistent with those models, while providers may need to keep training data and model parameters private. This makes zero-knowledge proofs for GBDT training and inference a natural solution. Existing approaches typically compile training certification into circuits and prove their execution using generic ZKP backends, incurring high prover costs. Directly proving the underlying algebraic relations offers an alternative, but proving each relation separately incurs substantial costs for committing to and opening auxiliary witnesses. Batching is challenging because these witnesses have different shapes and sizes and are encoded over different domains. We present Terrae, a zero-knowledge proof system for quantized GBDT training and inference based on KZG polynomial commitments. Terrae avoids both proving circuit computation and proving each constraint separately by leveraging the structure of GBDT training and two new batching techniques: domain-lifting batching for low-degree algebraic constraints and interleaving batching for same-form non-native constraints. Both techniques work over differently-sized domains and reduce many constraints to a single claim without introducing extra polynomial commitments. We also design a histogram proof that proves the correctness of aggregating sample-wise updates into histograms, which may be of independent interest. Our evaluation shows that, compared with prior work CertXGB instantiated with the same KZG backend, Terrae achieves proof-generation speedups of 3.18--13.55× for training and 1.96--4.31× for inference across completed benchmark comparisons, with lower peak prover memory, at the cost of moderately larger proofs and higher verification time.
evidence_items.title: Zero-Knowledge Proofs for Gradient Boosted Decision Trees

evidence_items.summary: Flow correlation attacks threaten Tor's anonymity by linking both ends of a communication circuit. Yet, existing correlation models rely on artificial datasets, resulting in significant performance degradation when evaluated against the sparse and highly variable nature of live Tor traffic. In this paper, we challenge this unrealistic evaluation by introducing two new datasets: Correlated GTT23, constructed from genuine exit traces, and Correlated CellFlow, comprising ground-truth flow pairs that we directly collected from the live Tor network. To tackle the unique challenges of these datasets, we propose ESPRESSO, a robust flow correlation attack tailored for realistic Tor traffic. ESPRESSO utilizes a density-based window representation via Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) to dynamically adapt to differences in transmission volume across a trace. Our results show that ESPRESSO outperforms state-of-the-art Tor flow correlation attacks, significantly improving detection accuracy across various scenarios, including standard settings and traffic drifted by temporal and network environment shifts. Notably, ESPRESSO achieves an impressive 88% True Positive Rate (TPR) at a False Positive Rate (FPR) of 10-5 , whereas DeepCoFFEA, the state-of-the-art attack, degrades to a near-zero TPR for the same FPR. This robustness holds even under adversarial constraints, including partial trace observations (as few as 500 cells) and limited visibility over the network under large numbers of concurrent connections (base rates as low as 10-4 ). These findings indicate that flow correlation remains a severe, imminent threat, establishing both our datasets and ESPRESSO as the new standard benchmarks for evaluating future flow correlation attacks and defenses.
evidence_items.title: Brewing Under Pressure: More Realistic Tor Flow Correlation Considering Low FPRs

evidence_items.summary: Industrial networks have evolved into converged IT-OT-IIoT environments in which Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) pivot across domains to disrupt physical processes. Despite growing research on APT detection, the literature remains fragmented, with limited structure for comparing approaches and identifying underexplored areas. This Systematisation of Knowledge (SoK) introduces a five-dimensional taxonomy of APT detection mechanisms in IT-OT-IIoT environments covering data source, detection scope, detection mechanism, detection objective, and evaluation basis, and maps 64 peer-reviewed studies to it. As an analytic tool, the taxonomy highlights underexplored combinations of taxonomy dimensions. Cross-dimensional analysis reveals three imbalances: (i) machine learning dominates (68.8% of papers) but concentrates on IT data, leaving the OT attack surface underexplored; (ii) detection ambition and validation rigour are inversely related, with no boundary-crossing detection validated in operational deployment; and (iii) no reviewed study addresses multi-site detection. Communities with operational data and researchers studying APT detection remain disconnected, discouraging investment in cross-domain datasets. From the classification matrix we derive seven research gaps covering cross-domain correlation, IT-OT temporal sequence modelling, multi-site attack detection, APT-informed physical-layer detection, threat-intelligence operationalisation, benchmark datasets, and deployment feasibility. Overall, current work lacks a detection configuration that is cross-domain, temporal, process-aware, and practically deployable.
evidence_items.title: Advanced Persistent Threat Detection in IT-OT Converged Industrial Networks: A Systematisation of Knowledge

evidence_items.summary: Fraud detection in financial transactions has been studied for decades, yet methods proposed in the literature remain difficult to compare due to inconsistent data, training, and evaluation practices. In this position paper, we identify three structural gaps behind this problem: the use of unsuitable or poorly standardized public datasets, inconsistent sequence and label construction (including the treatment of delayed fraud labels) and evaluation protocols poorly suited to the severe class imbalance of fraud detection. We audit representative sequential fraud detection methods against these gaps but could not establish that any single study addressed all three. Controlled experiments demonstrate that these choices can change scientific conclusions rather than merely reported scores: models that appear equivalent under ROC-AUC separate under precision–recall evaluation; iid splits mask the performance decline observed under chronological evaluation; and, on a widely used public benchmark whose protocol required reverse-engineering from released code, changing the labeling convention alone reverses the relative ranking of two methods. We therefore propose a standardized experimental protocol for sequential fraud detection and provide an open reference implementation with deterministic temporal splits and synthetic label delay on public datasets.
evidence_items.title: A Standardized Training and Evaluation Protocol for Sequential Fraud Detection

evidence_items.summary: ML-based Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDS) often report near-perfect benchmark accuracy but degrade sharply once deployed. This gap is driven partly by temporal data leakage, a pitfall raised for security ML generally but not systematically quantified for NIDS. Reproducing three published architectures, adapting a fourth across datasets, and independently designing a fifth, accuracy and recall reductions of 16.6-50.9 percentage points are observed under temporally-ordered evaluation, and in one case near-total collapse of a fixed anomaly-detection threshold, consistent with concept drift as a substantial contributor to this gap. AEGIS is proposed as a framework grounded in Design Science Research (DSR) and Design Thinking (DT) moving NIDS drift handling from detection toward decision support. Current drift explanations, though valuable, remain feature-level outputs that assume analyst expertise, falling short of human-centered design; AEGIS incorporates DSR and DT into drift handling, so Security Operations Center (SOC) analysts reach faster, more trustworthy decisions.
evidence_items.title: POSTER: AEGIS: A Framework for Human-Centered Explainable AI in Concept Drift Triage for Network Intrusion Detection

evidence_items.summary: Knowledge graph embedding (KGE) models are vulnerable to targeted data poisoning through the injection of a small number of training triples. Existing poisoning attacks typically employ a fixed attack mechanism for all targets, overlooking the heterogeneous vulnerabilities of individual target triples. We propose TAR-KGE, a target-level attack routing framework that adaptively selects attack mechanisms for each target. TAR-KGE first evaluates heterogeneous poison candidates using a unified target-relative virtual score derived from one-step virtual updates, and then constructs complementary poison sets via marginal greedy selection. Experiments on two benchmark datasets with four representative KGE models demonstrate that TAR-KGE consistently outperforms existing fixed-mechanism attacks and, relative to the corresponding clean models, reduces MRR by up to 41.9% and Hits@1 by up to 76.5%. These results validate the effectiveness of target-level attack routing and reveal the benefit of exploiting cross-attack complementarity.
evidence_items.title: POSTER: Target-Level Attack Routing for Knowledge Graph Embedding Poisoning

evidence_items.summary: Organizations may want to use hosted coding agents on private repositories. However, a coding session can expose sensitive text through file reads, search results, test logs, stack traces, and patches. Cleaning only the initial prompt leaves these later channels exposed. We introduce AnonAgentBench, a benchmark for evaluating repository anonymization across the complete agent interaction. The benchmark replaces planted sensitive strings before the agent sees them. It restores the original strings locally in the generated patch and evaluates that patch on the original task. The private mapping remains in the local harness. We test three forms of full-loop anonymization. Level B replaces protected strings throughout the interaction. Level C uses consistent placeholders across all channels. Level D adds limited type or role hints to those placeholders. Across 488 available prompt-only traces, the configured scanner found 3,375 Devstral and 2,852 Qwen exact planted-string occurrences. It found none in 1,462 available full-loop traces; this zero is a deterministic coverage and implementation check over observed model-visible channels. A separate inventory-independent fragment/Gitleaks audit of the same full-loop traces found no task-specific fragments (minimum nine characters) or stock-rule matches. Without anonymization, Devstral solved 235 of 500 tasks, and Qwen solved 259 of 500. We then applied full-loop anonymization to those solved tasks. Devstral continued to solve 127–141 of 235 tasks (54.0–60.0%), while Qwen continued to solve 197–203 of 259 tasks (76.1–78.4%). These raw-resolved percentages are conditional retention, not full-denominator or deployment estimates. In two sensitivity comparisons, positive submitted-instance differences disappeared or reversed after excluding pairs with an empty patch or evaluator error. AnonAgentBench therefore benchmarks observed-channel exact-string coverage, private restoration, and conditional utility; it does not establish semantic or formal privacy.
evidence_items.title: AnonAgentBench: Measuring Coding-Agent Utility Under Reversible Repository Anonymization

evidence_items.summary: Benchmarks often describe an LLM evaluation as blind after replacing company names and tickers with anonymous identifiers. We argue that blindness is not a preprocessing operation but an empirical property: under a declared threat model, the released record must resist linkage to its source while retaining what the benchmark means to evaluate. Our matched utility–linkability audit for point-in-time stock ranking holds the stock, date, numeric features, and realized return fixed, varying only the visible identity and news representation. An open-ended LLM, given one name-masked record (Blind) and neither a candidate list nor a corpus, names the issuer on 71% of rows; with same-date corpus access, fixed retrieval attacks recover the source on 99.8% of rows, and strict redaction, typed entity replacement, and LLM rewriting remain similarly linkable. Theme and Event abstractions cut exact-stock recovery to 5.1% and 3.9% against a 1.37% chance rate, but neither improves the Rank Information Coefficient over a numeric-only condition, so no tested representation combines near-chance linkability with detectable utility. Raw news is model- and prompt-order-sensitive and statistically unresolved within sectors; its sample portfolio difference concentrates in sector allocation without establishing within-sector selection. Separate attacks recover identity from numeric profiles and longitudinal scores even when text is masked. These surfaces motivate a threat-model-relative complete-record audit reporting source and group linkability and no-news-anchored, target-level utility. The code is available at https://github.com/minsuk-sung/ICAIF2026-AlphaLeak.
evidence_items.title: AlphaLeak: What `Blind' LLM Trading Benchmarks Still See

evidence_items.summary: Multispecific antibodies (msAbs) offer transformative therapeutic potential by engaging multiple epitopes simultaneously, yet their efficacy is an emergent property governed by complex molecular architectures. Rational design is often bottlenecked by the inability to predict how subtle changes in domain topology influence functional outcomes, a challenge exacerbated by the scarcity of comprehensive experimental data. Here, we introduce Synapse, a biologically inspired synthetic benchmark for topology-aware modeling of msAbs. First, we present a generative method that combines nonlinear per-domain sequence-to-score landscapes with connectivity-dependent synthetic readouts. Second, we propose a graph neural network architecture that explicitly encodes these topological constraints, distinguishing between format configurations that appear identical to the evaluated connectivity-agnostic multilayer perceptron. We demonstrate that this model learns topology-dependent structure–function relationships on synthetic landscapes and evaluate a transfer learning workflow as infrastructure for adaptation to biological datasets. We showcase our framework with a trispecific T cell engager-inspired synthetic topology-dependent optimization task and a constrained ranking of common light chain candidates against a composite objective. This work provides a controlled benchmarking environment for developing and evaluating topology-aware computational tools for msAb modeling. All experiments use synthetic data; no biological validation is performed.
evidence_items.title: A Synthetic Benchmark for Topology-Aware Modeling of Multispecific Antibody Function

evidence_items.summary: With the rapid expansion of content-centric architectures like Named Data Networks (NDN), efficient cache management has become essential for optimizing network performance. Among the various factors, the parameter β plays a crucial role in adjusting cache sensitivity based on content popularity distribution. An improper choice of this parameter can lead to lower cache hit rates, increased data pollution, and inefficient use of resources. This research introduces a novel framework utilizing the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) for distributed and adaptive tuning of β. The decentralized structure of the proposed model enables implementation at the network node level, facilitating fast convergence and accurate β tuning through coordinated updates of both primary and dual variables. Additionally, an enhanced version, ADMM-Enhanced, has been developed to offer greater stability, precision, and adaptability to network dynamics by automatically adjusting the parameters λ and ρ. To evaluate four network topologies (simple, hierarchical, enhanced, and mesh) were simulated under three operational scenarios: steady state, cache pollution attacks (CPA), and traffic load changes. Experimental results indicate that the ADMM-Enhanced algorithm increased the cache hit rate by 30% and reduced pollution to zero in stable conditions. It also demonstrated robust, adaptable, and resilient performance under severe attacks (with 30% attackers), maintaining a cache hit rate (CHR) of 18% and a cache pollution rate (CPR) of 18%. Furthermore, in complex topologies like mesh, the algorithm maintained cache efficiency and quality despite distributed threats, congestion, and link failures, showing high adaptability to dynamic network conditions.
evidence_items.title: Comparing the performance of caching algorithms in named data networks with a focus on reducing contamination attacks and optimizing the β parameter

evidence_items.summary: Absorption and scattering coefficients for the Jerlov optical water types, taken from the primary literature with the provenance of every value recorded. Values that a published table got wrong are flagged rather than silently repaired, and quantities the data do not determine are refused rather than guessed. Thirty-nine entries are documented, thirteen of them confirmed defects in the source literature: duplicated rows in Solonenko & Mobley (2015) Table 7, a transcription error in the small-particle scattering coefficient that propagated into their published coefficients, a Data Availability Statement that gives the DOI of an unrelated dataset, a reprint whose stated unit is out by a factor of ten, a misprinted equation for trichromatic colour thresholds in Vorobyev & Osorio (1998), a row of Smith & Baker (1981) Table I whose pure water absorption exceeds its own diffuse attenuation, a sign misprinted in Duntley's (1963) equation for the apparent radiance along a slanted line of sight, and a second factor of one half printed inside Fresnel's law in Gregg & Carder (1990). Three further entries were open questions that obtaining the 1968 first edition settled. The same Jerlov water type is in circulation with beam attenuations differing by a factor of five, which is why every coefficient here carries the source it came from. Every shipped table can be regenerated from its primary source by the scripts in tools/ , and each generation step checks the result against the equations of the paper it came from.

evidence_items.summary: Most image-based plant disease studies train deep networks on large laboratory datasets, yet many practical projects have only a few hundred field photographs and no GPU. This paper evaluates eight standard machine learning classifiers on a small field image dataset of 1,532 leaf photographs labelled Healthy, Powdery (powdery mildew) and Rust, using 129 hand-crafted colour, texture and shape features. Classifiers were compared by nested, repeated stratified cross-validation on the 1,382 training and validation images, and the best model was tested once on the untouched official 150-image test set. Gradient boosting achieved the highest cross-validated accuracy (92.04% ± 1.41%) and significantly outperformed random forest (89.87%; corrected resampled t-test, p = 0.021). On the official test set it reached 89.33% accuracy (95% CI 83.4–93.3%), a macro F1-score of 89.37% and Cohen's κ = 0.84, within four points of a published DenseNet121 result on the same data. Colour and texture features were the most informative; adding shape features reduced k-nearest-neighbour accuracy from 87.37% to 66.79%. Random forest was the most data-efficient model, reaching 68.4% test accuracy with only five training images per class. The commonest error was a diseased leaf predicted as healthy (10 of 100 diseased test leaves). A bias control using only eight border pixels per image reached 58.1% in cross-validation but 38.7% on the test set (chance: 33.3%), revealing that capture conditions shared within the training split inflate cross-validated estimates. Classical machine learning is therefore a strong, low-cost baseline for field disease recognition, provided performance is reported on an independent test set.
evidence_items.title: Evaluation of Standard Machine Learning for Plant Leaf Disease Recognition on a Small Field Image Dataset

evidence_items.summary: ⚠️ Archived: this repository is archived and no longer developed. Its successor is Stabilo Benchmark 🎯. Stabilo-Optimize is a Python benchmarking tool designed specifically to evaluate and tune methods and hyperparameters of the Stabilo ⚖️ library for video and track stabilization tasks. It systematically generates performance evaluations through random perturbations, eliminating the need for ground-truth homographies. This tool significantly simplifies the optimization of stabilization techniques, making it ideal for high-precision tasks in fields such as urban monitoring, traffic analysis, and drone imagery processing. About the successor: Stabilo Benchmark 🎯 continues this project. Stabilo-Optimize tunes Stabilo under random perturbations of static scenes, the campaign of the associated article . Stabilo Benchmark extends that campaign to complete registration pipelines (feature detector, descriptor, matcher, robust estimator and object masking) on static and real dynamic urban scenes, scored against an audited reference. It is the benchmark of the paper "Consensus Capture in Reference-Based UAV Video Stabilization: A Benchmark on Dynamic Urban Scenes" (arXiv preprint), whose inputs and results are in a data record on Zenodo. 📌 Important: If you use this code in your work, kindly acknowledge it by citing the following article: Robert Fonod, Haechan Cho, Hwasoo Yeo, Nikolas Geroliminis (2025). Advanced computer vision for extracting georeferenced vehicle trajectories from drone imagery , Transportation Research Part C: Emerging Technologies, vol. 178, 105205. DOI: 10.1016/j.trc.2025.105205 Why Stabilo-Optimize Ground Truth-Free Benchmarking : Randomly generates photometric and homographic perturbations (brightness variations, Gaussian blur, saturation adjustments, fog effects, rotations, translations, scales, and perspective shifts).

4D SOFT NEURAL INTERFACES F121-F125 | FAMILY 25 | FIVE-FLAGSHIP SCIENTIFIC TECHNICAL NOTEBOOK 33 × STARLI | The companion to the 819-page nonclinical research monograph EVIDENCE BOUNDARY: all 3D sensitivity surfaces and materials response scenarios are synthetic analytic examples. The manuscript reports no patient investigation, no demonstrated therapy benefit, no quantum advantage and no automated clinical decisions.   A LETTER FROM THE TWENTY-FIFTH RESEARCH FAMILY What is a trustworthy soft neural interface before its name becomes a claim about the nervous system? Its changing shape, force transmission, electrode impedance and damage history each require a different independent instrument. A pleasant contact animation may conceal higher pressure. A clean electrical spectrum can conceal phase drift. A strong early fatigue trial may hide late delamination. The five flagship questions demand separate negative controls and noncompensatory stops. F121 tests reversible contact adaptation under pressure-controlled curvature changes. F122 challenges the meaning of low-disturbance contact when shear and local force are measured independently. F123 separates genuine complex-impedance stability from hydration and lead artifacts. F124 investigates hidden long-tail mechanical fatigue and debris. F125 refuses higher signal quality whenever independent surrogate-safety measurements fail. The common platform is an inert stretchable-electrode coupon and nonliving tissue-surrogate board, never a clinical study. The companion PDF preserves the 819-page research architecture with 42 standalone reproducible mathematical grids, 30 candidate equations, 82 chapters of six progressive pages, 200 Research Gates and 33 unbuilt Phoenix concepts. The notebook develops the same research questions in a more continuous scientific prose. The public five-stage parallel spacetime name is a methodology for structured research reasoning, not a claim of real parallel spacetimes. I. NINE TITLE-LED SCIENTIFIC DESCRIPTIONS AND FIVE FURTHER PRELUDES 01 | Research Title and Scientific Identity — 4D Soft Neural Interfaces at the Limit The title '4D Soft Neural Interfaces at the Limit' identifies a nonclinical research program, not a device already validated for implantation or rehabilitation. Here the fourth dimension refers to the measurable history of a compliant interface: its bending, recovery, contact evolution and accumulated damage as conditions change over time. Five distinct questions give this title scientific content. F121 asks whether shape-adaptive contact can recover across unseen curvature histories. F122 asks whether an electrode can preserve an interpretable proxy signal while contact force and shear remain independently constrained. F123 follows complex impedance as deformation, wetting and cable motion compete to explain apparent stability. F124 examines when hydration and mechanical cycling lead to irreversible cracks, delamination or debris. F125 studies whether any gain in proxy signal quality survives a noncompensatory safety boundary. The five studies share a surrogate platform, but none substitutes for another. This notebook is the prose companion to the separate 819-page research edition. Its purpose is to make the research questions reconstructable by a later laboratory: which physical state was manipulated, what observation could distinguish the intended mechanism, what ordinary method might win, and what failure would require the claim to stop. The title is therefore a promise of falsifiability and inheritance, never an assertion of clinical effectiveness. 02 | Core Three-Coupling — Morphology, Neural-Signal Proxies and Independent Safety The family is organized around three interacting but separately measurable domains: time-dependent flexible-material deformation, electrical contact and signal integrity, and safety-limited mechanical interaction. 'Coupled' must mean an experimentally traceable interface among the three, rather than three attractive words placed next to one another. A curvature change can alter real contact area and the distribution of local pressure; pressure can affect electrode impedance, while sliding can create transient electrical artifacts. The same change may improve a proxy recording and simultaneously increase surface burden. For F121 and F122 the causal comparison therefore holds material batch, geometry and pressure allocation constant where possible. For F123, complex impedance is measured against independently calibrated lead motion and hydration. For F124, damage state is allowed to predict later failure rather than being redefined after failure. F125 treats safety not as a weighted reward that a good signal can purchase, but as a separate veto. A valid three-coupling experiment reports synchronized deformation, electrical response and mechanical burden, their instruments and uncertainties, and their relationship to held-out conditions. When an apparent improvement disappears after force matching or artifact cancellation, the mechanistic claim must be weakened. That possibility is precisely what makes the title a genuine research title rather than a success slogan. 03 | Core Research Question and Boundary — When Does Soft Contact Become Credible? Can a time-programmed compliant neural interface maintain stable contact and independently readable electrical proxies under bending radius, shear, moisture and ageing perturbations without increasing unsafe surrogate-surface loading? The question contains its own rival: a stronger signal may be nothing more than harder pressing or an unrecognized recording artifact. The minimum experimental object is a stretchable electrode attached to an inert tissue-like surrogate board with calibrated curvature control, force sensing and electrical reference pathways. The first claim should be tested against a pressure-matched passive electrode and a geometry-matched ordinary compliant contact. Hidden curvature order, reversed rest intervals, sensor lead perturbations and selected contact failures supply counterfactual worlds. A held-out test should preserve all attempted trials in the denominator, including disconnections and rejected acquisitions. Success in an isolated demonstration cannot stand in for a predetermined distribution of conditions. No inference crosses from inert surrogates to tissue inflammation, long-term implantation, neuromodulation, patient safety or stroke recovery. Those require separate biology, ethics, regulatory work and prospective clinical evaluation. Where the surrogate cannot identify a mechanism, the correct finding is an unresolved interface question, not permission to enlarge the claim. 04 | Six Falsifiable Claims and Thirty Candidate Equations — Geometry Is Not Proof The 30 proposed equations in the companion research book are six per flagship. They describe testable relationships, measurement definitions or decision constraints; none should be presented as a newly discovered clinical or physical law merely because it has a three-dimensional representation. Each flagship tests six different obligations. First, does the physical coupling remain identifiable under controlled disturbance? Second, can a frozen model predict hysteresis or adaptation under hidden stimulus order? Third, does the claimed increment outperform a fair classical or passive baseline at equal sensing and material budgets? Fourth, can an independent witness distinguish the intended mechanism from a rival, such as pressure-induced signal gain? Fifth, does a hard safety gate reject excessive pressure, shear, residue or unmeasured hazards even when apparent performance rises? Sixth, can another laboratory rebuild both a successful case and a refuting case without coaching from the originator? Stress in pascals, strain as a dimensionless ratio, impedance in ohms and phase in radians must not be silently mixed. A curved surface is useful only when its axes, units, parameter domain and generating rule are explicit. The numerical maps in this research pair are synthetic sensitivity illustrations. They can expose an unexpected tradeoff or a discontinuity worth testing, but they cannot establish that a neural interface will be effective or safe in a person. 05 | Five-Layer Research System — From Inert Surrogates to Independent Reconstruction A title that promises soft-neural-interface engineering needs an operational route from hypothesis to refusal. The five-layer system establishes that route before any favorable electrical trace is selected for display. Layer one fixes the sample identity, intended nonclinical use, allowed stimulus window and stop authority. Layer two performs traceable mechanical, geometric and electrical calibration with independent witnesses, including pressure [Pa], curvature [1/m], complex impedance [ohm] and relevant clock offsets [ms]. Layer three separates mechanism from nuisance variables through pressure-matched controls, randomized histories, simple passive competitors and frozen evaluation denominators. Layer four blinds the controller to hidden delamination, unobserved lead motion or altered moisture and requires it to reject conditions that exceed the approved envelope. Layer five transfers raw data, material batches, calibration versions, failed runs and re-execution instructions to an outside team. A beautiful interface photograph may motivate the project, yet it cannot replace those layers. The scientific object is not a shape alone; it is a sequence of decisions that another group can reproduce, disprove or stop for a physically stated reason. Failure records are consequently part of the primary research product. 06 | Five Research Depth Axes — Curvature, Time, Scale, Rivals and Material Fate Depth in this family means following one material-electrical claim into the regimes most likely to falsify it. Five depth axes organize the investigation without turning all five flagships into the same generic protocol. The first axis perturbs curvature, contact force, shear and wetting separately to find the local response domain and saturation limits. The second reverses loading order and extends rest periods to distinguish reversible accommodation from memory, creep and accumulating fatigue. The third moves carefully between film microstructure, electrode interface, complete lead assembly and task-level electrical proxies, documenting when a model ceases to be scale-invariant. The fourth inserts competing explanations: additional pressure, cable movement, hydration drift, hidden cracking and biased selection of intact samples. The fifth follows the life cycle of materials, contamination, detachable fragments, rejected components, provenance and eventual disposal. These axes lead to distinct questions: when is a shape recovered but a contact lost; when is impedance stable but the lead artifact dominant; when does a signal appear clearer only because a damaged sample was excluded? The project becomes more meaningful by retaining these differences rather than forcing every result into a common success score. 07 | Measurable Endpoints and Minimum Prototype — What the Title Actually Measures The minimum verifiable prototype is an instrumented stretchable electrode and inert compliant board, not an implanted neural interface or a clinical rehabilitation system. Its test is whether the same specimen can be observed through shape change, electrical transfer and mechanical-burden measurements with independent calibration. F121 records curvature [1/m], recovery error, residual strain [1] and contact stability after unseen bending sequences. F122 measures contact pressure [Pa], shear [Pa] and proxy-signal transfer under matched load. F123 measures frequency-resolved impedance magnitude [ohm], phase [rad] and drift with a separate lead-motion witness. F124 records fatigue cycles [count], crack occurrence, delamination fraction [1] and residue under blinded inspection. F125 publishes a constrained frontier of proxy electrical quality against independently measured surrogate-surface burden, along with refused cases. For every endpoint, a definition, sensor chain, calibration state, batch, complete denominator and uncertainty estimate are necessary before any comparison. The purpose of the minimum prototype is modest but exact: to distinguish the mechanism under a testable boundary and leave a useful negative result when it fails. Better surrogate signal fidelity is not evidence that living tissue would tolerate the interface or that neural rehabilitation would improve. 08 | Strong Baselines, Rival Explanations and Stopping Conditions — Permission to Be Defeated A credible title allows a simpler competitor to win. Pressure-matched passive gels, equal-material compliant electrodes, fixed-geometry references and a nonadaptive electrical contact form the strong baselines; deliberate underperformance of the comparator would invalidate the study. The leading rivals are increased normal force masquerading as signal gain, cable motion masquerading as impedance change, wetting or temperature changes masquerading as electrode adaptation, and visible shape recovery masking accumulated microcracks. Prespecify parameter ranges, blind the test order, keep equivalent power and measurement budgets, and count disconnected, damaged and rejected runs. Critical safety conditions include excessive local pressure or shear, unexplained fragments, calibration failure, uninterpretable electrical reference, untracked material identity and loss of authorization. A favorable mean signal never cancels one such refusal. Criteria requiring biological measurements remain undefined until a properly reviewed study can establish them. The stopping rule is not a literary ending. It is a reproducible event linked to a physical measurement or lost authority. A study that stops for the right reason leaves more trustworthy evidence than a study that continues until a convincing picture appears. 09 | Research Gates and Future Prototypes — Nine Title Claims Open Two Hundred Doors Research Gates in this family are future-facing scientific questions, not decorative checklists. Their function is to invite the next investigator to identify what is still unknown about adaptive soft contact and what observation would change the present theory. One door may begin with the surprising fact that a softer surface transmitted a cleaner proxy signal; another may ask whether the apparent gain was achieved by concealed pressure. A third can imagine an electrode whose impedance stays stable while microscopic damage quietly grows. Other doors ask what happens when the very sensor used to certify contact becomes the source of an artifact, or when a second laboratory receives the raw failures but none of the original team's explanations. Each door should retain a specific origin, an extreme counterfactual and a practicable future research plan with a falsifier or an explicit reason to stop. Across the book, 200 gates create different challenges rather than 200 paraphrases of success. The 33 Phoenix prototypes are unbuilt successor concepts: independent contact witnesses, blind adversarial samples, hard-stop interfaces, material-and-data provenance ledgers and cross-laboratory reconstruction packages. The strongest inheritance is not a perfect result; it is a complete trail showing a future researcher where the title remained true, where it failed, and what should be asked next. 10 | Unregistered thresholds are not safety claims All absolute pressure, shear, residue and signal thresholds remain subject to later experimental preregistration and independent review. Take signal-quality–safety pareto frontier as a specific case. The candidate says proxy electrical performance and independently measured surrogate surface burden must be treated as a constrained multiobjective outcome, not summed into a single flattering score. The rival explanation says higher pressure or a rare irreversible surrogate injury yields a better average signal while masking an unacceptable local burden. A research team should match signal quality at varying pressure and concealed rare-failure scenarios; allow an independent safety sensor to veto a high-quality signal and report proxy SNR [dB], pressure [Pa], shear [Pa], residue mass [mg], veto latency [ms]. Only a blinded difference that survives a strong comparison could justify a narrower technical claim. The most important practical inheritance is external noncompensatory safety veto with pressure, shear and residue audit. Compare with bounded-pressure passive electrode, Pareto analysis without scalar reward compensation and equal-area ordinary conformal contact. Preserve material batches, force transients, calibration, exclusions and all test attempts; refuse if one rare irreversible surrogate damage signal or a missing safety datum being outweighed by favorable mean signal quality. Any proposal involving people or implanted electrodes would require an entirely new ethics, biocompatibility and medical-device review.

evidence_items.summary: Deletion mandates increasingly require deployed models to forget training data, but retraining from scratch is impractical under continual data churn. We study class-level deletion in document classifiers, where an entire label must be retired — because the category itself is sensitive, or because the cohort behind it requests erasure. This creates a problem point-level unlearning does not face: documents from the deleted class still arrive at inference time and must be routed somewhere. The prevailing baseline, random relabeling, scatters them uniformly over the surviving labels, destroying the ranking the model already learned and leaving the deleted records in the corpus. We propose Hessian Reassignment, pairing a single class-level Hessian downweight update with a deterministic next-top-1 decision rule and release-time logit ablation. Against a shadow-model membership inference adversary on three text benchmarks it drives deleted-class attack AUC to ? 0.51, stays within 0.6 points of full retraining on retained accuracy, and runs 11× faster.
evidence_items.title: POSTER: Delete and Retain: Efficient Unlearning for Document Classification

evidence_items.summary: GeoSim: A Benchmark Dataset for Two-Dimensional Mantle-Plume Dynamics GeoSim is a reproducible benchmark dataset of two-dimensional thermo-mechanical mantle-plume simulations generated with the I2VIS solver. It contains 237 trajectories in two parameter-sampling groups (plume1: one varying parameter; plume2: two varying parameters), with six coupled physical fields, physical timestamps, and trajectory-level training, validation, and test splits. Each group is provided at two representations: 401x309 physical: physical field values on the non-uniform I2VIS grid. 128x128 norm: per-field max-normalized fields conservatively remapped to a 128 × 128 grid. The dataset comprises eight logical HDF5 products. The two large native-resolution training products are deposited as ordered binary parts, while the remaining six are provided as single HDF5 files. Reassembly instructions, checksums, and split manifests are included in this record. See the deposited README.md for the complete file list, HDF5 schema, field units, normalization constants, and usage examples. A copy of the dataset is also hosted on Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/datasets/irenier/GeoSim Companion code The preprocessing, training, evaluation, and plotting code, together with trained checkpoints and evaluation artifacts, is archived separately: Code and reproducibility materials: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24110606 The original GeoSim software is released under the MIT license. I2VIS-related patches and configurations are distributed with permission from the I2VIS author and are not covered by the MIT license. The upstream I2VIS solver is not redistributed. Associated publications This dataset accompanies the manuscript: Liu, H., et al. (2026). GeoSim: A Reproducible Benchmark Dataset and Multi-Field Graph Neural Operator for Mantle-Plume Dynamics. Manuscript in preparation for submission to Geoscientific Model Development (GMD).
evidence_items.title: GeoSim: A Benchmark Dataset for Two-Dimensional Mantle-Plume Dynamics

evidence_items.summary: Counterfactual explanations improve the interpretability of graph neural networks (GNNs) by identifying small structural or feature perturbations that alter model predictions. They are especially useful in applications sensitive to relational changes, including molecular property prediction, fraud detection, and recommendation systems. However, existing methods often rely on local importance scores or heuristic search, limiting their ability to capture global graph structure and generate prediction-relevant graph edits. We propose LLM-CFExplainer, a general framework that uses large language models (LLMs) to assist counterfactual generation for GNNs. The framework extracts neighborhood-level influence information from a trained GNN and converts it, together with the original graph information, into structured prompts. The LLM then performs relational reasoning and proposes counterfactual edits subject to prediction-flipping, domain consistency, and basic topological constraints. A lightweight verification module evaluates the validity of the proposed edits and ensures consistency with the original graph. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets show that LLM-CFExplainer improves counterfactual validity, coverage of perturbable regions, and coherence of generated explanations. These results demonstrate the potential of LLMs as reasoning tools for enhancing the interpretability of graph learning models. Our code is available at https://github.com/tanhaochen001-ux/LLM-CFExplainer .
evidence_items.title: LLM-CFExplainer: A Large Language Model-Guided Framework for Graph Counterfactual Explanations

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in high-stakes domains such as healthcare, law, education, and scientific research, where factual accuracy is paramount. However, LLMs frequently generate plausible-sounding but factually incorrect statements, a phenomenon widely known as hallucination. Existing detection approaches are constrained by significant practical limitations: white-box methods require access to model internals that are inaccessible from commercial APIs; self-consistency sampling incurs prohibitive inference overhead ($k\times$ additional LLM calls); and perplexity-based signals fail to distinguish factual errors from genuinely novel correct statements. In this paper, we propose RAG-CS (Retrieval-Augmented Consistency Scoring), a post-hoc, model-agnostic hallucination detection framework requiring no access to LLM logits, weights, or sampling distributions. Given any LLM-generated response, RAG-CS first sentence-segments the output, then retrieves the top-$k$ evidence passages per sentence from a knowledge corpus using a dense bi-encoder retriever indexed with FAISS. A cross-encoder natural language inference (NLI) model computes pairwise semantic consistency scores between each response sentence and its retrieved evidence. Finally, a lightweight logistic regression classifier aggregates these scores, including statistical features over the score distribution, into a binary hallucination label and per-sentence fine-grained indicators. We conduct comprehensive evaluations on four hallucination benchmarks (TruthfulQA, HaluEval, FEVER, and FaithDial) and demonstrate that RAG-CS achieves F1 scores of 87.3\%, 84.6\%, 89.1\%, and 83.7\%, respectively, outperforming strong baselines including SelfCheckGPT-NLI, SAPLMA, and FActScore by 4.1--9.8 percentage points.
evidence_items.title: Retrieval augmented consistency scoring for model agnostic hallucination detection in large language models

evidence_items.summary: Manual aerobics scoring is sensitive to evaluator experience, while a single sensing modality cannot fully represent posture, dynamics, and musical timing. This study develops an intelligent evaluation model that encodes video, skeleton, inertial, and music-rhythm data in parallel and integrates them through cross-modal attention, reliability-aware fusion, temporal attention, and multi-task scoring. The dataset contains 8,466 valid sequences from 60 adult athletes. On a participant-independent test set, the model achieved an MAE of 3.18 points, R2 of 0.946, and macro-F1 of 0.925 for four-class primary deviation recognition. Performance declined under cross-site and cross-device testing, with MAE increasing to 4.28 and 4.47 points, respectively. A four-week pilot involving 18 athletes and four teachers indicated shorter video-review time, but it was not designed to establish long-term technical improvement or deployment readiness. The model therefore provides an auxiliary source of quantitative evidence for training diagnosis rather than a substitute for expert judgment.
evidence_items.title: Optimization of an intelligent evaluation model for aerobics performance using artificial intelligence and multimodal deep representation

organizations: Zhejiang University of Science and Technology
evidence_items.summary: Abstract AI-assisted development weakens the meaning of a green continuous-integration (CI) check: generated tests may execute realistic code and pass while replacing semantic oracles with tautologies or coarse smoke checks. We introduce CI-DeceptiveTest, a Python execution-paired benchmark and Gatekeeper protocol for detecting such low-assurance tests. Its 600 pairs originate from real tests in 12 open-source repositories; each source-control test is paired with a candidate produced by controlled oracle weakening, yielding 1200 label-free static-binary views. Construction combines deterministic validation, execution evidence, a 20% manually annotated slice, random inspection of 30% of AI-assisted records. The evidence is GPT-5.5-first: GPT-5.5 supports construction, review, and full-dataset validation. Labels are transformation-defined, not model-assigned. On the full benchmark, transparent static rules achieve 0.928 low-assurance recall but a 0.458 false-block rate on accepted source-control tests. mimo-v2.5-pro is retained as an auxiliary external cross-check; it reaches 0.885 macro F1 and reduces false blocking to 0.048. Bounded mutation analysis over 42 pre-specified source/candidate pairs further supports the paired construction. The central stress result is that weak-oracle detection remains hard: plausible coarse assertions retain execution while losing semantic constraint. The benchmark enables CI gatekeeper evaluation in a controlled, reproducible setting.
evidence_items.title: CI-DeceptiveTest: An Execution-Paired Benchmark for Test Assurance in AI-Assisted Development

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Conversational agents that retrieve documents and call tools are being deployed to operate buildings, campuses and other intelligent environments, yet engineering teams rarely have labelled data with which to test them before real users arrive. Synthetic test generation is widely offered as a remedy, but there is little evidence on whether synthetic suites detect faults, which generation strategies matter, and whether automatically produced ground truth can be trusted. We present an inverse retrieval-augmented generation pipeline that turns knowledge-base context into persona-conditioned questions with verifiable answers, expands them along multi-hop, linguistic, edge-case, adversarial and privacy dimensions, and filters them with a claim-level critic. In a controlled study with a deterministic tool-using agent and a grammar-based teacher, synthetic suites of 100 tests detected 93% of fifteen design faults, against 29% for a rule-based suite and at most 40% for re-implemented Ragas- and PyRIT-style generators. On faults independent of the generator design the advantage was smaller: 92% versus 75-77% of 312 automatically generated code mutants, and 70% versus 54-62% of twelve faults from external taxonomies. Fault-level hypothesis tests confirmed the advantage on design faults and code mutants (Holm-adjusted ≤ 0.022), but not on the underpowered held-out set, and the code-mutant advantage lost significance when mutants were aggregated by function. A claim-level critic removed injected label errors in the structured corpus, but on paraphrased, outdated and cross-referenced documents it had to route 41% of items to human review to stay error-free.
evidence_items.title: Inverse-RAG Synthetic Test Generation for Agentic AI Assistants in Intelligent Environments: A Mutation-Based Evaluation of Fault-Detection Effectiveness

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large language models have extended software-development assistance from token-level completion to systems that can navigate repositories, edit files, execute tools, and iterate on test feedback. This survey studies the design, use, and evaluation of these AI coding agents, together with their commercial and societal context. Reproducible database queries support literature discovery, but the cited corpus is selected and coded for relevance; we therefore describe the work as a structured scoping survey rather than an exhaustive systematic review. We organize the field using five dimensions: interaction paradigm, computational architecture, deployment form, orchestration mode, and human-oversight mode. Treating oversight separately from architecture resolves a conceptual overlap in earlier classifications and gives each representative system one value per dimension. The technical synthesis covers repository context, planning, tool use, multi-agent coordination, SDLC applications, and benchmark limitations. We keep technical capability evidence separate from business and adoption reports. Vendor and news sources are used as dated context, not as proxies for maturity or user preference. The survey covers material available through 28 February 2026.
evidence_items.title: From Code Completion to Agentic Development: A Survey of AI Coding Agents, Ecosystems, and Evolving Software Engineering Practice

evidence_items.summary:
OBJECTIVE
Preclinical studies demonstrated that ultrahigh dose rate (UHDR) irradiation can spare normal tissue compared to conventional dose rate (CDR) irradiation while maintaining tumor control. However, the conditions and magnitude of that FLASH sparing remain uncertain, limiting clinical translation. Most proposed metrics and models for predicting FLASH sparing lack rigorous experimental validation. This study systematically benchmarks them against extensive in vivo data.


APPROACH
Normal tissue toxicity electron and proton data comparing CDR and UHDR irradiations were compiled from murine skin, gut, and zebrafish studies. The dataset encompassed single-fraction, fractionated, dose-rate scan, and split-dose experiments.Isoeffective dose ratios were derived, referred to as FLASH-modifying factors (FMF).Metrics exhibiting the strongest correlations with experimental data were identified and used to model FMF via empirical transition functions. Model performance was compared for two metric-based models established in this work and proposed models from literature, including the FLASH effectiveness and equilibrium state dynamics (ESD) models.


MAIN RESULTS
FMF correlated stronger with fractional dose (Spearman's ρ ≈ -0.64) than with total dose (ρ ≈ -0.11), following a piecewise-linear dependence in terms of FMF-weighted dose versus dose. Among the investigated temporal dose delivery metrics, mean and pencil beam scanning (PBS) dose rates showed the strongest correlations (ρ ≈ -0.75 to -0.80) and the associated FMF values were well captured by exponential relationships. Metrics such as dose-averaged dose rate and UHDR-contribution did not account for loss of FLASH sparing due to delivery pauses. The ESD model provided a more accurate description of FMF than metric-based models or the FLASH-effectiveness model.


SIGNIFICANCE
Among the assessed metrics, fractional dose combined with mean or PBS dose rate best captured FLASH-induced normal-tissue sparing, while ESD models provided the highest descriptive accuracy across all evaluated datasets. Validating FLASH metrics and models is essential to standardize FLASH treatment planning, inform delivery system design, and enable optimized clinical translation.
evidence_items.title: Data-driven evaluation of quantitative metrics and models for normal-tissue sparing in FLASH radiotherapy.

evidence_items.summary:
Predicting project completion time is a crucial aspect of construction management for mitigating delays and supporting effective project control. However, existing forecasting methods still rely on extensive historical data and lack optimality in capturing the cyclical and non-linear patterns of project progress. Therefore, an accurate and adaptive prediction model is required to support decision-making under conditions of limited data. Accurate prediction of construction completion remains challenging due to the cyclicality and nonlinearity of progress data, especially when historical datasets are frequently scarce or unavailable. This study develops and validates Optimum Fourier Series–Polynomial Regression (Optimum.FSPR), a hybrid prediction model designed to provide reliable completion forecasts under conditions of data scarcity or high volatility.
 
 
 
 The Optimum.FSPR technique integrates Fourier Series (FS) to model cyclic patterns with Polynomial Regression (PR) to capture nonlinear long-term trends. Model performance is evaluated using weekly project progress data, with Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA), eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) serving as benchmark models and Mean Absolute Error, Mean Absolute Percentage Error and Root Mean Squared Error as evaluation metrics. Additionally, 2,000 Monte Carlo simulations were utilized to generate a probabilistic distribution of the S-curve regarding project completion time.
 
 
 
 Traditional forecasting models proved ineffective for this application due to instability and heavy data requirements. Conversely, Optimum.FSPR demonstrated superior accuracy, consistency and stability. Optimum.FSPR produced lower errors compared to ARIMA, XGBoost and LSTM. An integrated simulation approach identifies a 94.5% probability of project completion by the 49th week. These results confirm the model’s reliability for application in practical construction project scenarios characterized by data limitations.
 
 
 
 This research offers a robust, data-driven tool for project managers and stakeholders to monitor progress in real-time. By facilitating accurate forecasting with minimal data, the model enables proactive decision-making to mitigate delays and optimize resource allocation throughout the project lifecycle.
 
 
 
 The study introduces a novel application of Fourier analysis in construction management. By merging spectral analysis with regression, the research advances predictive methodologies for handling complex datasets, effectively capturing both cyclic variations and nonlinear trends, thereby addressing a significant gap in the literature regarding methodologies for predicting the progress and completion of construction projects.
evidence_items.title: The application of Fourier series in forecasting construction project completion: a case study
