It contains 100 sample or time-point analysis units, an S0-S6 stage ontology with S7-S9 reserved, a 2,552-gene shared cost space, optimal-transport stage coordinates with 20 retrospectively exported reference-centroid bootstrap draws, five-axis/46-gene Maturity Fidelity Index scores with 16 sensitivity versions, a 25-module concordance atlas, gene- and module-level variance components, constructed reliability descriptors, provenance records, analysis-code snapshots, and two application workflows. Applications and evidence boundaries. The internal GSE158617 example uses 38 samples in a retrospective, in-sample interface demonstration and is not independent validation. The external GSE203264 application uses 35 wild-type samples and a rebuilt P1-compatible 2,550-gene reference. Its non-monotonic D35 result concerns unsorted, compositionally heterogeneous SC-islets and is not validation of the unmodified 2,552-gene model or a pure beta-cell accuracy result. Reliability values are constructed descriptors, not absolute dataset-quality scores or significance ranks. MFI values are within-matrix relative profiles, not absolute cross-protocol maturity measures. No in vivo developmental tiers, validated benchmark accuracy, clinical validity, or universal generalization are claimed. Reproduction scope. The package supplies package-local verification for the two application workflows and the external diagnostics. The analysis-code and provenance snapshots support inspection and traceability but are not represented as a relocatable clean-room rebuild of every manuscript display item. The reference-centroid draws are a retrospective deterministic reconstruction from frozen training inputs, not an original frozen cache. Source data and governance.

evidence_items.summary: Summary Internal multiple elimination (IME) is a challenging task in seismic exploration. If internal multiples (IMs) are not eliminated, they may be misinterpreted as primaries, leading to imaging artifacts. Among the few available methods, Marchenko multiple elimination (MME) is the most appealing, as it is data-driven and requires no model information. However, the computational cost is considerable due to the extensive calculations of multidimensional convolution and correlation, which include forward and inverse fast Fourier transforms among shot gathers. Moreover, its application to field data remains limited, indicating that more attention should be paid to practical issues. Starting from the PyMarchenko MME, a GPU-accelerated IME technique, GPU-MME, to alleviate the computational burden of MME is developed. GPU-MME faithfully replicates the PyMarchenko MME results and delivers a significant acceleration—up to nearly two orders of magnitude faster—due to the GPU’s efficiency in handling the key computations involved in MME. GPU-MME is applied to a series of synthetic datasets and an open field dataset to demonstrate its effectiveness and practical value. The comparison results are either provided or reproduced from existing work. GPU-MME is competitive with a state-of-the-art MME method. The impact of key parameters in GPU-MME and how to determine their optimal values are investigated. When accurate surface-free and wavelet-free reflection response is unavailable, an estimation of multiple and source (EMS) technique can successfully eliminate surface-related multiples (SRMs) and provide the surface-free, wavelet-free input for GPU-MME. However, additional scaling of reflection response and adaptive adjustment of the initially estimated IMs may be necessary to ensure effective IME. The scaling and adjustment procedures are discussed in detail, as they are critical when an exact reflection response is not available.
evidence_items.title: Marchenko-type GPU-accelerated internal multiple elimination (GPU-MME): Practical aspects, benchmark synthetic and field data applications

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have become ubiquitous, and with their adoption comes a range of ethical and security risks that has made alignment, and resistance to jailbreaking, a central concern. Guardrails are a widely adopted defense against such jailbreaks, yet their reported effectiveness is only as reliable as the data on which they are evaluated. This paper identifies a largely unexamined source of inflated performance: data leakage between the datasets used to seed offensive jailbreak frameworks and those used to train defensive guardrails. As both are derived from human-authored jailbreak prompt corpora, a guardrail may be evaluated on instances present in its own training data, in which case high detection rates reflect memorization rather than a generalized alignment policy. We quantify this contamination, which we term PromptLeaks, using a deterministic syntactic comparison of prompt datasets adapted from bioinformatics. Across three open-source red-teaming frameworks and five open-source guardrail datasets we observe severe leakage, with one test-prompt dataset almost entirely contained within the guardrail training corpora. Guardrail jailbreak detection rate diminishes on prompts that do not overlap the training corpus, indicating that current guardrails rely substantially on memorization rather than on generalizing an alignment policy.
evidence_items.title: PromptLeaks: Assessing Data Leakage in Guardrails and Automated Jailbreak Tools

evidence_items.summary: Recent speech synthesis systems have moved beyond conventional voice cloning toward the generation of expressive, text-described virtual identities. This shift creates a generalization challenge for spoofing countermeasures trained primarily on cloned speech from a limited pool of reference speakers and relatively neutral read-speech content. We introduce Virtual Identities with Varied Emotional Dynamics (VIVED), a large-scale dataset designed to improve robustness against text-driven virtual voices. VIVED is built around three principles. First, it generates over 100,000 synthetic virtual identities from stochastic natural-language descriptions sampled from a seven-dimensional acoustic and paralinguistic attribute bank, reducing reliance on real speaker reference audio for spoof generation. Second, it combines linguistically and affectively diverse transcripts from LibriSpeech, TIMIT, and the EmoBox English subset to expose synthesis models to phonetic complexity and emotional prosody. Third, it applies a symmetric domain-matching and acoustic laundering pipeline to both bona fide and synthetic utterances, including multi-codec alignment, room impulse response simulation, noise injection, and codec compression, thereby reducing shortcut learning from channel or processing artifacts. Empirical analysis indicates that VIVED covers a speaker representation space with nearly 1.8 times the Vendi Score of the ASVspoof 5 baseline, substantially reducing the risk of identity memorization. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that training on VIVED systematically enhances robustness to text-driven virtual voices while maintaining competitive cross-corpus performance on ASVspoof 5. Multiple baseline architectures achieve substantially lower EER and minDCF on the VIVED evaluation set compared with models trained only on ASVspoof 5.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Known Speakers: Enhancing Spoofing Detection Generalization with VIVED

evidence_items.summary: Machine-learning detectors for malicious smart contracts (e.g., Ponzi schemes, phishing, honeypots, DeFi attacks) often report detection scores of up to 98%. We ask how much of each score reflects the ability to recognize malicious contracts, and how much reflects the context of benchmark construction. We rebuild eight published benchmarks and reproduce the published scores where the releases permit. We then re-evaluate them under the conditions a deployed detector faces. We could run these evaluations on six of the eight benchmarks, and on five of them we observe significant score drops. The largest score drops are related to how the data is split over time and to how rare malicious contracts are on chain, while duplicated code and contradictory labels have a limited impact. We also recover the missing deployer addresses, to measure the impact of splitting contracts from the same deployer across training and test sets.
evidence_items.title: POSTER: Signal or Artifact? Auditing Machine-Learning Detectors for Malicious Smart Contracts

evidence_items.summary: The Segment Anything Model (SAM) is increasingly adapted for image forgery detection and localization (IFDL), yet its role as a shared public upstream model creates an overlooked attack surface. We reveal that perturbations crafted solely on SAM transfer across diverse downstream forensic models without access to their parameters or training data, degrading both forgery detection and forgery localization. To address this vulnerability, we propose ForensicsSAM, which casts robust IFDL as conditional correction of a unified upstream forensic representation. Rather than protecting individual prediction heads or modifying every image, it identifies adversarial images and corrects their attack-induced shifts at global-attention stages while preserving clean representations. Experiments on ten benchmarks and four attacks demonstrate superior cross-dataset generalization and cross-attack forgery localization robustness compared with existing SAM-based methods.
evidence_items.title: POSTER: ForensicsSAM: Conditional Feature Correction for Adversarially Robust Image Forgery Detection and Localization

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The objective was to identify the optimal MRI sequence to evaluate postoperative Achilles tendon (AT) healing. We compared T2 gradient sequence with 4.1ms (TE4) and 16ms (TE16) echo time with PD (proton density-weighted) through signal intensity (SI) measurements and correlated them with tendon-specific biomarkers. Additionally, the study assessed agreement between radiologists and AI in evaluating tendon-specific biomarkers. A total of 45 patients (mean age 36 ± 6 years; 36 men, 9 women) underwent nine consecutive MRI examinations at intervals from 1 to 52 weeks after surgery. SI in all postoperative MRI examinations was measured in AT in TE4, TE16 and PD. SI in the operated AT appears normal in PD and TE16 sequences around week 39. However, TE4 still shows high signals, indicating ongoing remodeling. Significant correlations were found between biomarkers and SI in the TE4 sequence ( p < 0.001 for structural changes and tendon edema, and p = 0.002 for tissue edema). High SI values were associated with poor biomarker outcomes. The mean absolute errors (MAE) between AI model scores, obtained using only axial TE4 scans, and radiologist evaluations ranged from 0.12 to 0.63. In conclusion, TE4 demonstrated greater sensitivity to persistent postoperative signal and structural abnormalities and may be useful in postoperative assessment of AT. AI scores showed relatively small absolute differences from the reference radiologist scores.
evidence_items.title: Postoperative evaluation of Achilles tendon using short echo time MRI and artificial intelligence

evidence_items.summary: Background: Artificial intelligence is used to detect and characterize abnormalities in diagnostic imaging and to support clinical interpretation. Technical performance does not always translate into patient benefit. Aim: To evaluate applications of artificial intelligence (AI) in diagnostic imaging, focusing on diagnostic performance, collaboration with clinicians, and limitations of clinical implementation. Methods: To identify recent articles on the use of artificial intelligence in diagnostic imaging, the PubMed database was searched. Only English-language publications were included. Results: AI algorithms have promising capabilities for detecting and characterizing abnormalities in mammography, radiography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, and ultrasonography. In selected settings, they improve sensitivity, support segmentation, and reduce interpretation workload. However, they do not consistently improve specificity, time to intervention, or patient outcomes. The clinical evidence varies in methodological quality and representativeness. Conclusions: AI should primarily be considered a decision-support technology rather than an autonomous replacement for clinical judgment. Wider adoption requires external validation, workflow-based evaluation, and ongoing safety monitoring.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence in diagnostic imaging

evidence_items.summary: Security teams increasingly rely on machine learning to detect malware and on language models and other automation to process threat intelligence. Both use cases pose the question, though: when should we trust what the system says? This paper proposes a set of trusting, explainable and trustworthy artificial intelligence in cybersecurity, including transparent detection of malware and evidence-based automated threat intelligence, that combine seven trust properties (fidelity, stability, robustness, calibration, plausibility, accountability, and security of explanations itself), compares eight families of explanation methods, shows an alert-level workflow where every explanation is verified before it impacts a decision, and describes an intelligence pipeline where every claim is tied to a source and to a technique in a standard taxonomy. It lists levels of automation for six intelligence tasks and an evaluation protocol for detection, explanations, calibration, analyst utility, extraction quality, and governance. The article describes the evidence that explanations may disagree and are unstable or manipulated, and that language model extraction of threat techniques may be highly error prone to error modes. It views explanations as an attack surface and a source of over-reliance, not just a benefit. It presents an analysis work in design and does not provide any new experimental results. Four tables and three figures show the framework concrete, and can be adopted by security operations.
evidence_items.title: Explainable and Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence for Cybersecurity: A Framework for Transparent Malware Detection and Automated Threat Intelligence

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM)-based agents are promising in Internet of Things (IoT) applications. However, existing agent systems suffer from an ephemeral limitation: agents are instantiated for individual tasks and terminated upon completion, losing valuable execution experiences across different tasks where past knowledge reuse is impossible. Inspired by dual-process theory in cognitive science, we propose a brain cognition-inspired dual-system agent framework for continuous knowledge reuse across heterogeneous task streams, termed the cognition-inspired dual-system agent framework for continuous knowledge reuse (CIA-CKR). The CIA-CKR framework separates fast (reactive execution) from slow (deliberative planning) cognition phases by maintaining a persistent knowledge base throughout the operational lifetime of agents. Two synergistic mechanisms are designed that mirror bidirectional knowledge flow in human cognition: a personalized agent generation mechanism that retrieves task-relevant knowledge and configures context-specific agent capabilities through top-down adaptation, and a knowledge accumulation mechanism that extracts experiential insights from execution traces through bottom-up feedback. Extensive experiments on HomeBench (smart home control) and OmniEAR (embodied multiagent collaboration) datasets demonstrate that CIA-CKR consistently outperforms both vanilla LLMs and recent memory-augmented methods, achieving 10.82% and 4.23% average accuracy improvements on HomeBench and OmniEAR, respectively, over the best baselines.
evidence_items.title: Brain Cognition-Inspired Adaptable LLM Agents for Continuous Knowledge Reuse Across Tasks in IoT

evidence_items.summary: The large-scale integration of distributed energy resources (DERs) imposes higher demands on the dispatch strategies of virtual power plants (VPPs). Existing dispatch strategies typically assume fully rational users, which leads to deviations of actual responses from theoretically optimal schedules. To address the above limitation, this article proposes a bounded-rationality Stackelberg game framework for VPP dispatch, where an adaptive dual-system narrative learning (ADSNL) model is developed to characterize users’ bounded rationality. Concretely, we first formulate the demand-side response as a bounded-rational response mapping induced by the ADSNL model, where users’ intuitive and rational decisions are dynamically balanced under narrative influence and habit inertia. To coordinate supply-side heterogeneous DERs, we then establish a cooperative coalition with fair profit allocation via the Shapley value. Moreover, we develop a hybrid differential evolution–mathematical programming (DEMP) algorithm to efficiently solve the Stackelberg equilibrium. Final simulation demonstrates that the proposed method yields a realistic, inertia-constrained load curve that avoids the overreaction of rational benchmarks. It preserves total system welfare, improves the operator’s profit, and ensures core-stable profit allocation among coalition members.
evidence_items.title: A Bounded-Rationality Stackelberg Game for Virtual Power Plant Dispatch With Adaptive Dual-System Narrative Learning

evidence_items.summary: The growing demand for high-dimensional artificial intelligence (AI) services on resource-constrained Internet of Things (IoT) terminals has driven the development of distributed edge intelligence. Among these enabling technologies, split inference has attracted significant attention due to its capability for lightweight deployment on edge computing devices. Meanwhile, over-the-air computation (AirComp), which exploits the principle of analog waveform superposition, has catalyzed the “over-the-air neural computing” paradigm to achieve end-to-end split inference across communication networks. However, high-mobility distributed inference can be limited by the spatial rank available at a single access point (AP) and by Doppler-induced phase mismatch. Limited spatial rank can truncate high-dimensional features, while Doppler shifts can impair coherent waveform aggregation. To address these challenges, we develop AgileAirNeuro, which combines heterogeneous multi-AP AirComp with sensed-velocity-based phase compensation. Under the stated nonzero-gain, generic-angle, and path-richness assumptions, we derive an ideal rank-additivity result that characterizes the algebraic spatial-DoF upper bound of heterogeneous multi-AP cooperation. Within the local residual-phase regime, we derive a first-order computation-mse model and its Cramér–Rao bound (CRB)-induced lower bound surrogate, relating velocity-estimation uncertainty to neural computation distortion. We formulate a stochastic computation-mse minimization problem and develop a spatio-temporal alternating relaxation (STAR) approach that combines greedy rank-aware topology selection with alternating optimization of the local surrogate. Simulations under the specified satellite–terrestrial integrated network (STIN) configurations show lower computation error than the evaluated baselines. Under preconfigured topology and transceivers, the simulated online air-interface feature-transmission latency is 92.65% lower than digital offloading. In the same simulations, AgileAirNeuro achieves higher inference accuracy than terrestrial baselines in the tested high-dimensional and line-of-sight (LoS)-dominant cases.
evidence_items.title: AgileAirNeuro: Mobility-Robust Over-the-Air Neural Inference for Edge Intelligence

evidence_items.summary: The development of artificial intelligence (AI)-based technology has driven the development of rule-based chatbots into AI-based chatbots. This development is used by various companies to use AI chatbots as the frontline of customer service. Meeting user expectations for AI chatbots requires an evaluation model to measure chatbot quality. Based on the literature, chatbot evaluation models still focus solely on technical quality, even as AI chatbots are evolving towards human-like services. This research will explore the integration of the technical dimensions of information system success with a new dimension, namely Human-Like Chatbot Interaction (HLCI) as a higher-order construct of anthropomorphism and conversational capability. This quantitative study uses an explanatory research approach. Data were collected through a cross-sectional survey of users of the Veronika chatbot, owned by Telkomsel, an Indonesian telecommunications company. A total of 213 respondents had data ready for analysis using the Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) method in SmartPLS 4, namely the measurement model and structural model tests. The analysis results show that service quality is not significantly related to user satisfaction but has a direct effect on trust. Meanwhile, information quality, system quality, and human-like chatbot interaction are positively related to trust and user satisfaction. Trust and user satisfaction are positively related to intention to continue using. The results of this study can contribute both theoretically and practically to modern AI chatbot quality evaluation models.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating human-like chatbot interaction in customer service: integrating anthropomorphism and conversational capability

evidence_items.summary: Internet of Things (IoT) systems often generate time series from multiple related entities, creating a practical need for unified cross-entity forecasting. Although these entities may operate within the same system, they can still exhibit long-term structural differences and short-term temporal variations under different operating regimes, which makes cross-entity forecasting particularly challenging. To address this issue, we propose an entity- and regime-conditioned model (ERM) for multientity time series forecasting (ME-TSF). Built on a shared forecasting backbone, ERM introduces two complementary conditioning mechanisms: Regime-MoE captures sample-level regime variations, and Entity-FiLM models long-term entity-specific structural shifts through entity-conditioned residual feature modulation. On ME-building time series (BTS), a reconstructed multientity HVAC benchmark derived from real building management system data, we conduct systematic experiments under source-entity joint training, unseen-entity zero-shot forecasting, and limited target-entity adaptation settings. The results show that ERM delivers stronger unseen-entity generalization and more stable performance across entities while remaining highly competitive after adaptation with limited target-entity data. These findings suggest that combining shared temporal modeling with regime- and entity-conditioned mechanisms is an effective direction for ME-TSF.
evidence_items.title: Multientity Time Series Forecasting in IoT Systems via Regime and Entity Conditioning

evidence_items.summary: Internet of things (IoT)-enabled public health systems need timely indicators from both device data and human-generated streams. Social media can supply upstream observations during emergencies, but noisy language complicates their validation against official surveillance. We construct daily emergency signals from Weibo posts and test whether they add leading information about official COVID-19 case counts. The analysis covers 39.6 million COVID-19-related posts in Weibo-COV 2.0 from January to April 2020. Distilled bidirectional encoder representations from transformers (DistilBERT), fine-tuned with keyword pseudo-labels, performs binary emergency screening and classifies symptom-, resource-, and policy-related subtypes. Postlevel metrics report agreement with keyword-derived pseudo-labels, not accuracy against independent human annotations; no such benchmark was available. Daily indicators are extrapolated from stratified samples of 500 posts. Their finite-sample uncertainty is reported, and alternative sample sizes represent theoretical precision bounds rather than empirical downstream stability. Validation uses stationarity tests, VAR lag selection, BH-corrected Granger predictability tests, HC1-robust OLS regressions, Johansen rank diagnostics, and a rank-one VECM sensitivity fit. A complete rerun with the stated settings reproduced all empirical outputs, while formula-derived quantities and theoretical bounds were recomputed. Binary and multiclass weighted <inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$F1$ </tex-math></inline-formula>-scores on pseudo-labeled held-out data are 0.927 and 0.880, respectively. At a one-day lag, emergency signals improve the statistical explanation of later cases (<inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$F=24.68$ </tex-math></inline-formula>, adjusted <inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$p\lt 0.001$ </tex-math></inline-formula>); symptom signals are strongest (<inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$F=26.87$ </tex-math></inline-formula>). The seven-day coefficient is 1.623 (<inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$p\lt 0.001$ </tex-math></inline-formula>), and subtype decomposition raises <inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$R^{2}$ </tex-math></inline-formula> from 0.636 to 0.665. Because the Johansen trace test rejects both rank restrictions, <inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$\alpha =-0.2965$ </tex-math></inline-formula> (29.6%/day) remains a descriptive VECM sensitivity estimate. A keyword baseline attains higher aggregate fit (<inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$R^{2}=0.691$ </tex-math></inline-formula>), so the evidence does not establish transformer dominance. DistilBERT instead contributes semantic subtype discovery with less manual rule design. The resulting IoT contribution is an interoperable analytics layer for aggregate alerts, not a new sensing device, protocol, or edge architecture.
evidence_items.title: Human-Centric Social Sensing for IoT-Enabled COVID-19 Situational Awareness: DistilBERT-Based Emergency Signal Discovery

evidence_items.summary: Over-the-air computation (AirComp) represents a paradigm shift toward ultrafast wireless data aggregation (WDA) with enhanced spectrum efficiency. In this article, we propose a novel relay-assisted covert AirComp system, in which a relay employs an amplify-and-forward (AF) strategy to forward the users’ local data to an access point (AP). A malicious warden, Willie, attempts to detect whether the users are transmitting. To guarantee covertness, the relay and the AP transmit artificial noise to impair Willie’s detection capability. We formulate an optimization problem to minimize the computational mean squared error (CMSE) at the AP while ensuring that the detection error probability (DEP) at Willie remains above a predefined threshold. Since the formulated optimization problem is nonconvex, an alternating optimization-based algorithm is developed to efficiently address the nonconvexity, in which the constrained concave-convex procedure (CCCP) method is adopted. Computer simulations demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms the benchmark algorithms.
evidence_items.title: Relay-Assisted Over-the-Air Computation: A Covert Communication Design

evidence_items.summary: Federated learning (FL) enables privacy-preserving distributed intelligence in unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)-assisted Internet of Things (IoT) edge networks. However, the efficient policy design remains challenging due to the hybrid decision space, which couples combinatorial device scheduling with continuous resource allocation, as well as the long-term impact of nonindependent and identically distributed (Non-IID) data on model convergence. In this article, we propose a spatiotemporal resource optimization framework for UAV-assisted edge computing services. We formulate a long-term utility maximization problem that jointly considers learning performance, energy consumption, and latency. To solve this mixed-integer nonlinear problem, a federated spatiotemporal policy optimization (FSTPO) approach is developed based on a constrained Markov game. The proposed method incorporates a dual-channel spatiotemporal representation to capture wireless dynamics and data distribution characteristics. In addition, a hybrid action learning mechanism is introduced to efficiently handle the coupling between discrete scheduling and continuous resource allocation. The simulation results demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms benchmark schemes in terms of system utility, learning accuracy, and resource efficiency, while achieving stable convergence under Non-IID environments.
evidence_items.title: Federated Spatiotemporal Policy Learning for Efficient Resource Management in UAV-Assisted IoT Edge Networks

UPPER-LIMB MOTOR RESTORATION AFTER STROKE AT THE LIMIT F091-F095 | A FIVE-FLAGSHIP SCIENTIFIC TECHNICAL NOTEBOOK | 33 x STARLI STATUS: prospective nonclinical research design, synthetic numerical examples, not an experiment with patients and not an established clinical effect. A LETTER FROM THE RESEARCH GENERATION A hand arriving at its goal is an astonishingly incomplete explanation. The shoulder might rotate, the trunk might lean, the fingers might squeeze too hard, or the robot might do the last crucial part of the movement. A science of upper-limb restoration must tell those worlds apart. This notebook examines the untrained reach, safe grasp, independent digit force, multijoint coordination and novel-object device-off transfer as distinct proposed mechanisms. Its mission is not to declare improvement from synthetic diagrams, but to design measurements that might overturn the claim. The integrated F091-F095 family proposes five distinct causal tests. F091 asks whether trajectory quality remains improved after trunk compensation is measured. F092 challenges a seemingly good grasp by concealing object stiffness and logging release failures. F093 separates independent finger control from total force. F094 dissects shoulder-elbow-wrist synergy and passive joint coupling. F095 tests untrained object manipulation with the device fully switched off. These tests are proposed for an inert mechanical arm and offline synthetic datasets, not a clinical evaluation. Our five-stage parallel spacetime reasoning is an intellectual strategy: lock the origin of the question, formalize candidate relations, allow a rival causal world, discover limits through safe bounded stress, and transfer the contradiction to a future laboratory. The name describes distinct branches of scientific interpretation, not physical travel between timelines. The longer this book survives, the more likely its apparatus will seem primitive. A valuable manuscript should let tomorrow's investigator explain exactly why it became obsolete. FOURTEEN RESEARCH PRELUDES 01 | A reached object is not proof of arm restoration One can move a hand to a target using different mixtures of elbow rotation, shoulder elevation, trunk translation and external actuation. This book therefore treats movement quality and genuine device-off object use as separate inferential claims. The science proposed here is prospective and nonclinical; its synthetic curves represent hypotheses rather than human improvement. A representative unresolved case is shoulder abduction as a compensatory shortcut. Its candidate is to distinguish joint-coordinate recovery from a merely faster endpoint path under explicitly held-out reach directions while isolating shoulder abduction as a compensatory shortcut. Investigators should replay the same hand path with a different elbow strategy, with independent measurement of angular path error [deg], movement smoothness [1], trunk excursion [mm]. An ordinary comparison using time-normalized minimum-jerk trajectory; transparent joint-space PD control; trunk-restrained kinematic reference is entitled to overturn the preferred model. The question is not resolved by a synthetic plot or by naming a more complicated controller. 02 | Five flagships with five independent failure paths F091 challenges trajectory quality without trunk substitution. F092 distinguishes intended grasp from robot-generated squeeze. F093 separates finger individuation from total strength. F094 identifies multijoint shoulder-elbow-wrist coordination rather than passive synergy. F095 asks whether gains generalize to unfamiliar objects without any powered assistance. A representative unresolved case is arc-length normalization and misleading smoothness. Its candidate is to distinguish joint-coordinate recovery from a merely faster endpoint path under explicitly held-out reach directions while isolating arc-length normalization and misleading smoothness. Investigators should physically lock the trunk in an inert arm phantom, with independent measurement of angular path error [deg], movement smoothness [1], trunk excursion [mm]. An ordinary comparison using time-normalized minimum-jerk trajectory; transparent joint-space PD control; trunk-restrained kinematic reference is entitled to overturn the preferred model. The question is not resolved by a synthetic plot or by naming a more complicated controller. 03 | The mechanical arm phantom and its limits The minimal reproducible test platform is an unloaded upper-limb kinematic surrogate with calibrated joint encoders, individual fingertip force references and an anonymized task dataset. It contains no patients, no therapeutic interventions and no clinical outcome claims. A future study involving people needs its own ethical, safety and regulatory authorization. A representative unresolved case is grip intention before measurable contact. Its candidate is to connect grasp command, object stiffness and time-resolved contact force without treating robot-supplied squeeze as independent hand control while isolating grip intention before measurable contact. Investigators should use two independent fingertip force references, with independent measurement of force overshoot [N], peak grip [N], target damage rate [1]. An ordinary comparison using classical proportional force control with explicit saturation; impedance-based grip; independently calibrated slip detector is entitled to overturn the preferred model. The question is not resolved by a synthetic plot or by naming a more complicated controller. 04 | When better trajectories conceal worse movement A lower endpoint deviation may coexist with greater trunk excursion, altered arm-segment length or aggressive smoothing. Motion quality requires independent anatomical reference frames and both temporal and spatial measurements. The F091 hypothesis is falsified when the same apparent reach can be reconstructed from compensation rather than improved arm dynamics. A representative unresolved case is the friction cone and object slip. Its candidate is to connect grasp command, object stiffness and time-resolved contact force without treating robot-supplied squeeze as independent hand control while isolating the friction cone and object slip. Investigators should interrupt feedback while keeping mechanical force limits active, with independent measurement of force overshoot [N], peak grip [N], target damage rate [1]. An ordinary comparison using classical proportional force control with explicit saturation; impedance-based grip; independently calibrated slip detector is entitled to overturn the preferred model. The question is not resolved by a synthetic plot or by naming a more complicated controller. 05 | Grasp precision belongs to the object as well as the hand For F092 the object is not a passive background prop. Stiffness, surface friction, deformability and safe contact thresholds determine whether a commanded pinch is useful. The study must distinguish strength from timing, a successful pickup from an unsafe overgrip, and a maintained hold from a failed release. A representative unresolved case is tactile reference drift after repeated contacts. Its candidate is to connect grasp command, object stiffness and time-resolved contact force without treating robot-supplied squeeze as independent hand control while isolating tactile reference drift after repeated contacts. Investigators should mask the object fragility label until after scoring, with independent measurement of force overshoot [N], peak grip [N], target damage rate [1]. An ordinary comparison using classical proportional force control with explicit saturation; impedance-based grip; independently calibrated slip detector is entitled to overturn the preferred model. The question is not resolved by a synthetic plot or by naming a more complicated controller. 06 | Why finger strength is not fine motor coordination F093 requires digit-specific measurement. Independent force generation, off-target coactivation, temporal sequence control and precision placement can vary even when aggregate hand strength rises. A strong grip may be an inadequate explanation for a targeted finger movement; forcing all digit measures into one score can erase the mechanism under study. A representative unresolved case is thumb opposition without whole-hand closing. Its candidate is to measure finger individuation independently of aggregate strength, exploiting asynchronous digit-force patterns and hidden sequencing while isolating thumb opposition without whole-hand closing. Investigators should independently calibrate each fingertip force channel, with independent measurement of finger cross-talk index [1], interdigit phase lag [ms], precision placement error [mm]. An ordinary comparison using a strength-matched linear finger-coupling model; fixed digit-threshold decoder; transparent covariance-normalized classifier is entitled to overturn the preferred model. The question is not resolved by a synthetic plot or by naming a more complicated controller. 07 | A shoulder, an elbow, a wrist and a moving trunk F094 tests whether the trajectory of one segment can compensate for a deficit elsewhere. The independent observation should include joint angular histories, trunk shift and the effects of passive mechanical coupling. A single end-effector path cannot identify every joint source that produced it. A representative unresolved case is the strength-controlled individuation experiment. Its candidate is to measure finger individuation independently of aggregate strength, exploiting asynchronous digit-force patterns and hidden sequencing while isolating the strength-controlled individuation experiment. Investigators should present previously unseen finger activation sequences, with independent measurement of finger cross-talk index [1], interdigit phase lag [ms], precision placement error [mm]. An ordinary comparison using a strength-matched linear finger-coupling model; fixed digit-threshold decoder; transparent covariance-normalized classifier is entitled to overturn the preferred model. The question is not resolved by a synthetic plot or by naming a more complicated controller. 08 | The true test happens beyond the practiced object F095 distinguishes trained laboratory performance from unassisted tasks with unfamiliar objects. The next scientific test must conceal object identity, disable actuator output, blind assessors and report unsuccessful release, object damage, missing outcomes and compensation. This is a research requirement, not proof of recovery. A representative unresolved case is trunk compensation during arm transport. Its candidate is to separate multijoint kinematic synergy from scapular and trunk compensation under known impedance and task geometry while isolating trunk compensation during arm transport. Investigators should invert the joint target order without changing total task time, with independent measurement of shoulder-elbow-wrist coordination residual [deg], trunk shift [mm], torque margin [N m]. An ordinary comparison using standard Jacobian pseudoinverse control; conventional joint-space impedance control; trunk-restrained synergy analysis is entitled to overturn the preferred model. The question is not resolved by a synthetic plot or by naming a more complicated controller.

evidence_items.summary: Research consistently shows that cyber deception can slow down adversaries, degrade their performance, and reveal their intentions and long-term planning. Yet the gap between this research and the real world remains vast. A deception storyline encompasses decisions on which assets to deploy, where to place them, what each one communicates to an attacker, and how they collectively shape the attacker's understanding of the environment. However, whether deploying deception as a structured storyline produces better defensive outcomes than simply deploying deception ad hoc remains an open and largely unstudied question. Three unsolved problems keep this gap wide open: (i) there is little, if any, research comparing strategic to ad-hoc deception deployment, (ii) to this day, there is no publicly available automated system capable of designing and deploying complete, coordinated deception storylines, and (iii) no empirical study compares the defensive performance of automated storylines against those that human experts design. To address these gaps, the primary scientific contribution of this thesis proposal is to systematically study, understand, design, implement and evaluate the mechanics of effective AI-based cyber deception storylines. Specifically, we propose using LLM-based scaffolds to create cyber deception storylines. Our approach will use autonomous agents to determine the selection, placement, tactical purpose, personality of deception assets, and the overall narrative by analysing target network topologies and defence goals from the user. Every decision in creating a deception storyline will be explicitly grounded in well-known previous work on deception theory and best practices. We propose implementing this methodology within a framework that, in addition to automated storyline creation, actively orchestrates and manages the deployed decoys. A critical contribution to this thesis proposal is strong validation. To validate this approach, our evaluations follow a structured plan: (i) creation of a SoK for summarising and systematising existing knowledge on how to evaluate deception against human adversaries, (ii) assessing our framework against autonomous AI-based network attacking agents, (iii) assessing our framework against professional human adversaries, (iv) comparing our AI-based cyber deception storylines against human deception expert-designed storylines. Thus, we hope to develop a principled understanding of how AI-coordinated deception alters the behaviour of both AI and human adversaries.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Models For Narrative-Driven Cyber Deception

evidence_items.summary: Hydrologic models, including deep learning systems now deployed for operational flood forecasting, are evaluated primarily by how closely their simulated hydrographs match observed streamflow. However, high hydrograph skill does not guarantee physical consistency: in a synthetic calibration experiment, a conceptual model that loses 15% of its water input to an unreported sink still reaches a Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency of 0.93, and no shared benchmark tests whether models obey fundamental conservation laws. Here we introduce HydroTuring (v0.1.0), a black-box benchmark of 37 physics probes that test mass (24 probes), energy (7) and momentum (6) conservation in hydrologic models. Each probe runs a controlled experiment on forcing generated at run time from a recorded seed and applies binary pass or fail criteria validated against 18 physically exact and 59 deliberately broken reference models. Across 32 evaluated models (3 exact references, 7 AI-based models and 22 process-based models), only the 3 exact references pass every probe among the 28 models scored on 5 or more probes. Process-based and AI-based models pass similar shares of their scored probes (76% and 74%), and a pre-trained flood-forecasting LSTM fails 6 of the 11 runoff-only probes it can be scored on. Furthermore, 49% of all 1,184 model-probe pairs remain unscored because models omit the required state or flux variables, while the scored failures occur in perturbation responses and state bounds rather than long-term water-budget closure. HydroTuring provides a reproducible smoke test for model development, peer review and operational deployment under an open community protocol.

evidence_items.summary: Machine learning-based intrusion detection systems often achieve strong performance on standard benchmarks, yet fail when deployed in a different environment. This paper investigates how well ML-based detectors transfer between IoT and enterprise traffic, using IoT-23 and UNSW-NB15 as two heterogeneous domains. Our experiments show that cross-domain performance drops sharply even after explicit feature alignment and limited target supervision, and that this drop is strongly asymmetric across transfer directions. Early detection experiments show that malicious signal is recoverable from partial traffic observations within a domain, but this property does not transfer equally between domains. The hybrid model that combines tabular, temporal, and prototype-based evidence provides interpretable insights into these failure modes, but does not consistently outperform simpler temporal baselines. Together our findings suggest that benchmark accuracy alone is a poor indicator of real-world robustness, and that intrusion detection system evaluation should place greater emphasis on cross-domain portability, data efficiency, and timeliness.
evidence_items.title: Benchmark Accuracy Is Not Robustness: A Cross-Domain Study of ML-Based Intrusion Detection across IoT and Enterprise Traffic

evidence_items.summary: Agentic AI systems increasingly execute actions for users, including transfers, deployments, account changes, and data release. Human approval gates are meant to prevent these actions from running until a reviewer has inspected the proposed action and issued a decision. Because approval can arrive after a delay, frameworks often persist workflow state and resume later. The resume path therefore becomes a security boundary: it must distinguish evidence that a human approved from approval-shaped values stored in mutable state. We define Approval-Provenance Failure as a condition in which a workflow resume path treats mutable approval-relevant state as evidence that a trusted human approval path produced a decision. Our adversary can write approval-relevant workflow state, but cannot use the approval path, change the model, modify tool code, invoke the tool directly, write the business database, mint a valid approval artifact, or access the approval issuer key. We evaluate 18 agent frameworks with human approval, interruption, or pause-resume behavior. Thirteen are exposed, three are resistant, and two are non-applicable. In exposed cases, state-only approval forgery causes gated action execution after a negative control blocks ordinary resume. The failure also forges the evidence of human oversight itself: across 500 paired audit traces, genuine and forged records are statistically indistinguishable, with exact-match rate 1.0 and AUC 0.5 under the tested native audit-field projection, while provenance evidence separates them with AUC 1.0. Finally, we evaluate a provenance-bound approval artifact that authenticates the decision with a MAC or digital signature and is verified at resume time. The full artifact check blocks 13 adversarial variants on five representative targets with microsecond-scale verification cost.
evidence_items.title: Ghost Approvals: Approval-Provenance Failure in Agentic AI Frameworks

organizations: School of Computing and Data Science, Xiamen University Malaysia, Sepang, Selangor, Malaysia
evidence_items.summary: ROS 2 and its underlying Data Distribution Service (DDS) middleware and Real-Time Publish-Subscribe (RTPS) wire protocol have become a high-value attack surface for safety-critical robotic systems. Meanwhile, large language model (LLM) driven agents are reshaping the attacker profile from human penetration testers into autonomous entities capable of multi-step intrusion—yet these agents' own architectural weaknesses open paths for defensive counteraction. To date, no agentic honeypot has been built on ROS 2 to counter LLM-driven adversaries. We present ROS2Pot, whose contributions are threefold. (i) To our knowledge, it is the first publicly described interactive ROS 2 honeypot, built on rclpy atop Fast-DDS and combining rosbag replay with on-demand PyBullet physics simulation to deliver both high interaction and DDS-observable physical fidelity. (ii) To our knowledge it is also the first to cast LLM-driven agents as the explicit adversary class in ROS 2 robotic systems, mapping the systematized LLM-agent weaknesses of Ayzenshteyn et al. [1] onto concrete exploitation points in the ROS 2 attack surface. (iii) It introduces an agent-versus-agent paradigm in which the honeypot itself runs as an LLM agent and weaponizes two of these weaknesses into ROS 2-native deception primitives. Evaluation against five LLM-driven red-team agents spans three levels. At the protocol level, introspection responses are byte-identical to those of a real reference. At the physical level, the honeypot remains operationally indistinguishable from the reference under the injected control commands we replay. At the counteraction level, a two-stage trap confirms an LLM attacker through an invisible honeytoken and then elicits its operational objective by reverse prompt injection, with susceptibility varying sharply by model and objective and a measurable detect-but-not-extract funnel.
evidence_items.title: POSTER: ROS2Pot: An Agentic Honeypot for Proactive Defense Against LLM Agents in ROS 2/DDS Systems

organizations: School of Science and Technology, The University of Georgia, Tbilisi, Georgia
