evidence_items.summary: Agents that use language models to call external tools via the Model Context Protocol (MCP) are entering sensitive environments, such as assistants that take action based on the emotional state they infer using electroencephalography (EEG). Prompt injection, tool poisoning, and unauthorized tool invocation threaten such agents while they act on state derived from identity-bearing EEG data. The position of this paper is that tool-use security cannot rely on the model’s decision, because the channel that carries legitimate instructions also carries the attack. The agent should issue action requests, but leave authorization to a deterministic policy engine. Three trust boundaries with ordered controls, mapped to an MCP threat taxonomy, implement the approach. A feasibility suite of 57 test cases, 32 adversarial and 25 benign, exercises the implementation: with controls disabled every scripted adversarial call executes; with all controls enabled the engine denies all 32 and executes all 25 benign actions. Allow/deny lists and schema checks issue most first denials; output sanitization never decides a rejection, so poisoned output content at the tool-output boundary (B3) remains unevaluated. The result is deterministic denial of the covered malicious and malformed invocations without any claims about robustness. In a rule-blind preliminary trial across four language models, all 21 malicious calls that reached the engine were denied. That small, one-time trial is not a robustness benchmark. Robustness needs an adaptive adversary, independent benchmarks, comparisons with existing deterministic defenses, and evaluation of returned-content attacks.
evidence_items.title: Position: Agents Orchestrate, Policy Enforces — A Deterministic Tool-Use Control Pattern for Agentic Assistants over Sensitive EEG Data

evidence_items.summary: How news affects volatility over time depends on what the news is about. We show that this dependence is mainly one of amplitude. Event types scale a common temporal response profile by type-specific amplitudes, and differences in temporal response shape beyond amplitude are small. We use event-type labels distilled from a large language model for 904,670 headline–ticker pairs covering 499 large- and mid-cap US stocks from 2015 through June 2026. First, the event-type × age interaction is large relative to an additive level benchmark, but type-specific amplitudes of a common profile absorb 94% of it. A wild cluster bootstrap that imposes this amplitude-only null and clusters by ticker and date block still rejects it (p = 0.0005), so the remaining shape deviations are detectable but small. Second, we compare nested heterogeneous autoregressive models with news predictors (HAR-X) across three chronological evaluation stages comprising development (2019–2021), temporal validation (2022–2023), and final test (2024–2026H1). An amplitude-only model reduces quasi-likelihood (QLIKE) loss relative to a common age profile at every stage, with 95% confidence intervals excluding zero and reductions increasing from 0.0036 to 0.0058. It matches or outperforms a model with a separate age profile for each of the eleven event types, and shape deviations beyond amplitude add no stable gain. Third, two amplitudes, one for earnings and one for all other news, retain the gain, and the distilled earnings labels add forecasting information beyond a filing-based earnings calendar observed after each announcement. Earnings news weighted by a common age profile, rather than earnings intensity alone, therefore provides stable incremental value for out-of-sample volatility forecasting.
evidence_items.title: Amplitude Beyond Level: Event-Type News Persistence in Volatility Forecasting

evidence_items.summary: Papers that report trading performance for large language models describe one pipeline: one prompt, one way of reading the model’s answer, one holding period, one entry rule. Behind that one number is a search whose size is rarely reported. We measure the effective multiplicity of one such search and benchmark it against a permutation null that any paper can run on the grid it has already computed. Over 2,978 SEC Form 8-K filings from 2025-08-01 to 2026-07-30, a window opening more than ten months after the most recent model in our grid was released, we build one event-driven equity pipeline over three open-weight models under 8 billion parameters and evaluate a pre-registered grid of 7,776 configurations differing only in choices papers rarely report. Annualised Sharpe runs from -3.85 to 2.46, standard deviation 1.01; with model, prompt and truncation all fixed, the 432 configurations reachable after the model has spoken still span 4.89 on average. No family of choices is the culprit: on a descriptive partition, 83.3% of the variance sits in interactions rather than in any main effect. The configurations are highly correlated, so the effective number of independent trials is 20 by the cheapest estimator and 160 by measurement, against a nominal 7,776, and the deflated Sharpe ratio of the best configuration moves from 0.995 through 0.390 to 0.072 depending on which count is assumed. We replace that assumption with a measurement: a within-session permutation benchmark, run over the identical grid, gives a best-of-grid Sharpe of 2.72 when the model’s scores are permuted among the filings of each session, against 2.46 for the real pipeline (p = 0.746). In this study, the grid run on permuted scores reaches a higher best-of-grid Sharpe, on average, than the real pipeline. We close with a reporting protocol built on the same two instruments.
evidence_items.title: The Grid Is the Alpha: Measuring Effective Multiplicity and Permutation Nulls in LLM Event-Driven Trading

organizations: Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, USA
evidence_items.summary: Large language models can integrate heterogeneous financial evidence, but their cost, latency, and data-governance requirements can limit repeated portfolio-level inference. We evaluate whether a role-specialized multi-agent small language model system can provide a competitive alternative to a single-agent large language model for monthly portfolio rebalancing. The proposed system, SLM-Multi, instantiates Gemma 4 E4B across four specialized investment roles with selective debate. The comparator, LLM-Single, is Gemini 2.5 Flash operating as one consolidated agent. Both systems operate under a common downstream portfolio-construction pipeline, enabling a matched comparison of the two complete reasoning systems. We evaluate both systems across ten pre-specified six-stock portfolios and 15 monthly rebalances from January 2025 through March 2026. SLM-Multi achieved a mean net cumulative return of 18.28%, compared with 16.57% for LLM-Single, and a mean annualized Sharpe ratio of 0.757 versus 0.675. SLM-Multi achieved higher cumulative returns in all ten portfolios, lower average turnover, and a slightly shallower mean maximum drawdown. These results demonstrate that a structured multi-agent SLM system can achieve competitive portfolio-level performance relative to a consolidated LLM under a common portfolio-construction protocol.
evidence_items.title: Can a Multi-Agentic Small Language Model framework Compete with a Single-Agent LLM in Portfolio Rebalancing?

evidence_items.summary: We introduce FinMFT, a multi-source fine-tuning framework for transforming an open-weight language model into a structured, semantically informed, and market-aligned financial-news model. FinMFT addresses two central challenges in financial language modeling: (i) transforming general linguistic fluency into structured financial judgments supported by the underlying text and (ii) aligning those judgments with economically meaningful outcomes. It progressively aligns a shared representation with three distinct sources of supervision: vendor annotations establish financial-event structure; teacher-generated semantic assessments encode mechanisms, evidence, directional impact, and uncertainty; and realized market outcomes align the representation and a compact outcome head with multi-horizon, industry-neutral return ranks and direction classes. We assess predictive validity out of sample using rolling model fits and a strict pre-close evaluation design. At each of the one-, five-, and twenty-day horizons, FinMFT achieves higher rank IC than every external benchmark on the common evaluation population, including commercial vendor sentiment, dictionary-based methods, FinBERT, a return-supervised TF–IDF model, and prompted variants of the same backbone. These findings establish multi-source fine-tuning as a practical framework for coordinating structured, semantic, and market supervision in financial language models whose outputs are empirically evaluated against subsequent market outcomes.
evidence_items.title: FinMFT: Multi-Source Fine-Tuning of Language Models for Financial News

evidence_items.summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) improves question answering by grounding model outputs in retrieved documents, but it also introduces a trust boundary between system instructions and untrusted retrieved content. Complementing existing RAG security benchmarks, we isolate lightweight defenses at the retrieval, prompt, and output stages and evaluate their effects on three attack scenarios -- instruction-following injection, exfiltration, and PoisonedRAG-style knowledge corruption -- within a single controlled HotpotQA-derived setup. The results show that defense effectiveness is attack-dependent. Retrieval and prompt defenses reduced instruction-following success, output filtering prevented user-visible structured leakage, and retrieval diversification reduced but did not eliminate PoisonedRAG success. These results indicate that stage-local defenses are useful for isolating mitigation effects, but no single evaluated stage provided broad protection across all attacks without utility or scope trade-offs.
evidence_items.title: POSTER: Evaluating Mitigation Strategies Against Prompt Injection Attacks in Retrieval-Augmented Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Regular expressions (regexes) are widely used in modern software systems, yet their backtracking-based execution exposes them to Regular Expression Denial-of-Service (ReDoS) attacks, where crafted inputs trigger super-linear runtime. While prior work has made significant progress in detecting such vulnerabilities, automatically repairing them remains fundamentally challenging: existing approaches rely on heuristic rewriting or search-based mutation, often producing patches that either break functional correctness or fail to eliminate worst-case backtracking, with no formal guarantees. We focus on ReDoS vulnerabilities induced by structural ambiguity under backtracking semantics. We present ReAR, a certified algebraic framework that recasts ReDoS repair as a language-preserving transformation problem. Our key insight is that catastrophic backtracking is not inherent to the language defined by a regex, but instead arises from its structural representation. Based on this observation, ReAR performs repair via a constructive algebraic derivation that transforms vulnerable regexes into language-equivalent repairs that are free from the modeled structural hazards. ReAR follows a three-stage pipeline: ambiguity exposure, vulnerability elimination, and structural reduction. The first stage reveals latent ambiguity and hidden backtracking paths; the second removes the modeled exponential and polynomial backtracking hazards, yielding regexes that are structurally free from the ambiguity patterns targeted by our derivation system; and the third reduces structural redundancy while preserving language and remaining free from the modeled hazards. All transformations are grounded in Kleene algebra, ensuring language equivalence (L(R') = L (R)) while enforcing a complexity safety invariant, and produce machine-checkable derivation certificates. We implement ReAR and evaluate it on 460 real-world vulnerable regexes collected from CVEs and prior benchmarks. ReAR successfully repairs 85.22% of vulnerabilities, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods, while maintaining an average repair time of 0.86 seconds per regex. We further analyze the algebraic derivation process and find that repairs typically converge within a small number of transformation steps (median: 5), with 78.57% of regexes repaired within 10 steps, demonstrating the practical efficiency of our certified approach. Beyond effectiveness, ReAR provides verifiable proof traces, transforming regex repair from heuristic patching into a principled and auditable process.
evidence_items.title: Repairing ReDoS by Construction: Certified Algebraic Derivation for Language-Preserving Regex Transformation

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are no longer limited to text generators, but they can also plan, call tools, delegate tasks to other agents, act within external environments, and change states in response to their actions. In Anthropic’s recent report on an AI-orchestrated cyber-espionage campaign involving Claude Code, individual subtasks appeared legitimate when evaluated in isolation but became malicious when combined into an autonomous attack sequence. Consequently, the security of such complex LLM-based agentic systems may fail even when each component appears secure in isolation. This position and open-problem paper argues that LLM agent security should be studied as emergence-driven security: the analysis of security properties that arise from the interactions among agents and its components over time. We define emergence-driven security and provide a conceptual taxonomy to classify emergent security-related phenomena in LLM agents, covering both beneficial and harmful forms of emergence. Based on these insights, we propose EASE, an Emergence-Aware Security Evaluation framework that provides a systematic process for assessing how interactions among agents combine over time to produce harmful or beneficial system-level security outcomes. Finally, we conclude by outlining open problems for studying emergent behavior in LLM agents in the context of security. The paper is intended to provide a foundation for examining how the emerging capabilities and operational needs of LLM agents may shape security evaluations that go beyond static, model-level testing.
evidence_items.title: Emergence-Driven Security of LLM Agents

evidence_items.summary: Model Context Protocol (MCP) is rapidly emerging as a standard interface for connecting large language model (LLM) applications to external tools. An MCP tool exposes two semantic views of the same functionality: a developer-provided description that guides the LLM's tool selection, and an implementation that determines the actual runtime behavior. Security issues arise when these two views diverge, leading to instruction injection, misleading descriptions, malicious code, or unsafe implementations. Existing defenses analyze descriptions or implementations largely in isolation and thus fail to address this broader threat space in a unified manner. We present ContractGuard, the first security-oriented framework for bidirectional semantic contract auditing of MCP tools. Our observation is that diverse MCP threats can be unified as violations of a semantic contract between a tool's description and its implementation. ContractGuard combines reachability-aware static analysis with LLM-based cross-view reasoning for auditing. It extracts a tool-specific code slice, generates a code-grounded description, compares it against the developer-provided one, and validates and classifies detected inconsistencies. We evaluate our method on 3,586 MCP tools from 1,000 real-world MCP servers and 5,661 benchmark cases. Our tool uncovers 116 security issues in the wild, including 21 misleading descriptions, 29 instances of potentially malicious code, and 66 unsafe implementations. It achieves a 96.0% true positive rate on malicious-code benchmarks and more than a 92.8% true positive rate on description-attack benchmarks. Results show that contract auditing can effectively identify security-relevant description--implementation mismatches in MCP tools.
evidence_items.title: ContractGuard: Auditing Semantic Contracts of MCP Tools for Security Violations

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can retain personal, copyrighted, or harmful information that may later require removal. My dissertation studies trustworthy LLM unlearning as an integrated process of specifying the forgetting target, performing robust single and continual deletion while preserving capabilities, and verifying forgetting through representation diagnostics and recovery tests. My work develops dual-granularity target construction, utility-preserving deletion, and recovery-based verification for these stages. A complementary SoK organizes safety forgetting across benchmarks, algorithms, and evaluation, while identifying behavior probing, graceful forgetting, and model regularization as functional uses. Future work will formulate retraining-based verification criteria and extend the framework to agents whose state spans model weights, memory, retrieval, tools, and interaction histories.
evidence_items.title: Trustworthy LLM Unlearning and Beyond

evidence_items.summary: Code Large Language Models (Code LLMs) have demonstrated exceptional capabilities in code generation and completion. While these models are known to memorize portions of their training data, existing approaches to evaluate credential memorization rely on output-level inspection or adversarial prompt crafting, leaving the internal decoding behaviors that underlie secret leakage unexplored. In this paper, we conduct a token-level investigation of hard-coded credential memorization in Code LLMs during routine code completion. We report two findings: (1) traces of memorized secrets persist in the token candidate space, indicating that standard output-level evaluation underestimates the true extent of memorization; (2) the generation of real secrets exhibits statistically distinct uncertainty dynamics compared to hallucinated strings, providing a reliable intrinsic signal for memorization detection. Based on these findings, we propose Code-SeC (Code Secret Characterization), a decoding-time diagnostic framework that monitors uncertainty signals along the decoding trajectory and performs targeted distribution adjustments to uncover latent credential memorization. Experimental results show that Code-SeC effectively detects memorized code secrets across representative Code LLMs and secret types, providing comprehensive empirical evidence that hard-coded credential memorization is prevalent in current code completion models.
evidence_items.title: Code-SeC: A Decoding-time Probing Method for Characterizing Secret Memorization in Code LLM

evidence_items.summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has become a standard approach for improving the reliability of large language models (LLMs). Prior work demonstrates the vulnerability of RAG systems by misleading them into generating attacker-chosen outputs through poisoning the knowledge base. However, we observe that the effectiveness of these attacks is substantially undermined in the real-world deployment, where LLMs exhibit a strong self-correction ability (SCA). This ability is typically triggered by the mainstream configuration of LLMs, indicating a substantial gap between idealized research settings and practical scenarios. To address this issue, we systematically reflect on the limitations of prior RAG attacks and introduce DisarmRAG, a novel poisoning paradigm that focuses on the retriever, instead of the conventional approach of only poisoning the knowledge base. By compromising the retriever, our method can inject arbitrary anti-SCA instructions into the context provided to LLMs, effectively suppressing the SCA and enforcing attacker-chosen outputs. In particular, we craft a novel and systematic attack framework consisting of 1) an iterative co-optimization process to ensure the effectiveness of the anti-SCA instructions and 2) a stealthy model editing technique based on contrastive learning to facilitate the delivery of the attack payload. We extensively evaluate DisarmRAG across six LLMs and three QA benchmarks, and the results, with success rates exceeding 90%, confirm its efficacy. We additionally validate the effectiveness of our attack under various detection defenses, highlighting stealthiness, which is another critical aspect to consider in real-world attacks.
evidence_items.title: DisarmRAG: Stealthy Retriever Poisoning to Disable Self-Correction in Retrieval-Augmented Generation

evidence_items.summary: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) enables task specialization but introduces privacy risks through training data memorization. Practitioners deploying fine-tuned LLMs in sensitive domains such as medicine, law, and finance must choose among fine-tuning methods without clear guidance on the privacy implications of that choice. We compare full fine-tuning, partial fine-tuning, and Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) by measuring how much sensitive personally identifiable information (PII) each method leaks from training data, using planted canaries to track memorization. Six Llama configurations (3B and 8B parameters) are evaluated across the medical, legal, and finance domains under three extraction attack types: prefix attacks, random prompting, and completion attacks. Full fine-tuning leaks the most on average, followed by LoRA. Partial fine-tuning leaks the least in every configuration we tested, though the relative ordering of full fine-tuning and LoRA varies. Contrary to our initial hypothesis, LoRA's parameter efficiency does not yield the strongest privacy protection; we attribute this to LoRA's architectural breadth across all transformer layers. The performance-privacy trade-off these findings expose has direct consequences for deployment. Even partial fine-tuning on the 3B model, our best configuration, leaked canaries, so practitioners should assume some leakage by default.
evidence_items.title: Out of Tune: How Different Fine-Tuning Methods Affect Information Security

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have recently shown promise in code generation and other software engineering tasks. However, their effectiveness in real-world security vulnerability detection still remains limited. A key observation is that while LLMs exhibit strong semantic understanding and security analysis capabilities on code snippets, these strengths are rarely extended to large-scale real-world programs. In this work, we propose SemScan, a novel vulnerability detection approach that harnesses LLMs' local reasoning capabilities to enable global security analysis. SemScan establishes an iterative loop of evidence collection and evidence-guided semantic synthesis. Our evaluation on a Python CVE vulnerability dataset and 200 popular real-world Python projects demonstrates that SemScan significantly outperforms state-of-the-art tools, uncovering 62 previously unknown serious vulnerabilities, including remote code execution and insecure deserialization flaws. To date, 22 of these vulnerabilities have been confirmed and assigned CVE identifiers.
evidence_items.title: Global-View Reasoning with LLMs for Real-World Vulnerability Detection

evidence_items.summary: Web application scanners are indispensable tools for black-box vulnerability discovery. However, modern web applications increasingly rely on dynamic client-side rendering, where many HTTP requests are generated only in response to specific, meaningful user interactions. These interaction-triggered requests and the vulnerabilities they may conceal create a hidden attack surface that traditional scanners struggle to explore, as they lack the semantic understanding needed to identify and execute purposeful action sequences. In this paper, we present SemScanner, a novel approach that leverages the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) to achieve semantic-aware web scanning, effectively uncovering this hidden attack surface. SemScanner performs per-page semantic analysis to generate meaningful interaction tasks, which are then executed by LLM-driven agents. Through this process, it constructs a Web Application Semantic Graph (WASG) that models the application's attack surface enriched with semantic context. Building on this graph, SemScanner formulates targeted audit tasks and deploys specialized agents to perform context-adaptive testing, thereby exposing vulnerabilities that conventional approaches may miss. We evaluate SemScanner on 20 real-world web applications, comparing it against state-of-the-art scanners. SemScanner identifies 59 previously unknown zero-day vulnerabilities, nearly three times the number discovered by the strongest baseline. All identified zero-day vulnerabilities have been responsibly disclosed, with CVE identifiers assigned.
evidence_items.title: Uncovering Hidden Attack Surfaces in Web Applications via Semantic-Aware Black-Box Scanning

evidence_items.summary: Total positivity of order two (TP2) imposes a restriction on European call prices across strikes and maturities: after the appropriate normalization, the price ratio of a higher-strike call to a lower-strike call should increase with maturity. This property holds in Black–Scholes and in a broader class of European option models [3]. Recent evidence further shows that TP2 violations in European SPX options can behave like near-arbitrage opportunities [1]. The same interpretation does not carry over directly to SPY. Its options are American, and early exercise around discrete dividends can itself produce an apparent TP2 violation. We first ask when a violation in SPY calls can still be evaluated using the European TP2 benchmark. We derive two contract-level tests: a sufficient condition for the early-exercise premium to be zero and a dividend-based bound that identifies violations too large to be explained by early exercise. Among 177,487 detected episodes from 2014–2026, these tests resolve 64.0% of the sample. In the 2021–2026 trading period, 71.0% of episodes are European-equivalent under the zero-premium conditions. We then ask whether TP2 violations are profitable after trading costs. Trading every detected candidate at quoted bid and ask prices wins 94.7% of the time before commissions; adding them turns 250,004 trades into a $12.52 million loss with a 12.9% win rate. The signal survives the spread but not the modeled commission charge, so we treat trading as a conditional selection problem. In six walk-forward test periods, LightGBM, an MLP, a TP2-specific transformer, and logistic regression all select subsets with positive aggregate out-of-sample P&L. The MLP produces the largest normalized P&L at $3.56 million, while the transformer variants achieve active-day Sharpe ratios of 2.19 and 1.88, with the plain transformer’s date-block bootstrap interval on total P&L excluding zero. In a separate premium-budget experiment, LightGBM and the MLP grow the budget by 14.9% and 13.0% per year. Overall, TP2 violations in SPY do not support unconditional trading after costs, but their profitability is concentrated in subsets that can be identified using information available when the violation occurs.
evidence_items.title: Machine-Learned Conditional Trading of TP2 Violations in SPY American Call Options

evidence_items.summary: Financial natural language processing (NLP) often treats the tone of an earnings-call answer as fixed by its text. Yet the same answer can be routine after one question and surprising after another. We define answer surprise as observed tone minus its prediction from pre-answer information. We compare four benchmarks with progressively richer context: pre-call information (A0), earlier dialogue (A1), the current question (A2), and full context including the questioning analyst’s prior-call history and richer question features (A3). All four benchmarks use the same tone measure and Ridge model, trained only on earlier years. On 2020–2024 calls, added context improves time-forward out-of-sample prediction of Loughran and McDonald dictionary tone and changes the residual’s association with one-day stock returns. We fix these choices before evaluating a 2025 holdout of 1,901 calls. A one-standard-deviation increase in the full-context answer residual is associated with 61.5 basis points of one-day market-adjusted return. We repeat the holdout analysis using tone scores from Gemini 3.5 Flash and DeepSeek V4 Flash. For both scorers, answer-return coefficients are positive across A0–A3 and all five return horizons. Incorporating dialogue context improves answer-tone prediction, while the residual remains positively associated with stock returns across all three tone measures.
evidence_items.title: When Answers Surprise: Sequential Tone Residualization and Abnormal Returns in Earnings Calls

evidence_items.summary: Mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) is a foundational tool for modeling complex decision-making problems across domains such as logistics, finance, healthcare, and network planning. While modern solvers can efficiently handle large and intricate MILP instances, they are typically deployed as black boxes, offering little transparency or auditability of their outputs. This limitation is particularly problematic in Optimization-as-a-Service settings, where users must trust remote solvers to return correct and optimal solutions. Although zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs) provide a natural mechanism for verifiable computation without revealing sensitive information, directly applying general-purpose zkSNARKs to prove the full execution of MILP solvers is computationally infeasible due to the complexity and dynamism of solver internals. In this work, we present a specialized zero-knowledge verification framework for MILP solutions that avoids proving the entire solver execution. Instead, we certify optimality by proving solution feasibility, the validity of lower bounds at leaf nodes of a branch-and-bound tree, and the consistency of branching decisions, without revealing the solver's proprietary search strategy. To enable this approach, we introduce new techniques for zero-knowledge certification of linear programming infeasibility, node-bound correctness, and lightweight verification of branch-and-bound tree structure. We implement our system and evaluate it on standard MILP benchmark instances. Experimental results show that proof generation incurs only modest overhead relative to the solver runtime—for example, requiring only 3.1× the solver runtime for an instance with 23,970 variables and 16,765 constraints.
evidence_items.title: Melior, Verifiable Mixed-Integer Programming via zkSNARKs

evidence_items.summary: Aim: This article examines the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in four core management accounting functions: cost analysis, budgeting, management control, and decision-making. Method: A structured literature review synthesizes findings from systematic reviews, case studies, experiments, a dissertation, and professional reports to distinguish demonstrated predictive benefits from broader claims about organizational performance. The review is limited by the absence of a complete database export and a study-specific PRISMA flow; it should therefore be read as a structured synthesis of accessible literature rather than a fully reproducible systematic review. Results: Machine-learning models can match or exceed human estimates in selected cost-estimation tasks when adequate historical data are available. In budgeting, machine learning can improve prediction accuracy, but predictive accuracy alone does not establish causal effects or guarantee appropriate resource allocation. In management control, digital tools support more timely and anticipatory monitoring, although the available evidence does not always isolate the effect of AI itself. For decision-making, the usefulness of AI depends on data quality, model explainability, user trust, professional competence, and the preservation of human accountability. Novelty/Implications: The novelty lies in organizing the evidence by management accounting function and strength of evidence, separating technical outcomes (prediction accuracy) from organizational outcomes. AI is best positioned as support for professional judgment rather than a replacement for management accountants. Organizations need data governance, model evaluation, and training to ensure responsible adoption, and the article proposes an empirical research agenda, particularly in Indonesian organizations, on AI use, efficiency, cost control, and decision quality.
evidence_items.title: Transformasi Akuntansi Manajemen pada Era Artificial Intelligence: Tinjauan Literatur Terstruktur tentang Efisiensi, Pengendalian Biaya, dan Pengambilan Keputusan

evidence_items.summary: The rapid growth of Internet of Things (IoT) deployments has increased the need for reliable intrusion detection in connected and safety-critical environments. Although machine learning-based intrusion detection systems can achieve strong predictive performance, their decision-making processes often remain opaque, limiting analysts' ability to interpret and trust model outputs. Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods, particularly SHapley Additive explanations (SHAP) and Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME), address this limitation by providing feature-level explanations of model predictions. However, it remains unclear whether these explanations remain stable when intrusion detection models are periodically retrained, and prior work has not systematically examined explanation stability under controlled model retraining in an IoT intrusion detection setting. This study evaluates the stability of SHAP and LIME explanations for a Random Forest-based IoT intrusion detection model. The classifier was trained on the well-known datasets, CICIoT2023 and TON-IoT, and retrained six times using different random seeds while keeping the dataset, preprocessing pipeline, and train-test split fixed. Explanation stability was evaluated by comparing explanations across all pairs of retraining runs using feature-set, ranking, and vector-similarity measures. Across both CICIoT2023 and TON-IoT, SHAP produced substantially more consistent explanations than LIME, with more stable feature rankings and greater agreement in the most influential features across retraining runs. LIME showed greater sensitivity to retraining, producing more variable explanations even when the overall model behaviour remained broadly similar. These findings indicate that SHAP is better suited to system-level explanation consistency in retrained IoT intrusion detection models, while also highlighting that explanation stability alone does not guarantee correctness or operational trustworthiness. The results therefore suggest that stability evaluation should be incorporated into the deployment and validation of XAI methods for safety-critical intrusion detection systems.
evidence_items.title: Explanation Stability in IoT Intrusion Detection: A Comparative Study of SHAP and LIME Across Retrained Random Forest Models

evidence_items.summary: Once specialized for graphics acceleration, Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) now serve as foundational components of parallel computing, driving advancements from immersive gaming to generative Artificial Intelligence (AI). However, while their computational capabilities have expanded dramatically, GPU security has lagged behind their expanding functionality. Recent studies reveal that GPUs remain susceptible to memory corruption attacks, a gap amplified by their reliance on memory-unsafe programming frameworks, such as CUDA. Although contemporary GPUs incorporate basic defenses like ASLR and stack canaries, the absence of hardware-enforced Data Execution Prevention (DEP) leaves them critically exposed to code-injection attacks, undermining the implementation of a robust W⊕X security policy. This work analyzes the potential of code-injection attacks on NVIDIA GPUs, executed independently of CPU vulnerabilities, in the presence of ASLR and stack canary protections. To address this gap, we design and implement a software-based DEP mechanism, a critical enabler of the W⊕X policy, to enforce strict memory permissions, eliminating executable-writable memory regions, and thereby neutralizing code-injection attacks. Our solution operates transparently alongside proprietary vendor toolchains and software components while maintaining compatibility with precompiled libraries. Empirical evaluations across diverse benchmarks on three different NVIDIA GPU architectures show that our approach incurs minimal overhead, with average runtime and memory overheads of less than 0.5%.
evidence_items.title: Mitigating Code Injection Attacks on Modern GPUs

evidence_items.summary: Backdoor attacks traditionally manipulate model predictions, while recent explanation-aware attacks have shown that post-hoc explanations can also be compromised. However, it remains unclear whether prediction and explanation backdoors can coexist as independently activated behaviors within a single model. We introduce a compositional dual-trigger framework in which one trigger manipulates Grad-CAM explanations while preserving predictions, and a second trigger causes targeted misclassification while preserving the previously learned explanation behavior. The two backdoors are embedded sequentially using partial layer freezing and replay-based regularization, enabling independent or simultaneous activation. We evaluate the framework using BadNet-, WaNet-, and Grond-based triggers across five CNN and Vision Transformer architectures on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet. The results show that explanation-aware backdoors extend beyond visible patch triggers and that prediction and explanation manipulation can coexist in most evaluated settings. However, their compatibility depends on the architecture, dataset, and trigger composition. These findings demonstrate that backdoored models may contain multiple independently activated malicious behaviors and highlight the need to evaluate explanation integrity alongside predictive integrity.
evidence_items.title: Compositional Dual-Trigger Backdoors for Independent Prediction and Explanation Manipulation

evidence_items.summary: The classification of network traffic using machine learning (ML) models has become popular to address the security issues in IoT networks and/or IoT devices. However, the classifiers often act as black-boxes which hinders its adoption in critical decision making. To address this problem, we design and develop a system, called rCamInspector, that employs Explainable AI (XAI) to generate reliable and trustworthy explanations for the model outputs. It adopts two classifiers, Flow Classifier and SmartCam Classifier; both of them are IP address and transport port agnostic. rCamInspector is evaluated using a total of 38 GB network traffic collected over 72 hours. Our results show that Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGB) achieves the highest accuracy of 92% and 99% in the Flow and Smart-Cam classifiers respectively, among eight supervised ML models. We empirically show that the traditional mutual information (MI) based important features in XGB remain almost same in either classifier. Using SHAP and LIME, we show that the most important features in Flow Classifier are significantly different from those in the SmartCam Classifier for the correct prediction using XGB. To evaluate the faithfulness of SHAP and LIME on the dataset, we show that both have a consistency of more than 0.7 and a sufficiency of 1.0. Compared to the existing works, rCamInspector achieves a better accuracy (99%), precision (99%), and false negative rate (0.7%), supported by the XAI for the predictions.
evidence_items.title: rCamInspector: Building Reliability and Trust on IoT (Spy) Camera Detection using XAI

organizations: Department of Science, University of Western Ontario, London, Canada
evidence_items.summary: Risk, compliance, and reference-data teams must follow a legal entity through mergers, rebrands, spinoffs, and jurisdiction changes, where its name and identifiers change by design. Snapshot entity-resolution benchmarks do not pose this task, and the open registry that records such events (GLEIF) does so only as sparse, partly administrative successor links. We introduce Sylvester, a public benchmark and empirical study of lifecycle-aware entity resolution: 125,519 labeled pairs over 3.3M entities from GLEIF Level-1/2, SEC EDGAR, and Wikidata, with held-out time, event-type, and jurisdiction splits. Successors change names while hard negatives are mined to be name-similar, so name similarity is anti-predictive on the released pool. We therefore evaluate every method on three candidate pools: the released pool, an unrelated miner’s pool, and retrieval over the full universe. Methods that exploit the construction (inverted name similarity, 64–70% Hits@1 on time/event; a name-feature gradient-boosted matcher, 0.73–0.84) score well on the released pool and collapse off it. Among name-only methods, a 22M-parameter cross-encoder transfers: 57–61% Hits@1 on time and event, 27–35 pp ahead of the best bi-encoder and ahead of six zero-shot LLMs. Input matters as much as architecture: given the full registry record, a gradient-boosted matcher beats that cross-encoder on-pool by 18 pp, and a cross-encoder over the same record wins the fielded setting by 12 pp (both p < 10− 4). Even so, the best system reaches only 21–39% Hits@1 end to end, because first-stage retrieval (Recall@20 of 33–50%) misses most true successors. The bottleneck is finding the candidate, not scoring it.
evidence_items.title: Sylvester: A Benchmark and Empirical Study of Lifecycle-Aware Entity Resolution on Open Financial Data

evidence_items.summary: Machine-learning approaches for American option pricing depend on adequate training data coverage. However, contracts most informative for learning early exercise are intrinsically underrepresented, as market observations concentrate away from the early-exercise boundary. Targeted data augmentation could address this limitation but requires a representation of a contract’s location relative to the boundary, which existing option representations lack. We introduce the Boundary Proximity Score (BPS), a continuous coordinate in [0,1] quantifying each contract’s proximity to the early-exercise boundary, and incorporate it into a conditional generative adversarial network, giving BPS-cGAN. A BPS-consistency loss, enforced by an independently trained and frozen regressor together with model-free financial constraints, enables the generation of contracts with prescribed boundary proximity. Applied to approximately 3.3 million QQQ put option quotes, BPS reveals that observed contracts are concentrated well outside the early-exercise region, with relatively few samples lying in or near the region where early exercise becomes relevant. The proposed framework generates contracts with controlled BPS values while preserving the statistical properties of market data. Ablation experiments show that withholding BPS from the conditioning vector eliminates this control, confirming that explicit exercise-proximity information is what enables targeted augmentation. Augmenting the training data of a neural pricing model with the generated contracts using BPS-cGAN lowers out-of-sample pricing error, reducing RMSE by 9.2% relative to a no-augmentation baseline and by 9.9% relative to a benchmark cGAN augmentation, with corresponding MAE reductions of 7.2% and 13.1%. The code has been made publicly available on GitHub: https://github.com/J1225Q/BPS-cGAN.
evidence_items.title: BPS-cGAN: Generating American Option Data at a Prescribed Exercise Proximity

evidence_items.summary: Lack of benchmark and realistic datasets is a critical shortcoming in access control research, including Attribute-based Access Control (ABAC). In this paper, we address this concern by building MuSimA - a web-based tool for generating ABAC datasets with user-specified dataset size and probability distributions of attribute values. These specifications can be provided either in a structured JSON file or as a combination of a minimal JSON along with hand-drawn distribution sketches. The generated synthetic ABAC data matching the input specifications can be downloaded by the user. MuSimA is freely available for the research community.
evidence_items.title: DEMO: A Tool with Multi-modal Input for Generating Bespoke ABAC Datasets

evidence_items.summary: Peer selection is a recurring primitive in finance: comparable firms are used for valuation, benchmarking, liquidity inference, and data imputation. Yet peer selection is often treated as static similarity based on industry, geography, fundamentals, text, or judgment. We argue that this is incomplete: the best peer-selection mechanism depends on the target, information set, and downstream task. We study private-company valuation, where peer choice directly affects revenue-multiple estimates and post-IPO market valuations provide an observable benchmark. Using private firms that later completed IPOs, we evaluate multiple peer-selection methods in a contemporaneous relative-valuation setting: peer sets and method choices are fixed before the IPO, while target and peer enterprise values are measured at IPO+31 to evaluate the pre-IPO peer-selection decision. We find substantial heterogeneity: no fixed rule dominates, and the training-selected fixed method remains far from an ex-post oracle that selects the best method for each company. Motivated by this gap, we propose a valuation-aware adaptive peer-selection framework. The model selects among peer methods using ex-ante characteristics, pre-IPO implied valuations, peer-set diagnostics, and cross-method agreement features, learning which notion of comparability suits each firm while preserving traceability to a peer method and peer set. Empirically, adaptive hard selectors reduce valuation error relative to fixed rules, and the confidence-gated selector outperforms a simple median-of-methods ensemble while preserving attribution to a single peer-construction method and peer set. Rank-based selection best identifies the ex-post oracle method, while risk-aware and confidence-gated selectors provide stronger tail-risk control. Overall, peer selection is better viewed not as choosing a universal comparable set, but as learning a task-aware policy over complementary peer-construction mechanisms.
evidence_items.title: No Universal Comparable: Adaptive Peer Selection for Private-Company Valuation

evidence_items.summary: We introduce the Concentrated Liquidity Execution Benchmark (CLEB), an execution-aware testbed for reinforcement learning (RL) in liquidity provision on Uniswap v3. We control four evaluation axes at once, fee accounting, model selection without data leakage, executable action geometry, and operating costs. We build CLEB from 22.6 million Ethereum mainnet swaps across six pools (three token pairs at two fee tiers) and evaluate five RL algorithms and six heuristics on held-out walk-forward windows. We average across seeds within windows and report paired bootstrap intervals with Holm correction. When rebalancing conserves value and fees are attributed swap by swap, every strategy’s mean sits below holding and no algorithm dominates across pools. Evaluated deterministically, each learned policy executes one action in each held-out window of its first seed’s recorded trace. To test whether this collapse is economically appropriate, we evaluate every action at each decision state and fit a decision stump over the same state variables. The stump produces no reliable test advantage over a fixed range width selected on validation, and in no pool does a learned policy improve on the best validation heuristic at every block length. Because a maximum over realized outcomes disagrees with a fixed action even without predictable state-dependent gains, we report the hindsight comparison as descriptive. Matching executable action geometry across fee tiers changes which strategy has the highest mean in four of six pools and eliminates the apparent lead of one learned policy over the other learned policies at the 0.30% tier. Across capital and gas levels, recentering an out-of-range position is worse than leaving it unchanged in every 0.05% cell and only descriptively favorable in most 0.30% cells. With this state and action set, CLEB therefore characterizes active liquidity provision on this panel as heterogeneous loss mitigation rather than premium capture.
evidence_items.title: Execution-Aware Benchmarking of Reinforcement Learning for Concentrated Liquidity Provision

evidence_items.summary: Privacy-preserving Boolean satisfiability (SAT) solvers allow multiple distrustful parties to solve the conjunction of their private formulas without revealing their inputs. Prior work on privacy-preserving SAT solvers, i.e., ppSAT (USENIX Security 2022), fails to solve formulas of practical size and complexity because it supports only the most basic SAT-solving algorithm. We bring privacy-preserving SAT solving closer to practicality by introducing ppCDCL. Through carefully orchestrated oblivious data structures and solver architecture, our new solver enables conflict-driven clause learning (CDCL) and efficient propagation, the two most important features of modern plaintext SAT solvers. Evaluation results show that ppCDCL outperforms ppSAT in both capability and efficiency. It solves significantly more instances: 98% vs. 65% on the Haplotype benchmarks and 84% vs. 28% on the larger, more diverse SATLIB benchmarks. Furthermore, it solves 36% of SATLIB instances within 1,000 seconds compared to only 4% for ppSAT.
evidence_items.title: Towards Practical Privacy-Preserving SAT Solving

evidence_items.summary: Fuzzing and symbolic execution are two prominent methods for software testing and a comprehensive set of command-line option sequences can significantly improve their performance. However, the exponential number of potential command-line option sequences makes it challenging to select the most effective ones for security testing. State-of-the-art option sequence generation methods primarily employ either black-box or white-box analysis methods for automatic option relationship extraction. Black-box analysis methods can analyze program manuals for option relationships, while white-box analysis methods rely on precise data and control dependency analysis. The limitation of extracted relationships makes them suffer from generating redundant and ineffective sequences. In this paper, we propose a novel option sequence generation method based on a novel coverage-based conditional probability model CBP, which is constructed on runtime metrics to reflect option relationships more realistically and can provide fine-grained guidance for option sequence generation. Besides, we propose a significance-based option sequence generation algorithm based on CBP to generate more effective command-line option sequences for security testing. We implemented a prototype tool called GoSe and evaluated its performance on benchmarks of 24 real-world programs. The results demonstrate that, compared with the state-of-the-art methods OSmart and ProphetFuzz, GoSe can generate command-line option sequences that improve KLEE's branch coverage by an average of 22.8% and 22.4%, respectively. Additionally, by providing superior command-line option sequences, GoSe enabled AFL++ to cover 33.3% and 30.2% more branches than when using the option sequences generated by OSmart and ProphetFuzz, respectively. With the option sequences generated by GoSe, AFL++ has discovered five 0-day vulnerabilities.
evidence_items.title: GoSe: Command-Line Option Sequence Generation with Runtime-Based Option Relationship Modeling for Security Testing

evidence_items.summary: Proving the correctness of computations over a large dataset via succinct non-interactive arguments of knowledge (SNARKs) entails the large overhead of ''loading'' the dataset in the SNARK. However, certain computations may only need to access a small fraction of the dataset (e.g., a database query that only accesses a subset of table rows and then computes an aggregation function). The standard way of efficiently proving such computations is to use lookup arguments with sublinear prover complexity to load only necessary data to the SNARK. Unfortunately, all prior schemes are static : even a single change to the dataset forces the prover to re-run an expensive pre-processing step, linear to the dataset size. The only exemption is the recent work of Dutta et al., (CCS'24) that proposed a lookup argument with amortized sublinear updates-based on re-running the pre-processing phase periodically, when too many changes have been accumulated. In this work, we present Rogue, the first lookup argument with sublinear prover time and updates that always take time proportional only to the number of incurred changes. Indeed, Rogue is actually a matrix lookup argument, supporting entire row lookups in time proportional to the number of rows (and independent of their size)! It has very good practical performance, e.g., for a 220x 27 matrix and 210 row accesses, Rogue achieves x21-942 and x76-30000 faster lookups and updates, respectively, compared to prior works. We then use Rogue to build RogueDB, the first verifiable database system for arbitrary SQL queries that supports authenticated indexes, hence achieves prover time sublinear to the database. Compared with prior schemes with succinct proofs, vSQL (Zhang et al., IEEE S&P '17) and PoneglyphDB (Gu et al., SIGMOD'25), we get x42.8-x8624.1 and x149.6-x11362.4 faster prover times, for various SQL queries from the TPC-H benchmark.
evidence_items.title: Rogue: Updatable Matrix Lookup Arguments and Applications to Verifiable Databases

evidence_items.summary: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) achieve strong performance across many graph-based tasks but remain vulnerable to membership inference (MI). Prior work has shown that graph structure plays a central role in shaping MI risk. Since nodes differ in their structural and feature properties, we ask whether they also face unequal MI risk and find that structurally isolated nodes and nodes with high intra-class feature dissimilarity are particularly exposed. Motivated by this uneven vulnerability, we make the case for systematically exploring self-supervised learning (SSL) as a privacy-mitigation strategy for graph machine learning. As a first step, we investigate contrastive SSL pretraining on a public graph before fine-tuning on private data. In standard GNN training, a low backbone learning rate disproportionately protects the most vulnerable nodes, while SSL preserves utility and provides additional privacy gains across node groups. We then integrate SSL into PrivGNN, improving the privacy--utility trade-off by reducing the privacy budget by more than 50% on benchmark datasets.
evidence_items.title: POSTER: Towards Mitigating Unequal Membership-Inference Risk in GNNs with Self-Supervised Pretraining

evidence_items.summary: Automated gadget-chain synthesis is central to code-reuse exploitation, a core technique for bypassing exploit mitigations such as non-executable (NX). Existing automated solutions typically rely on restrictive assumptions, including the availability of large, fully controllable stack memory regions or gadgets that directly manipulate the stack pointer register. These assumptions rarely hold in practical exploitation scenarios. As such, specialized gadgets are required to facilitate exploitation, and we term these components dynamic-source gadgets. Widely prevalent in programs and endowed with richer semantics, it serves as a valuable asset for generating target gadget chains under constrained conditions. The data flow of dynamic-source gadgets is governed by runtime register states and context-dependent memory values. However, the flexible data-sourcing characteristic of these gadgets gives rise to an unwieldy constraint space and a combinatorial explosion of the search space. This renders existing automated methods inapplicable to this scenario. In this paper, we introduce DynOP, a framework that automates the inference and synthesis of attack chains by leveraging dynamic-source gadgets .To achieve this, we design a Virtual Controllable Memory (VCM) mechanism with layout correction, a backward constraint propagation solver, and a context-aware filtering mechanism. These innovations transform dynamic-source gadgets into viable building blocks for synthesis, effectively expanding the semantic boundary of usable gadgets. Consequently, DynOP supports diverse attack primitives and adapts to complex memory environments. We evaluate DynOP against state-of-the-art techniques on both ROP benchmarks and 9 real-world vulnerabilities. Our framework consistently outperforms state-of-the-art tools across both overwritable and non-overwritable stack memory layouts, successfully synthesizing attack chains where prior methods fail while achieving a significant improvement in efficiency. We demonstrate its practicality through end-to-end exploits for multiple vulnerabilities, validating that the framework can effectively breach current defense systems.
evidence_items.title: DynOP: Blow Away the Cobwebs in NX Bypassing with Dynamic-Source Gadget Oriented Programming

evidence_items.summary: Forced execution is an effective technique for exposing hidden payloads in malware by systematically enforcing the outcomes of conditional transfer instructions. However, modern malware increasingly employs commercial virtualization obfuscators (e.g., VMProtect, Themida, Enigma, Obsidium) to protect their code body. In particular, native instructions are transformed to customized virtual bytecode instructions, which are decoded and interpreted at runtime. As a result, native control transfers become obscure from forced execution tools, rendering conventional approaches largely ineffective. In this paper, we propose a novel forced execution technique specifically designed to address virtualization-based obfuscation. The technique does not require comprehensive deobfucation. Instead, it only identifies the instructions responsible for the virtualized conditional transfer instructions, leveraging a critical observation that the virtualization needs to follow specific data/control-flow to preserve the original semantics of conditional transfer. Once identified, these instructions are manipulated to simulate the effect of enforcing branch outcomes in the original plaintext code. Evaluations on the benchmarks with ground truth show that our technique achieves 100% recall and nearly 100% precision in identifying virtualized conditional transfers, and generalizes well across a variety of popular commercial virtualization obfuscators. Evaluations on real-world malware samples show that the number of behaviors exposed by our technique is 10.97 times of plain execution, and 1.89 times of native forced execution.
evidence_items.title: Forced Execution for Malware Protected by Commercial Virtualization Obfuscators

evidence_items.summary: Conventional dressings provide coverage but cannot steer repair, so wounds stalled by infection, inflammation, or impaired perfusion remain inadequately treated. This review examines functional hydrogels through two paradigms: bioactive hydrogels that directly modulate healing, and delivery-system hydrogels that release payloads via material-controlled, externally driven, or microenvironment-responsive mechanisms. After outlining the healing cascade and acute–chronic divergence, we critically appraise each bioactive function and release strategy for mechanistic evidence, design, and limitations. Benchmarking 20 registered clinical trials and FDA/NMPA-approved products exposes a systematic translational gap: clinical candidates remain early-stage and largely single-function, approved dressings are mostly Class II moisturizing/bioactive products, and preclinical multifunctional platforms often rely on rodent contraction models, surrogate endpoints, and unassessed manufacturing. AI is a promising but not yet translation-ready bridge for property prediction, closed-loop monitoring, and patient stratification, constrained by data quality, sensor stability, interpretability, and regulation. We conclude that multifunctionality is not intrinsically superior and must be justified by measurable clinical benefit, and prioritize mechanism-resolved, temporally programmed bioactivity, rigorous controls, clinically relevant models/endpoints, and scalable manufacturing.
evidence_items.title: Functional hydrogel dressings for skin wound healing: from materials to clinical translation

organizations: Independent Researcher, Seoul, Republic of Korea
Mirae Asset Securities, Seoul, Republic of Korea
EY Consulting, Seoul, Republic of Korea
Korea University, Seoul, Republic of Korea

Pusan National University, Busan, Republic of Korea
evidence_items.summary: Trading cost for a broad cross-sectional portfolio should be computed by aggregating conditional displayed-depth cost across its constituent orders. Order-level cost varies with contract, side, notional, and the contemporaneous L2 state. We propose SlipClock, a point-in-time benchmark that selects the universe using historical information, applies a common submission-time feasibility policy, and prices each resulting frozen order against minute-level L2 states. Its estimand is static VWAP cost relative to the midpoint, conditional on filling the order entirely from displayed depth. Across 494,116,530 minute–contract states for Binance USD-margined futures from January 2024 through April 2026, costs varied systematically with clock time, universe, and per-contract order size. In an accounting decomposition of the cross-fitted high–low clock contrast, the half-spread accounted for about 1%, while the remaining 99% was attributed to filling against displayed depth beyond the best quote. Broader portfolios also cost more at the same submitted gross. Point-in-time universe selection produced mean costs 1.85–2.64 times those under ex-post selection. Mean conditional costs ranged from 6.709 to 56.111 bp across five strategies, including an MLP. Applying the same constant trading cost to every strategy cannot represent these strategy-specific differences. SlipClock evaluates each strategy’s submitted, liquidity-gated orders under the same displayed-depth cost rule. The code is available at https://github.com/Ginger-Tec/SlipClock.
evidence_items.title: SlipClock: A Conditional Displayed-Depth Cost Benchmark for Evaluating Financial AI Strategies in Crypto Futures

evidence_items.summary: Financial multi-agent systems distribute evidence extraction, expectation retrieval, consistency checking, decision, and settlement across roles. When a final claim is wrong, outcome accuracy cannot say where the evidence chain first broke or which role was responsible. We formulate financial multi-agent workflow auditing: given a typed workflow trace, detect whether a fault occurred, classify its root cause, and localize the earliest responsible agent and step. We introduce the Financial Agent Audit Benchmark (FAAB) for that task, built from 300 real point-in-time SEC and I/B/E/S workflows and pairing 300 untouched clean controls with 700 minimal single-point interventions over 14 fault classes spanning evidence, financial semantics, time, coordination, and settlement. Expert executable contracts detect every controlled fault at a zero clean false-positive rate and localize every responsible role and step, at no inference cost. A single-call LLM judge and a three-call debate reading the identical trace are substantially less reliable, particularly on clean-workflow calibration and causal localization. Capability alone does not close that gap in the useful direction. Across three models from two vendors, stronger free-form judges buy root causes with clean work: root-cause accuracy rises from 38.9% to 83.4% while clean false positives rise from 7.5% to 15.4%. Requiring the same model’s claims to survive execution reverses the trade: handed the same stated control surface plus deterministic arithmetic, date, retrieval, and hash tools, the strongest model reaches 100% detection at 1.7% clean false positives on unused issuers. On a handoff representation held out from training, expert contracts and that execution-bound auditor each recover all ten cases, while controls compiled from the training examples and the same model judging free-form recover none. Reliable auditing therefore depends less on how capable the auditor is, or on whether it is rule-based or model-based, than on whether the workflow exposes financially meaningful state through controls that are explicitly stated and mechanically verified. Adding auditors does not create auditability; designing for verification does.
evidence_items.title: FAAB: A Benchmark for Fault Detection and Responsibility Attribution in Financial Multi-Agent Workflows

evidence_items.summary: Most financial benchmarks test what a model knows about finance, not whether an agent can complete operational finance work safely. We introduce the Collections and Accounts Receivable Benchmark (CARB) for AR agents. Its 168 tasks cover cash application, collections, customer communication, promise extraction, deduction decisions, and ledger analytics. Each one starts from a complete fictional ledger and ends with a structured work product. Of 969 grading criteria, 940 (97%) are deterministic checks against the ledger and hidden truth. Correctness also includes safe rejection when the evidence does not support an action. Every task runs in two modes: rendered ledger context and read-only tools. Across four models from three providers, performance falls into clear tiers. Most models handle well-evidenced work, such as matching a payment to its invoices or extracting a promised payment date. They struggle with ledger-wide work: exact analytics requires tools, and complete collections worklists are produced by only one frontier model—and it is not the model that leads analytics. Tools raise every model’s overall score; in each case, an agent that can query the records outperforms the same model reading them in one pass. Yet tool access weakens safe rejection for two of the four models. We run every task twice to test robustness. Scores barely change on well-evidenced work in the second run, but they fall on ledger-wide tasks. CARB separates these failures—access, policy application, safety, and repeatability—in operational AR work.
evidence_items.title: CARB: A Verifiable Benchmark for Accounts-Receivable Agents

evidence_items.summary: Trusted Platform Module (TPM) and Physically Unclonable Function (PUF) are two complementary building blocks of hardware-rooted security: the former offers a standardized, Trusted Computing Group (TCG)-compliant interface for key management, integrity measurement, and attestation, while the latter derives device-unique secrets directly from uncontrollable manufacturing variations rather than from static, extractable storage. This paper presents a simulation framework that integrates a TPM 2.0 model with a PUF challenge-response subsystem inside the gem5 full-system simulator, targeting the RISC-V architecture, and extends it with a fine-grained latency-characterization methodology. The TPM command dispatcher and the PUF challenge-response path were instrumented with a dedicated statistics group that records per-command and per-sub-phase latency using both gem5's discrete-event tick counter and host wall-clock timing, the latter reinjected into the simulated timeline as a Programmed I/O (PIO) delay. Using four bare-metal authorization scenarios (unsalted Hash-based Message Authentication Code (HMAC), password-based, salted HMAC, and Non-Volatile (NV)-storage), each replicated to separate genuine signal from measurement noise via the Coefficient of Variation (CV), we show that (i) HMAC-based authorization is roughly 35X more expensive than password-based authorization, (ii) the PUF computation itself, rather than TPM protocol or authentication logic, dominates challenge-response latency, (iii) disk I/O and Rivest-Shamir-Adleman (RSA) key-setup operations are the principal sources of measurement variance, and (iv) PUF computation cost is essentially flat across challenge sizes from 16 to 128 bytes, indicating a fixed-overhead-dominated cost model for the current generic PUF implementation. These results characterize the performance envelope of a TPM-PUF root of trust on RISC-V, identify the specific sub-operations that would most benefit from hardware acceleration or architectural redesign, and establish that such a root of trust can be built, instrumented, and characterized inside gem5 at all - a preliminary foundation for future work benchmarking these results against physical hardware.
evidence_items.title: Toward Trustworthy Simulation-Based Security Evaluation: A TPM-PUF Root of Trust for RISC-V in gem5

evidence_items.summary: A generative limit order book (LOB) model approximates the distribution of a window of order messages given a conditioning state, for use as a market simulator. LOB-Bench evaluates such a model by reducing the generated and real streams to microstructure features and comparing their distributions, and its market impact metrics are likewise read from the stream the model produces. These are observational, while a simulator is used to ask how the book responds when an order is placed, which is an interventional question. Testing a simulator’s responsiveness to placed orders is established practice for agent-based, stochastic and learned simulators, but it is absent from LOB-Bench and has not been applied to the token-level autoregressive models LOB-Bench scores highest. This paper designs and analyses this test for a converged autoregressive state-space model. Orders are forced into the rollout under a do-operator, applied to the book and encoded into the model’s conditioning stream, and the response is read from a paired same-context decomposition against an unforced branch. The primary variable is the ratio of order size to the volume resting at the best ask rather than order size in shares, since the share count that clears the level differs in every window. When the ratio is a quarter the model does not detectably respond to the order and at a half it responds weakly, whereas at and above one the response grows with size at every horizon measured, reaching 0.95 of the prevailing spread at three times the resting volume. This is four times the displacement the order would produce mechanically on the book as it stood at injection, and relative to that frozen-book baseline most of it is generated by the model. Withholding the order from the model’s conditioning, so that it changes the book without being described, decreases its contribution by a margin that widens with size above the threshold, which locates the model’s sensitivity to order size in the message rather than in the book state. Two noise floors, a placebo intervention that cannot move the price and replicate pairs with no intervention, bound the precision available at each horizon.
evidence_items.title: Interventional Evaluation of a Generative Limit Order Book Model

evidence_items.summary: Financial-reporting models are often validated against labels derived from post-filing records generated by selective regulatory review, issuer filings, or public disclosure. Because these records need not represent the same institutional event, chronological separation alone does not determine what reported performance can support. We define a filing-origin evaluation specification linking five elements: filing origin, point-in-time information set, label-maturity rule, outcome definition, and intended score use. We apply it to three issuer-level 365-day outcomes: constructed correspondence episodes based on U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) submissions, periodic-report amendments, and Form 8-K Item 4.02 non-reliance disclosures. The public-source benchmark contains 96,734 issuer–fiscal-year observations. Eight rolling-origin folds (2017–2024) use point-in-time predictors and training origins whose outcome windows have closed. All-feature extreme gradient boosting models yield fold-mean average precision (AP) above prevalence for correspondence (0.4276 vs. 0.2610), amendments (0.3385 vs. 0.1540), and Item 4.02 (0.0603 vs. 0.0219). Issuer-cluster intervals for the three mean AP–prevalence gaps remain positive after multiplicity adjustment; Item 4.02 ranking also persists after excluding Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) 6770 blank-check observations from the evaluation cohort. Ranking remains above prevalence across episode definitions and learner pipelines. Over six eligible folds, raw Brier skill is negative relative to a mature-history forecast for all three outcomes. Past-only Platt recalibration yields mean historical-relative skill of 0.0991, 0.0815, and -0.0083, respectively. Among high-confidence links to an external restatement panel, outcome prevalence among reference positives is 1.03, 1.92, and 8.54 times unconditional prevalence. Because the Item 4.02 comparison shares a non-reliance recording mechanism, it supports cross-source alignment rather than independent construct validation. Ranking therefore supports outcome-specific retrospective prioritization, without by itself establishing probability quality or validation across outcomes.
evidence_items.title: Validating Financial-Reporting Models with Delayed Labels and Distinct Regulatory and Reporting Outcomes

evidence_items.summary: Aggregate trade policy uncertainty can inform forecasts of downside firm earnings. This study examines Gaussian forecast coverage and compares exposure refinements with direct tail estimation. Earnings-at-Risk is the conditional fifth percentile of next-quarter return on assets. The retrospective evaluation covers 402,780 of 538,484 firm-quarters across 65 origins from 2010Q1 to 2026Q1. Tariff windows are 2018Q1–2019Q4 and 2025Q1–2026Q1, defined by forecast origin. The Gaussian refinement adds measured exposure and historical firm volatility. Its exceedance rate is 14.79 percent, compared with 15.84 percent for the aggregate benchmark and 4.96 percent for direct quantile estimation. A pooled conformal correction reduces Gaussian coverage errors but leaves size-group failures. Linear conformal quantile forecasts breach 11.35 percent among the largest tenth despite near-nominal pooled coverage. Size-quartile calibration and nonlinear fitting improve quartile coverage in this panel. The contribution is a common-panel comparison of exposure, tail estimation and calibration. The findings support direct quantile benchmarks and size-group coverage checks in the tested setting.
evidence_items.title: A Pooled Exceedance Rate Hides Two Failures in Firm Earnings-at-Risk Under Trade Policy Uncertainty

evidence_items.summary: Despite the rapid development of fuzzing techniques for PHP web applications, the community still lacks a unified, high-quality benchmark for rigorous evaluation. Existing evaluation methods suffer from imbalanced vulnerability distributions, the omission of hard-to-find bugs, and unverified ground truths, leading to skewed and unreliable evaluation results. To address this, we introduce PHPBench, the first framework for automatically constructing verifiable and hierarchical vulnerability benchmarks for PHP web fuzzers. PHPBench's approach is threefold. First, it generates diverse vulnerability variants from real-world vulnerabilities by systematically weakening existing security protections, creating a varied distribution of exploitation complexity. Second, given a set of target PHP web applications, PHPBench further selects ideal code locations to insert the generated vulnerability variants, ensuring high realism. Finally, PHPBench automatically synthesizes verifiable Proofs-of-Concept (PoCs) to guarantee the exploitability of every inserted vulnerability. In the evaluation, PHPBench successfully generated 375 unique vulnerability variants from merely 28 high-quality known vulnerability causes and inserted them into 10 popular PHP applications, covering 197 distinct functionalities. Each inserted vulnerability was verified to possess 100.00% exploitability while maintaining functional integrity. Finally, we utilize this curated fuzzing benchmark to evaluate seven existing fuzzing tools and reveal their systemic weaknesses, providing critical insights for future work and highlighting the limitations of current ad-hoc evaluation practices.
evidence_items.title: PHPBench: Automated Generation of Verifiable and Hierarchical Benchmarks for PHP Web Fuzzing

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Visual Foundation Models (VFMs), such as DINO and CLIP, excel in semantic understanding of images but exhibit limited spatial reasoning capabilities, which limits their applicability to embodied systems. As a result, recent work has incorporated some 3D tasks (such as depth estimation) into VFM training. However, VFM performance remains inconsistent across other spatial tasks, raising the question of whether these models truly possess spatial awareness or overfit to specific 3D objectives. To address this question, we introduce the Spatial Relation Recognition Task (SpaRRTa) benchmark, which evaluates the ability of VFMs to identify static directional relations between visible objects. Unlike traditional 3D objectives that focus on precise metric prediction (e.g., surface normal estimation), SpaRRTa probes a fundamental capability underpinning more advanced forms of human-like spatial understanding. SpaRRTa generates an arbitrary number of photorealistic images with diverse scenes and fully controllable object arrangements, along with freely accessible spatial annotations. Evaluating a range of state-of-the-art VFMs, we reveal significant disparities in their ability to encode directional spatial relations. Through our analysis, we provide insights into the mechanisms that support or hinder this form of spatial awareness in modern VFMs. We hope that SpaRRTa will serve as a useful tool for guiding the development of future spatially aware visual models. Our project page can be found at https://sparrta.gmum.net/ .
evidence_items.title: SpaRRTa: A Synthetic Benchmark for Evaluating Spatial Intelligence in Visual Foundation Models
