TRUSTWORTHY QUANTUM AI FOR REHABILITATION RESEARCH F076-F080 | SCIENTIFIC TECHNICAL NOTEBOOK | RESEARCH WORKING EDITION Prospective | Nonclinical | Falsifiable | Reproducible | Unbuilt Research Concepts 33 x STARLI OPENING ESSAY | THE AUTHORITY A MODEL DOES NOT HAVE A predictive score is a statement about a model conditional on the data and assumptions that produced it. It is not evidence that the model has identified a causal neural mechanism. It is not permission to issue a physical command. It is not a clinical outcome. This family studies the boundaries between those three categories. The central object is a synthetic offline audit environment, designed so that the model may succeed, the ordinary rival may win, or a safety policy may correctly refuse the request. Five separate flagship questions meet at the same test bench. F076 tests the intervention fidelity of explanations; F077 asks whether unfamiliar inputs can be recognized before acceptance; F078 audits the source lineage and disparate failures that can manufacture attractive evaluation scores; F079 gives authorization a separate and explicit place in the decision path; F080 measures the usefulness of quantum-labelled computation after whole-pipeline cost. Each flagship has its own failure conditions. Their coupling is useful only if interfaces are causal, auditable and independently replaceable. Interpretability is especially vulnerable to beautiful output. Heatmaps, feature masks and counterfactual diagrams can look precise while merely expressing local correlation or an approximate post hoc surrogate. A serious explanatory claim tells the next investigator which feasible feature intervention will change the prediction and which independent witness can confirm it. A neural feature that was never intervened on cannot be declared causal from the color of a plot. Distribution shifts change the meaning of confidence. The familiar recording can be transformed by a new electrode montage, a different clock, an unknown class or missing-channel patterns. A detector that recognizes only the noise signatures on which it was trained may appear successful while failing precisely where a reliable refusal is needed. This is why F077 preserves selective risk, coverage, false acceptance and the full latency of the veto, not just aggregate classification accuracy. Leakage often survives a superficial audit. A synthetic source can be transformed into many nearly identical examples. The copied signals may receive new filenames, be presented as a different session or pass through a normalization fitted on the entire dataset. A high score on this partition does not demonstrate that the proposed quantum model has learned generalizable neural dynamics. F078 requires source ancestry, label availability at inference time, group balance and versioned data contracts before model comparison. Human authorization has a different grammar from prediction. A permission token may be valid for one task and forbidden for another; a model version may change while a previously signed policy does not. An operator may revoke consent after inference begins. These are not situations to be resolved by increasing confidence thresholds. A correct engineering design makes the action envelope an intersection of scope, role, time and safety, independently auditable after both successful and refused requests. In this book the commands remain inert simulations. Quantum performance remains an open empirical question for the present application. A systematic review of quantum machine learning in digital health, DOI 10.1038/s41746-025-01597-z, did not find a consistent empirical advantage over classical methods. That does not forbid the search for new architectures. It does require clean experiments. Encoding overhead, noisy operations, repeated runs, queueing, mitigation, hardware drift and classical tuning all belong to a practical utility comparison. A result below the preregistered benefit threshold must be allowed to stop the search. The five-stage parallel spacetime method organizes scientific uncertainty into origin questions, mathematical proposals, competing explanations, bounded stress worlds and independently reconstructable evidence. This phrase describes intellectual branches, not physical travel through alternative universes. The stages are most useful when a late counterfactual changes what we thought we knew at the beginning. No stage gives special permission to call a hypothesis established. A technical notebook does not repeat an entire research monograph line by line. It attempts to show why a researcher would care about an experiment, how instruments might mislead, and what interpretation could survive a fair adversary. Repeated concepts are welcome when their role deepens; recycled paragraphs masquerading as new research are not. This notebook uses Mechanism, Measurement and Refutation not as decorative labels but as obligations that make one another more exact. The research is deliberately nonclinical. It uses synthetic and authorized nonclinical proxies, inert test-bench decisions and invented stress scenarios. The proposal does not support diagnosis, implantation, robotic stroke rehabilitation or therapeutic claims. Clinical translation would require a separately approved, prospective, human-subject program with its own risk and endpoint design. Neither this document nor its figures can supply that evidence. The future reader may inherit much better hardware and different methods for causality, uncertainty or governance. If our circuits look primitive, the questions remain: what was actually measured, which part was guessed, where did the permission come from, what ordinary explanation could prevail, and who can reproduce the result? A living research civilization does not demand that its first equations remain sacred. It tries to leave an apparatus for self-correction. THE FIVE DISTINCT FLAGSHIP CONTRACTS F076 | Explainability of Quantum AI Models for Rehabilitation at the Limit Falsifiable proposed mechanism: test whether feature-level interventions change model explanations and predictions consistently under a frozen causal hypothesis. Declared primary observables: counterfactual fidelity [1], explanation stability [1], calibration gap [1], audit time [s]. The ordinary or confounded world proposes that a saliency map follows correlated noise or a post hoc surrogate rather than the model decision. The concealed discriminating test should blindly perturb one neural feature while preserving its nuisance-correlated partner. Instrumental evidence: frozen synthetic EEG-like feature traces [normalized], plausible intervention support [1], explanation audit logs [1] and independent causal labels [1]. A strong baseline is feature ablation, sparse logistic models, calibrated gradient boosting and causally constrained classical surrogate explanations under identical data and access. These are plans and measurement contracts only, not records of achieved effect or human treatment. F077 | Out-of-Distribution Detection in Quantum Rehabilitation AI at the Limit Falsifiable proposed mechanism: detect unfamiliar EEG acquisition regimes and refuse unsupported inference before any simulated control action. Declared primary observables: OOD AUROC [1], selective risk [1], false-acceptance [1], refusal latency [s]. The ordinary or confounded world proposes that shift scores measure recording artifacts or test-set tuning rather than genuinely unsupported states. The concealed discriminating test should hide a center-specific acquisition defect and replace a high-impairment synthetic test subgroup. Instrumental evidence: held-out sensor arrays [mV], acquisition timestamps [ms], unseen-site shift manifests, accept/reject flags [1] and dispatch times [s]. A strong baseline is deep ensemble and conformal selective prediction, classical density models and transparent acquisition-quality rules with equally tuned thresholds. These are plans and measurement contracts only, not records of achieved effect or human treatment. F078 | Data Leakage and Bias Control in Quantum Rehabilitation AI at the Limit Falsifiable proposed mechanism: separate individual/session/center provenance and audit false performance improvements across synthetic subgroups. Declared primary observables: leakage exposure fraction [1], subgroup calibration gap [1], false-positive disparity [1]. The ordinary or confounded world proposes that participant overlap, batch identity or label timestamp leaks the holdout answer. The concealed discriminating test should plant blinded duplicate source fingerprints and evaluate a locked independent subgroup. Instrumental evidence: source genealogy hashes, session identifiers, timestamp manifests [ms], subgroup sizes [count] and sealed evaluation outcomes [1]. A strong baseline is grouped nested cross-validation, strict temporal split, classical feature leakage audits and equal-cost subgroup calibration analysis. These are plans and measurement contracts only, not records of achieved effect or human treatment. F079 | Human Oversight and Authorization of Quantum Rehabilitation Decisions at the Limit Falsifiable proposed mechanism: enforce a versioned authorization-policy intersection before any model suggestion can be executed in an inert test sandbox. Declared primary observables: unauthorized action rate [1], revocation latency [ms], false-denial rate [1], audit trail coverage [1]. The ordinary or confounded world proposes that human consent is inferred from a stale token or a policy exception hidden in the interface. The concealed discriminating test should expire a synthetic authorization and revoke permission during an otherwise successful trial. Instrumental evidence: synthetic signed policy tokens, scope lists, version hashes, consent expiry clocks [ms] and complete inert action logs. A strong baseline is ordinary role-based access policy, signed consent records, deterministic fail-closed interlocks and human stop procedures. These are plans and measurement contracts only, not records of achieved effect or human treatment. F080 | Practical Quantum AI Advantage and Research Stopping Conditions at the Limit Falsifiable proposed mechanism: compare candidate quantum/hybrid inference and matched tuned classical methods using end-to-end performance, safety and resource accounting. Declared primary observables: task utility gap [1], total wall time [s], energy [J], safety refusal error [1]. The ordinary or confounded world proposes that encoding, queueing, mitigation or retraining overhead erases a solver-only apparent gain. The concealed discriminating test should blindly add data-loading and queue costs while allowing a tuned classical model to win. Instrumental evidence: raw input bytes, preprocessing and circuit simulation logs, queue durations [s], modeled hardware power [W] and matched classical results. A strong baseline is strong tuned classical SVM, gradient boosting, calibrated neural networks and full-metered classical optimization matched for safety and data. These are plans and measurement contracts only, not records of achieved effect or human treatment.

QUANTUM SENSING AND STROKE NEUROREHABILITATION F166-F170 | FAMILY 34 | FIVE-FLAGSHIP SCIENTIFIC TECHNICAL NOTEBOOK 33 × STARLI | The companion to the 819-page nonclinical research monograph EVIDENCE BOUNDARY: every 3D map is an analytic synthetic sensitivity model. No measured human cortex, clinical neuroplasticity, therapeutic benefit or quantum hardware sensing advantage is reported.   A LETTER FROM THE THIRTY-FOURTH RESEARCH FAMILY A more sensitive magnetic sensor is not necessarily a more truthful neural-source instrument. The first flagship separates a known cortical magnetic surrogate from independent drive coils. The second asks if EEG–magnetic fusion survives hidden reference and artifact swaps. The third distinguishes genuine synthetic network changes from a shared magnetic driver. The fourth measures blind source timing versus cue alignment. The fifth asks whether a more costly magnetic sensor changes a safe nonclinical decision at all. The common nonclinical platform contains a known-source magnetic phantom with blind drive-coil artifacts, synthetic EEG-like signals, independent acquisition clocks and a held-out sensing-decision benchmark. None of these tests establishes empirical quantum utility, clinical motor intention, physical patient safety or improvement after stroke. The companion PDF preserves the 819-page research architecture: 30 dimensionally specified equations, 42 fully recomputable 3D analytic sensitivity grids, 82 chapters of six progressive Mechanism–Measurement–Refutation pages, 200 Research Gates and 33 unbuilt Phoenix prototypes. This notebook opens with nine title-led scientific descriptions and all five official 4D F166–F170 titles for accurate publication discovery. The research workflow couples known-source magnetic phantoms, EEG reference swaps, common-driver graph tests, independent timing, full-cost sensing value and successor reconstruction. FAMILY 34 OFFICIAL QUANTUM-SENSING FLAGSHIP TITLES / PUBLICATION DISCOVERY F166 | Quantum Magnetometry of Post-Stroke Motor Cortex Signals at the Limit Core research mechanism: source-resolved quantum magnetometry of a nonliving motor-cortex field surrogate. Independent counterworld: common-mode field contamination or adjacent 4D microrobotic magnetic actuation masquerades as a cortical source. Proposed blind test: randomize independent cortical-field phantom and drive-coil polarity while blind-hiding source identity; require reconstruction against an external current and field reference. Evidential limit: nonliving phantom cortical dipoles, isolated magnetic drive coils and analytical magnetic-source surrogates; no measured patient cortex. F167 | Quantum Sensing–EEG Multimodal Fusion at the Limit Core research mechanism: EEG–magnetic fusion with independent reference, time-base and leakage controls. Independent counterworld: shared task cues, an EEG reference swap or muscle and eye artifacts produce spurious multimodal agreement. Proposed blind test: blindly swap EEG references, remove one sensing modality, inject ocular and electromyographic nuisance signals and quantify whether apparent fusion gains survive true independent source labels. Evidential limit: synthetic EEG-like electrical waveforms and independently driven magnetic phantom signals only; no human intention or clinical EEG evidence. F168 | Quantum Sensing of Post-Stroke Neural Network Changes at the Limit Core research mechanism: network-change identifiability in synthetic post-stroke neural connectivity surrogates. Independent counterworld: a single common magnetic driver or source leakage makes an unchanged synthetic network appear reorganized. Proposed blind test: embed an unchanged neural network behind a changing common-source artifact, then conceal both and ask estimators to identify which condition actually changed. Evidential limit: known synthetic multichannel oscillators with separate magnetic nuisance injection; not evidence of human stroke neuroplasticity. F169 | Quantum Sensing and Post-Stroke Motor Intention Synchronization at the Limit Core research mechanism: temporal agreement of surrogate motor-intention labels with independent magnetic and actuation clocks. Independent counterworld: visual prompts, muscle-like artifact bursts or clock drift align with the task and falsely certify a motor-intention event. Proposed blind test: randomize no-intent periods and hidden cue jitter; offset one device clock and require the method to abstain when onset ordering cannot be independently confirmed. Evidential limit: offline event labels, synthetic magnetic streams and isolated nonliving controller timing fixtures; not verified patient motor intention. F170 | Incremental Value of Quantum Neural Sensing for Rehabilitation Decisions at the Limit Core research mechanism: incremental decision value of a magnetic quantum sensing candidate above simpler measurements. Independent counterworld: gain arises from privileged data, a weak baseline or omission of sensor readout, shielding, preprocessing and false-trigger costs. Proposed blind test: conceal which sensor is quantum-enabled, rerun decisions with all acquisition costs and adversarially equalized simpler baselines, then compare full-outcome utility and abstention. Evidential limit: synthetic bench decisions on simulated phantom and signal states; no clinical prescription or stroke-recovery evidence. I. NINE TITLE-LED SCIENTIFIC DESCRIPTIONS AND FIVE FURTHER PRELUDES 01 | F166–F170: Official Quantum Sensing and Stroke Neurorehabilitation Titles This family begins with five distinct research questions: source-resolved motor-cortex magnetometry, EEG and quantum magnetic fusion, network change identifiability, motor-intent synchronization, and decision value after complete sensing costs. The title inventory is a searchable publication map, not a declaration of clinical findings. Take source-resolved quantum magnetometry of a nonliving motor-cortex field surrogate as a specific case. The proposed source model says a calibrated optically pumped or other quantum-sensitive magnetic measurement can separate a known cortical-field surrogate from external actuator fields only when source identity, sensor distance and nuisance gradients are independently measured. The rival explanation says common-mode field contamination or adjacent 4D microrobotic magnetic actuation masquerades as a cortical source. A research team should randomize independent cortical-field phantom and drive-coil polarity while blind-hiding source identity; require reconstruction against an external current and field reference and report field amplitude [fT], spectral noise density [T/sqrt(Hz)], source error [mm], sensitivity [T/sqrt(Hz)] and false source fraction [1]. Only a blinded difference that survives a strong comparison could justify a narrower technical claim. The most important practical inheritance is an externally calibrated reference magnetometer and a blind source-coil current ledger. Compare with a calibrated conventional magnetic reference, gradiometric subtraction and source-known synthetic forward-field reconstruction at identical shielding and sample budgets. Preserve sensor batches, artifact transients, calibration, exclusions and all test attempts; refuse if source attribution fails, residual ambient field exceeds the preregistered domain, sensor saturation occurs or a localization error cannot be independently bounded. Any proposal involving people or implanted robotic devices would require an entirely new ethics, device safety and applicable regulatory review.

evidence_items.summary: Despite established consensus about the individuality of brain physiology and structural changes, current neuroimaging biomarker paradigms heavily rely on population averages. Here, we define normativity not as a single reference point but as a landscape of permissible configurations arising from diverse physiological manifestations. We introduce the Nearest Neighbor Normativity (N3) framework, designed to parse the natural heterogeneity in brain structural measurements into a diversity-aware biomarker of brain structural decline. Through repeated comparisons within different demographic subgroups, N3 contextualizes an individual’s measurements from several viewpoints along the aging continuum. Relying on local density estimation, it accommodates multiple, shared normative configurations within and across age groups. We use T1-weighted MRI data from 29,883 individuals for training and 7,013 individuals for validation, and benchmark our framework against Brain Age models and Normative Modeling. We evaluate each biomarker’s ability to detect neurodegenerative diseases, using them as representative models of atypical brain structural decline. In group-level analyses, the N3 biomarker shows the largest effect sizes in the detection of Mild Cognitive Impairment, Alzheimer’s Disease, and Frontotemporal Dementia. Similarly, the N3 biomarker achieves the highest predictive performance in the classification of neurodegenerative diseases on a single subject level. Notably, the N3 estimates remain stable across age and robust to compositional changes in the reference sample. Finally, correlation analyses indicate that it captures distinct and complementary aspects of brain structural variation compared to existing approaches. Our findings underscore that rethinking normativity assessments to explicitly accommodate natural inter-individual variability can advance our collective efforts toward truly personalized patient care. Brain aging varies greatly between individuals, yet standard medical tools rely on population averages that may miss important individual differences. We developed a method called Nearest Neighbor Normativity (N3) that assesses brain health by searching for similar configurations along the aging spectrum and their likelihood, rather than to a single average. Using MRI scans from nearly 37,000 people, we tested whether this framework could detect brain changes associated with mild cognitive impairment, Alzheimer’s disease and frontotemporal dementia. The N3 method outperformed existing approaches, distinguishing disease-related brain changes from natural aging effects more accurately. This work suggests that personalized medical assessments accounting for natural human diversity may improve our ability to detect brain diseases early and support more targeted interventions. Leenings et al. methodologically reformulate neuroimaging standards to explicitly account for natural inter-individual variability of brain physiology. Applied to brain structural decline, the result is a diversity-aware biomarker which improves the detection of disease signals in both statistical and machine learning analyses.
evidence_items.title: Contextualizing biological heterogeneity in brain structural normativity assessments across the aging continuum with the nearest neighbor normativity framework

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The chapter consists of a new integrated cyber-physical systems and deep Earth observation for real-time stewardship of the environment. By combining the distributed sensor networks with sophisticated artificial intelligence models, the strategy redefines the way environmental monitoring is conducted, moving from passively gathering data to a more active and responsive approach. A key point of interest is the trade-off between inference-latency-accuracy, where using models at the network edge necessitates trade-offs between fast hazard detection and limited computational resources, while still maintaining scientific reliability. This change is part of deep learning. Periodic structures such as long short-term memory (LSTMs) and gated recurrent units are able to model the temporal relationships in hydrological systems and can be applied to successfully predict river discharge and climate variability. Super-resolution generative adversarial networks also enhance the capability of observation for higher resolution information that is generated from lower quality data sources. These features can be extended to executable governance, making it a decision support system. Deep reinforcement learning is the most effective method of optimization of complex resource allocation tasks, and digital twins are used to simulate environmental scenarios to evaluate policies. Autonomous environmental grids and quantum machine learning could become an ecosystem of smart, self-governing systems, which may help to balance the ecological system at a planetary level.

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are frontier deep learning systems that have achieved remarkable success across a wide range of AI services. However, their substantial computational and memory requirements make them difficult to deploy and run on local hardware. Due to these resource requirements, users often rely on untrusted cloud infrastructure providers to perform model inference. However, outsourcing introduces the challenge of verifying that the returned output is the genuine result of the specified model. In this work, we present DeepProve, the first system to enable efficient end-to-end verification of full LLM inference (i.e., for all generated tokens of a prompt) on untrusted cloud servers using zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs). In contrast, prior work either provides only a proof-of-concept partial implementation for a single token (zkGPT, USENIX '25), or focuses exclusively on specific components of the inference pipeline, such as Softmax (zkLLM, CCS '24). DeepProve achieves end-to-end verification by certifying the correctness of the output sequence rather than encoding the expensive inference computation in-circuit, an approach that would require either circuit size quadratic in the sequence length or costly in-circuit modelling of RAM operations. The core building blocks of DeepProve are sum-check protocol and lookup arguments, which enable efficient proof of correctness of all operators needed for GPT-2 and Gemma 3, such as multi-head attention and layer normalization for GPT-2, and grouped-query attention, root mean square normalization, and rotary positional embeddings for Gemma 3. Our evaluation shows that DeepProve can prove inference of GPT-2 and Gemma 3 at approximately 174 and 86 tokens per minute, respectively, which is 20-60× faster than the state-of-the-art, without any significant loss in accuracy. Verification takes only 1 to 3.7 seconds. By distributing proof computation across multiple nodes, DeepProve can further improve the prover time while reducing the memory requirements for individual machines. With distributed proving, DeepProve can scale the throughput to 1855 tokens per minute. Our work represents the first full system for end-to-end LLM inference verification, thus paving the way for secure and trustworthy AI services.
evidence_items.title: DeepProve: Verifiable End-to-End Large Language Model Inference

evidence_items.summary: Background: Large language models (LLMs) are solely judged by their scores on biomedical benchmarks, yet these scores are rarely reproducible since the prompts, inference settings and model builds are seldom reported. We developed BenchmarkHub, an open-source platform for auditable evaluation of language and vision-language models for biomedical research. Methods: BenchmarkHub is a Python web application (Django 5.2, SQLite) released under the MIT licence and available at https://github.com/juanjuanignacio/benchmarkhub. The application can be accessed through a browser interface, a set of command-line tools and a REST API, so interactive exploration and scripted pipelines produce identical, comparable records. The platform samples questions with fixed seeds, runs models directly or as tool-using agents in a code sandbox, grades answers with deterministic rules and stores every prompt, reply and tool call. The interface provides a leaderboard to rank performance of the models, allowing model comparison without any preexisting programming knowledge. Findings: We used BenchmarkHub to evaluate 12 open-weight models in five experiments on 15 biomedical benchmarks (11 text, two multimodal and two computational biology) and two general benchmarks. The pooled accuracy ranged from 46.1% (95% CI 43.0-49.3) to 80.9% (78.3-83.3). Re-grading the responses with simple answer-extraction rules lowered a model's accuracy by up to 33.1 percentage points, leading to a reorder of the leaderboard. Published scores were found for 23 out of the 143 benchmark/model combinations tested. The accuracy measured by BenchmarkHub was lower than in the published results in 19 out of the 23 available comparisons. The effect of four prompting protocols (1: default prompt; 2: asking the model to answer the letter only; 3: chain-of-thought prompting; 4: three-shot prompting) changed MedQA accuracy by up to 11.3 points but was not significant after multiple-testing correction with 150 questions.
evidence_items.title: BenchmarkHub: an open-source platform for reproducible evaluation of large language models in healthcare

evidence_items.summary: The enormous growth of IoT networks and security risks has encouraged research into intrusion detection, which is based on deep learning methods. IoT network security is an essential concern, and intrusion detection solutions are required to secure the network. In this study, we developed an LSTM-based model to detect various attacks in the IoT system. The filter correlation approach is used for selecting features, while data augmentation techniques SMOTE and GAN are used to address the class imbalance issue. The Pearson correlation method reduces the features after selecting one feature out of two having a correlation value more than the 0.95 (threshold) value. The minority attack classes DoS and Fuzzers are increased by generating synthetic data using data augmentation techniques SMOTE and GAN. The model used the UNSW-NB 15 dataset and is evaluated on various parameters. The findings indicated that the GAN-LSTM model attained an accuracy of 92%, outperforming other models with high precision values, and it improved both the overall accuracy and the accuracy of the minority class. The explainable AI methods LIME and SHAP are implemented to explain the model prediction and also find the prominent feature to build trust in the model prediction.
evidence_items.title: Enhancing IoT intrusion detection using an LSTM-based deep learning model with GAN and explainable AI

4D MICROROBOTIC NEURAL SIGNAL SENSING F126-F130 | FAMILY 26 | FIVE-FLAGSHIP SCIENTIFIC TECHNICAL NOTEBOOK 33 × STARLI | The companion to the 819-page nonclinical research monograph EVIDENCE BOUNDARY: all 3D sensitivity surfaces and neural-like waveform scenarios are synthetic analytic examples. The manuscript reports no patient investigation, no demonstrated therapy benefit, no quantum advantage and no automated clinical decisions.   A LETTER FROM THE TWENTY-SIXTH RESEARCH FAMILY A measured voltage is not yet a neuronal event. In a sealed saline-tank phantom, the five flagships test whether a known injected source is separable from common-reference pickup, whether multipoint timing is genuine, whether filtering preserves true events, whether calibration survives sensor-version changes, and whether a confident false event forces rejection. Each mechanism requires a different adversarial test and independent witness. F126 separates known injected microvolt waveforms from electrochemical and shared-reference artifacts. F127 measures independently verified interchannel lag under hidden clock slips. F128 tests waveform preservation under electromagnetic interference and aggressive filtering. F129 challenges frozen calibration across wetting histories and sensor revisions. F130 demands explicit abstention on high-confidence counterfeit electrical events. Their common platform is a sealed saline-tank phantom with nonliving electrodes and known injected voltages; no patient or neural recordings are represented. The companion PDF preserves the 819-page research architecture: 30 dimensionally stated candidate equations, 42 reproducible synthetic 3D sensitivity grids, 82 chapters of six progressive pages, 200 Research Gates and 33 unbuilt Phoenix research concepts. This notebook develops each test and counterworld in scientific prose, beginning with nine title-led descriptions suitable for a research listing. The public five-stage parallel spacetime name is a reasoning workflow, not literal spacetime physics. I. NINE TITLE-LED SCIENTIFIC DESCRIPTIONS AND FIVE FURTHER PRELUDES 01 | Flagship Identity — The Five Neural-Sensing Questions The title of this family, 4D Microrobots for Neural Signal Sensing, contains five independent claims that should not be collapsed into a single attractive recording. F126 asks which part of a microvolt waveform originates from an isolated injected source rather than microprobe motion or electrode polarization. F127 asks whether two time-aligned traces are truly synchronized or simply share a misleading clock. F128 challenges the familiar assumption that the smoothest denoised waveform is the most faithful one. F129 treats calibration as a time-limited statement that must survive changes in sensor version. F130 asks whether a high-confidence electrical event should be rejected when the physical witness is missing or contradictory. The common minimum instrument is a sealed saline tank, a deformable nonliving microelectrode, a known synthetic source and at least one independently calibrated reference. Source, detector, clock and adjudicator must be physically distinguishable. The central question is source and measurement integrity at laboratory scale, not the presence of genuine neuronal action potentials. Any improvement must be reported against an ordinary, well-tuned electrical and computational comparator under equal acquisition resources. Five flagship identities therefore create five failure denominators: unexplained voltage, source-lag error, lost genuine waveform structure, long-horizon offset drift and forbidden false acceptance. Each denominator must count failed as well as successful trials. This family makes no claim about implanted devices, patient brain activity, treatment outcomes or quantum computational advantage. Its useful inheritance would be independent refutation routes that future laboratories can rebuild. 02 | Core Three-Coupling — Sensor Motion, Independent Electrical Truth and Contested Attribution A valid coupling cannot consist merely of a deformable microelectrode beside a neural-looking trace and a sophisticated classifier. The first system is a time-varying probe or microactuator with measured geometry and motion. The second is a controlled input and its independent voltage-and-time reference, kept inaccessible to the tested estimator during blind evaluation. The third is a decision about whether the observed waveform can be attributed to that input despite electrochemical offset, common-mode pickup, motion artifact, synchronization leakage and drift. In the candidate voltage relation, the observed potential contains source, motion, electrochemical and common components, all in compatible microvolt units at a validated time. The same single recording can be explained by different mixtures. Consequently a deformation trajectory does not prove improved neural sensing, and a calibration reference that shares the candidate amplifier cannot establish independence. The interventional test changes one nuisance source while holding injected voltage fixed, then asks whether the model predicts the hidden change before the source is revealed. The coupling succeeds only within its nonclinical claim boundary when a simple external source, independent clock, ordinary fixed electrode and blind rival experiments all agree about the cause of any measured gain. If magnetic drive adds electromagnetic contamination, the candidate may look better in a familiar scenario and fail under a reversed actuation schedule. Such a loss is evidence about the coupling, not a reason to conceal the trial. 03 | Core Research Question and Scientific Boundary — What a Saline-Tank Signal Can Mean The core research question is whether a deformable microelectrode can distinguish deliberately injected electrical signals from self-generated artifacts, at a preregistered bandwidth, source amplitude, sampling rate, sensor motion and calibration history. The second part of the question is as important as the first: what observation would make the attractive explanation untenable? A separate voltage source, a blind multipoint delay, an unseen interference spectrum, a swapped sensor revision or a fabricated high-confidence event should all be able to challenge the candidate model. The permitted experimental domain is nonclinical. A sealed saline tank, inert electrode coupon and synthetic known-potential generator can approximate selected electrical boundary conditions. They cannot reproduce neuronal tissue, implant biocompatibility, inflammation, therapeutic engagement or functional stroke recovery. Even a system that perfectly recovers every injected waveform can claim only bench-source reconstruction under those particular tested conditions. Any biological interpretation requires a different approved study, different specimens, separate ethics and an independently defined clinical endpoint. Before testing, record every allowed contact state, power budget, waveform amplitude, electromagnetic interference condition, clock offset and stop trigger. Scientific refusal follows uncontrollable contact, missing calibration, invalid reference or a violation of the nonclinical scope. A strong measurement model should remain capable of saying that the source cannot be identified. 04 | Six Falsifiable Claims and Thirty Candidate Equations — A Geometry of Possible Failure The thirty candidates are organized as six per flagship and are not presented as discovered physical laws. F126 develops voltage source decomposition, reconstructed amplitude error, SNR, common-mode rejection, probe-motion coupling and an attribution margin. F127 defines lag, clock drift, jitter, phase, lag-estimator bias and synchrony admissibility. F128 develops reconstruction error, SNR improvement, true-peak preservation, false-event rate, filtering delay and a bounded loss. F129 measures offset drift, gain residual, temperature compensation, forecast error, calibration availability and cross-version discrepancy. F130 quantifies calibration error, selective risk, false acceptance, coverage, hard admissibility and abstention latency. Dimensional analysis is a requirement rather than an ornament. Voltage error is measured in microvolts; lag in microseconds or milliseconds; drift in microvolts per hour; SNR in decibels; probability and coverage as dimensionless fractions. For example, translating microsecond lag into a phase at frequency f in hertz requires the factor 10^-6 seconds per microsecond. A confusion between these units could manufacture a magnificent frequency dependence that is entirely a bookkeeping error. The corresponding 3D diagrams vary two dimensionless synthetic nuisance parameters and display a dimensionless analytical proxy. Exact recomputation of the plotted 31-by-31 grid shows that the code works; it says nothing about living neurons. Six falsification obligations apply to each flagship: identify the mechanism, forecast a hidden temporal case, beat a fair baseline, separate a rival explanation, refuse an unsafe or unsupported signal, and enable another laboratory to rebuild the failure. 05 | Five-Layer Research System — From Source Identity to Independent Reconstruction Layer one fixes the scientific object: electrode identifier, waveform generator, isolated saline chamber, measured geometry, allowed motion, legal and ethical scope and hard stop authority. A probe can move without being permitted to claim neural function. Layer two freezes traceable electrical and timing calibration, with microvolt sources, reference gain, sampling rates, environmental history and a second independent instrument. A measurement derived from the same clock or amplifier is not automatically a second witness. Layer three creates the contest. A standard microelectrode, fixed-reference acquisition, conventional clock correction, ordinary digital filtering and simple statistical calibration receive the same time, data, bandwidth, energy and tuning budgets as the proposed 4D architecture. The fourth layer blinds all contestants to deliberately concealed faults: shared common-mode error, clock jump, narrowband interference, version-induced drift or counterfeit waveform. The controller must stop or abstain when a necessary witness is invalid. Layer five places source signals, raw and corrected traces, rejected records, calibration versions, stopped trials and reproducibility code in the hands of an independent laboratory. The five layers should produce a result even when the claim is false. The scientific point is not a polished demonstration but a reconstructable decision about why a waveform was trusted or rejected. 06 | Five Research Depth Axes — Source, Synchrony, Spectral Integrity, Drift and Trust The first depth axis perturbs source identity through controlled probe movement, electrode polarization, common-mode voltage and magnetic-drive contamination. The question is whether a supposedly recovered signal remains attributable to a known independent electrical generator. The second axis challenges temporal meaning through hidden source delays, clock steps, jitter, buffering and channel exchanges. High coherence or zero-lag agreement is not evidence of a neurological network without validated timing provenance. The third axis protects waveform fidelity against the temptation of excessive artifact suppression. It introduces hidden true peaks alongside electromagnetic interference and probe-motion noise, then scores original source reconstruction, true-event preservation and false-event rates under an identical digital-compute budget. The fourth axis extends time through temperature changes, wetting history and sensor-version replacement; a calibration that depends on seeing held-out data must be reported as unverified. The fifth axis makes abstention a measurable engineering outcome. Missing independent witnesses, contaminated validators and counterfeit high-confidence events require refusal instead of confident classification. These five depth axes are related but not exchangeable: better waveform SNR cannot compensate a lost reference clock, and lower drift cannot validate a fabricated source. Each axis supplies its own unit-bearing measurements and a different research door for the next generation. 07 | Measurable Endpoints and Minimum Prototype — Voltage, Time, Waveform and Abstention The minimum prototype uses an inert microelectrode in a sealed saline tank and an isolated known-potential source. A physical source signal and an independent acquisition chain are retained even when the candidate sensor or processing algorithm is turned off. F126 is scored on injected-source amplitude error [microvolt], SNR [dB] and source-motion coupling [microvolt/mm]. F127 uses known relative lag [microsecond], jitter [microsecond RMS] and timestamp continuity. F128 preserves waveform morphology and reports reconstruction RMSE [microvolt], filter delay [ms] and false events per hour. F129 follows offset drift [microvolt/h], gain calibration error, temperature [degC] and the fraction of measurement intervals with valid calibration. F130 requires false-acceptance probability, selective risk, coverage and hard-stop delay. Every outcome needs a frozen sampling period, complete assigned denominator, calibration state, model version and uncertainty account. A favorable average must not erase a rare missed event or an interval lost when the calibration chain failed. The crucial distinction is between a measurement of an injected artificial electrical input and a demonstration of valid human neural-signal sensing. The proposed prototype can test the former. It cannot establish the latter, and even a perfectly recomputed synthetic 3D surface remains a mathematical illustration until an independent physical experiment challenges it. 08 | Strong Baselines, Rival Mechanisms and Stopping Conditions — Let Ordinary Electronics Win A good research title makes clear which simpler approach is allowed to defeat it. Strong baselines here include an independently calibrated stationary microelectrode, conventional differential acquisition, known-lag clock correction, well-tuned notch or adaptive denoising, scheduled reference recalibration and a conservative quality-mask detector. Each receives equal source examples, bandwidth, latency budget, compute allowance and evaluation time. Changing those resources after inspecting results would invalidate any technology-specific advantage. The leading rivals differ by flagship. F126 can be explained by a shared reference error or actuation-generated electromagnetic pickup. F127 can inherit common triggers, hidden buffer latency or resampling leakage. F128 can score high by deleting the very event it was meant to recover. F129 can appear stable only because its calibration is refitted using later test blocks. F130 can look trustworthy while confidently accepting injected fake signals whose source was absent. Each rival must be represented by a blind, physical or algorithmic counterfactual. The hard stop is independent of average performance. Invalid microelectrode contact, missing external reference, lost timestamp provenance, calibration outside its validity range or high-confidence counterfeit acceptance must trigger refusal according to prespecified rules. The most honest null result may show that ordinary electronics performs just as well. That finding should survive publication and transfer. 09 | Research Gates and Phoenix Inheritance — Two Hundred Doors to Future Experiments The research doors are neither slogans nor a list of compliance checks. Each door begins from a concrete unresolved observation: an unexpected microvolt peak, a synchronized pair of independent channels, an oddly clean denoised trace, a calibration that worked only on the first sensor batch or a model that was most confident about a nonexistent event. The door asks why the observation mattered, what competing physical world could explain it and what a future laboratory should test next. The two hundred Research Gates span five orientations: origin of the signal question, physical counterworld, independent witness, noncompensatory refusal and successor reconstruction. Every door retains Origin, Extreme Extrapolation and Future Research Plan. For an inspiring question to remain scientific, the counterworld needs a distinct measurable prediction or an explicit reason the original two mechanisms cannot be identified. The future plan names a blind input, strong baseline, reference instrument, failure ledger and stop condition rather than merely inviting hope. Thirty-three Phoenix concepts are not built devices but revisable proposals: known-source observatories, hidden-lag injectors, waveform-preservation courts, cross-version drift sentinels and high-confidence false-event traps. Their diagrams distinguish source, rival, external witness and refusal. A future generation may replace every present sensor and equation and still inherit something meaningful—the complete record that allows it to prove us wrong. 10 | Neither a 4D label nor a quantum label is evidence The public five-stage reasoning name and the 4D device concept organize testable design hypotheses. Neither licenses claims of real spacetime compression, verified quantum speedup or living neural sensing. Take trustworthy sensing and abstention as a specific case. The candidate says source provenance, independent calibration, out-of-distribution checks and a physical rejection gate can distinguish an admissible proxy signal from a confidently wrong synthetic signal. The rival explanation says a model may give high confidence to a fabricated event because it shares contamination with its own validator or because rejected trials were removed. A research team should blind-inject a high-confidence false event and a missing calibration witness, require an explicit rejection rather than a plausible classification and report false accept probability [1], selective risk [1], calibration ECE [1], missed veto [count], stop latency [ms]. Only a blinded difference that survives a strong comparison could justify a narrower technical claim. The most important practical inheritance is an independently clocked signal auditor with authority to force abstention when its witness is missing. Compare with thresholded fixed-reference detection, independent second-instrument validation, classic anomaly detection and simple quality masks at equal input budgets. Preserve sensor batches, artifact transients, calibration, exclusions and all test attempts; refuse if high-confidence false acceptance, calibration invalidity, missing reference chain or an unsafe continuation after the stop trigger. Any proposal involving people or implanted electrodes would require an entirely new ethics, biocompatibility and medical-device review.

evidence_items.summary: Abstract This viewpoint addresses developers and evaluators of large language model (LLM)–based clinical decision support systems. Although recent benchmarks increasingly evaluate multiple clinical reasoning domains, many still rely substantially on reference decision agreement—whether model outputs conform to predefined decisions. Our aim is to clarify when such agreement remains useful, when it becomes insufficient for complex or preference-sensitive decisions, and how it can be complemented by reasoning-centered assessment. Clinical decision-making often depends on structured reasoning under uncertainty, integrating probabilistic evidence, contextual constraints, and patient values. Using oncology as an illustrative domain, we argue that some decision variability is a structural feature of clinical reasoning rather than noise or error. Used alone in such settings, single-reference benchmarks may conflate reasonable divergence with incorrectness and reward answer imitation over transparent reasoning. We conclude that reference decision agreement should be retained for tasks with stable ground truth but supplemented by evidence grounding, reasoning quality, patient-centeredness, and safety checks for open-ended clinical decision support. This multidimensional approach is intended to support safer and more clinically meaningful evaluation.
evidence_items.title: Challenges of Single-Reference Benchmarks for Clinical Reasoning in Large Language Model–Based Decision Support

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are extensively used for many Natural Language Processing tasks such as question answering, natural language inference, document summarization, etc. Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting compels LLMs to generate step-by-step reasoning chains. While some of the reasoning chains may follow a correct thought process, they can also suffer from hallucinations, leading to errors in answer generation. Recently, many articles have targeted the problem of verifying these reasoning chains from various aspects. Despite this recent attention, to the best of our knowledge, no comprehensive survey currently summarizes these studies on reasoning chain verification. This work addresses that gap by presenting a detailed overview of the methods for verifying reasoning chains and categorizing them according to their methodology. This paper introduces a novel taxonomy of existing reasoning chain verification methods and mainly divides them into approaches that assess entire chains versus those that examine individual steps. This paper also reviews benchmarks for evaluating reasoning chains and verification methods and further discusses the challenges and future directions associated with these methods. By compiling and analyzing these approaches, our survey aims to advance the understanding and development of robust reasoning techniques in LLMs.
evidence_items.title: Verifying Reasoning Chains Generated by Large Language Models: A Survey

evidence_items.summary: Phytoplankton composition and biomass are widely used indicators of eutrophication and aquatic ecosystem condition. Under the EU Water Framework Directive, phytoplankton is a biological quality element in ecological status assessment, which requires reliable taxonomic identification. This study evaluated the capabilities and limitations of general-purpose multimodal AI for phytoplankton identification from microscopy images using a two-stage design. In Stage 1, six off-the-shelf multimodal models—ChatGPT 5.1, ChatGPT 5.4, Gemini 3 Thinking, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Perplexity Pro and Grok 4.1—were compared using 30 expert-verified microscopy image cases. Gemini 3 Thinking showed the strongest overall performance across several measures, although no stable model hierarchy was established across all metrics. In Stage 2, GPT-5.6 Sol was evaluated using an expanded dataset of 157 microscopy images in three independent runs. Accuracy ranged from 70.1 to 81.5% at the higher-group level and from 40.1 to 57.3% at the genus level, but decreased to 14.3–31.8% at the species level. Performance differed significantly among runs and phytoplankton groups, with recurrent taxon-specific misclassification patterns. Across both stages, performance declined markedly with increasing taxonomic resolution. General-purpose multimodal AI may therefore support preliminary phytoplankton image screening and broad-group assignment, but current systems remain insufficiently reliable for autonomous genus- or species-level identification. Expert verification remains essential for ecological monitoring and water quality assessment.
evidence_items.title: Comparison of Multimodal Large Language Models for Phytoplankton Identification from Microscopy Images

evidence_items.summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems are often constrained by the “relevance myopia,” primarily focusing on fully relevant external information to supply missing or outdated facts while overlooking the potential of partially relevant knowledge to activate the internal knowledge of Large Language Models (LLMs). We challenge this paradigm by proposing that partially relevant knowledge can “awaken” latent semantic information within LLMs. We provide a theoretical framework, grounded in information theory, that explains this awakening effect: partially relevant knowledge reduces the conditional entropy of the answer by increasing the mutual information between the context and the model’s parametric knowledge. We thoroughly investigate the influence of different types of partially relevant knowledge by leveraging the gold reasoning path from Knowledge Graphs (KGs). Furthermore, we introduce a new problem called Unseen Entity Knowledge Graph Question Answering (UE-KGQA), where the entity mentioned in a question does not have a corresponding entity in the KG. Specifically, UE-KGQA simulates the realistic RAG with incomplete KGs and evaluates the effectiveness of the partially relevant knowledge. Experiments conducted on three KGQA datasets reveal that prompting with partially relevant knowledge substantially outperforms traditional similarity-based RAG methods, often susceptible to noisy and irrelevant outcomes.
evidence_items.title: Prompting Large Language Models with Partial Knowledge for Answering Questions with Unseen Entities

evidence_items.summary: Securing the Internet of Things (IoT) requires detecting and responding to evolving threats across distributed devices with limited computing and communication resources. Large language models (LLMs) can interpret security alerts and help investigate incidents. Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) extends these capabilities by combining reasoning, planning, memory, and tool use to coordinate security actions. Existing studies offer a fragmented account of how these capabilities fit IoT architectures, what risks arise when agents act autonomously, and how to evaluate their performance. This survey addresses these gaps by tracing the transition from LLM-assisted analysis to agentic defence across threat detection, triage, investigation, and response. We develop a unified taxonomy covering IoT infrastructure, LLM-driven and agentic security, trust and resilience, application domains, and evaluation methods. We compare hierarchical, orchestration-based, distributed multi-agent, and cognitive architectures by examining where security decisions are made, how agents coordinate, and where actions are executed across device, edge, fog, and cloud layers. We also examine threats introduced by agentic operation, including prompt injection, memory poisoning, privacy leakage, and compromised trust between agents, together with corresponding defences. Our synthesis finds that limited attack testing and dataset coverage leave uncertainty about how well these systems generalize, while coordination failures and inference overhead constrain deployment. These findings motivate research on trustworthy orchestration, privacy-preserving collaboration, explainable security decisions, and efficient edge inference.
evidence_items.title: From Large Language Models (LLMs) to Agentic AI for IoT Security: A Survey

organizations: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, The University of Texas at San Antonio, San Antonio, TX 78249, USA
evidence_items.summary: Exact, deterministic preparation of an arbitrary dense n-qubit state is the data-loading step for quantum signal and image processing, and, without ancillae, a generic target needs at least ⌈(2n − n − 1)/2⌉ controlled-NOT (CNOT) gates. We evaluate the two new Quantum Signal-induced Heap Transform (QsiHT) syntheses, Real and Complex, built on the discrete signal-induced heap transform (DsiHT), inside a nine-configuration benchmark drawn from the uniformly controlled rotation, multiplexor, isometry, Schmidt, and Quantum Shannon Decomposition (QSD) families. Qiskit’s StatePreparation is the only method benchmarked as shipped rather than re-implemented. Every configuration reproduces its Haar-random targets to machine precision, with the Real Synthesis confined to sign-bearing targets. Under noise, one coarse tier is stable, set by the executed two-qubit count; the O(2n) frontier stays well below QSD’s O(4n), and no finer order reproduces across two IBM Heron r2 processors at n = 3. Both syntheses reach the 2n − n − 1 multiplexor-family floor. That count matches StatePreparation and, as built, undercuts every other from-scratch construction from n = 3 up. Under a uniform optimization-level-3 pass Plesch–Brukner falls below it at n = 4 and on real targets at n = 6, and as built, it keeps the lowest constant on complex data among the from-scratch methods above that floor. At large registers, the Real Synthesis has the cheapest build-time cost and the Complex Synthesis handles arbitrary targets.
evidence_items.title: A Unified Benchmark for Exact Dense Quantum State Preparation

evidence_items.summary: The physics programs of current and future collider experiments necessitate the development of surrogate simulators for calorimeter showers. While much progress has been made in the development of generative models for this task, they have typically been evaluated in simplified scenarios and for single particles. This is particularly true for the challenging task of highly granular calorimeter simulation. For the first time, this work studies the use of highly granular generative calorimeter surrogates in a realistic simulation application. We introduce DDML (4hep with machine learning), a generic library which enables the combination of generative calorimeter surrogates with realistic detectors implemented using the 4hep toolkit. We compare two different generative models—one operating on a regular grid representation and the other using a less common point cloud approach. In order to disentangle methodological details from model performance, we provide comparisons to idealized simulators which directly sample representations of different resolutions from the full simulation ground truth. We then systematically evaluate model performance on post-reconstruction benchmarks for electromagnetic shower simulation. Beginning with a typical single-particle study, we introduce a first multiparticle benchmark based on diphoton separations, before studying a first full physics benchmark based on hadronic decays of the tau lepton. Our results indicate that models operating on a point cloud can achieve a favorable balance between speed and accuracy for highly granular calorimeter simulation compared to those which operate on a regular grid representation.
evidence_items.title: First full physics benchmark for highly granular calorimeter surrogates

evidence_items.summary: Small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) silence target genes through RISC-mediated hybridization and cleavage, but can silence unintended transcripts and cause toxicity or complicate regulatory approval. In drug development, empirical assessment by qPCR and RNA-seq is slow, forces early candidate prioritization, and is limited by available species- and genome-appropriate cell models. While extensive empirical screening remains standard practice, there is a significant opportunity for modern AI methods to change this paradigm. We introduce DeepRNAi, a deep learning model that accurately predicts on- and off-target knockdown from siRNA and mRNA sequence. Trained on 16 million siRNA-transcript pairs from 2,031 siRNAs designed to interrogate known siRNA failure modes, and incorporating transcript context from biological foundation models, DeepRNAi is the first in silico method that approaches experimental accuracy. It generalizes across cell models, transcripts, genomes and species, and in a small study distinguishes approved therapeutics from hepatotoxic candidates. The value of DeepRNAi for prioritizing better candidates up front improving likelihood of success later in development is evidenced by a genome-wide survey of 24.4 million siRNAs targeting 7,946 genes, which indicates that 90.1% of the 100 most potent siRNAs have at least some off-target concerns. To support the community, we are publishing a training and benchmark dataset containing 1.84 million siRNA-transcript pairs from 240 siRNAs.
evidence_items.title: DeepRNAi: Predicting on- and off-target siRNA activity and establishing a benchmark
PANO-Bench: A Public Information-Grounded Benchmark for Annual Narrative Generation and Open-Ended Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Terraces play a vital role in mitigating runoff and intercepting sediment. Large-scale, high-precision extraction of terraces from remote sensing imagery is essential for environmental monitoring and soil erosion control. However, accurate spatial identification of terraces still presents significant challenges, including scale variability, shadow interference, and complex geometric configurations. To address these issues, we propose DETS-Net, a dual-encoder network that integrates CNN and Transformer architectures. The network employs ResNet-34 as the CNN encoder for local feature detail extraction, utilizes a Transformer encoder to strengthen long-range dependency modeling, and incorporates an adaptive feature fusion (AFF) module for the dynamic integration of the two feature branches. We develop the THDIR dataset, which covers four typical terrain types, namely, plateau mountains, hills, and mountain-basin transition zones, and contains 9,336 standardized 256 × 256 pixel images. We conduct systematic comparisons with eight representative deep learning models. Experimental results demonstrate that DETS-Net achieves an overall accuracy (OA) of 89.91%, a mean intersection over union (MIoU) of 81.28%, and an F1-score of 87.99% on the THDIR dataset, outperforming current mainstream methods in segmentation precision. We apply the optimized model to 2023 remote sensing imagery of Luotian County in the Dabie Mountains, Hubei Province, and generate a high-precision county-level terrace spatial distribution map. This framework supports the assessment of soil and water conservation benefits through area statistics, slope distribution data, and high-precision boundary extraction and provides a reproducible technical pathway for automated terrace mapping using high-resolution remote sensing imagery in complex mountainous regions.
evidence_items.title: A comprehensive benchmark and dual-encoder baseline for terraced field extraction in complex mountainous regions

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Text-to-SQL systems allow users to query databases in natural language, yet existing benchmarks cover English and a small number of well-resourced languages, and no resource has been reported for Kurdish. This paper presents SoraniSQL, a novel dataset and benchmark that is, to the best of current knowledge, the first for Text-to-SQL in Central Kurdish (Sorani). The dataset contains 7,518 question-SQL pairs from 609 query types, systematically constructed over a nine-table retail point-of-sale database with four database instances for test-suite execution accuracy (EXₜₛ); a five-member native-speaker panel rated a stratified sample of 200 questions at 4.9 out of 5 for fluency and 4.9 for adequacy. Dedicated splits separate new values, unseen phrasings, unseen combinations of query components, unseen SQL constructs and spelling variation. Experiments with retrieval, template, compositional, neural and pretrained models, all tuned on development data, show that a template classifier reaches 97.1% EXₜₛ on new values but 0.7% on unseen combinations, where a compositional model reaches 97.7%. A 1.5B-parameter code model fine-tuned with quantised low-rank adaptation (QLoRA) reaches 95.0% on unseen combinations on a laptop central processing unit (CPU), and the structure split and the orthographic-noise sets form the most demanding conditions of the benchmark. A Windows application, DanaText2SQL, demonstrates offline use of the benchmark's best fast model with Microsoft SQL Server.
evidence_items.title: SoraniSQL: A Novel Synthetic Text-to-SQL Dataset and Benchmark for Low-Resource Central Kurdish (Sorani)

organizations: International University of Business Agriculture and Technology
evidence_items.summary: Abstract The Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) is based on accumulated precipitation, but there is a difference between the scale of accumulation and the forecast lead time. When a forecast is issued at month t and verified at t+h-1, each post-issue month during the target accumulation period must either be forecast or be provided via a specified alternative. Although the method for constructing the SPI from observed and forecast precipitation is well established in operational practice, its impact on comparisons of lead times across different models has rarely been quantified. We assess three accumulation methods; a full-trajectory forecast, a climatology-gap operational baseline, and a perfect-intermediate-information (PII) diagnostic. This study uses a dataset comprising 10 stations with complete records from Bangladesh, six expanding rolling-origin folds, ten forecasting techniques, SPI values of 3, 6 and 12 months, and lead times of 1, 3, 6, 9 and 12 months. Sensitivity analyses were carried out on a 34-station dataset with variable records and an empirical SPI. For the Gamma SPI-12, the difference between the PII and full-trajectory approaches increased with lead time and reaches +0.760 F1, +0.732 PR-AUC, and +1.873 R2. No method performed best in all criteria and simple baselines of climatology and residual-trees were highly competitive. This shows that the accumulation protocol can qualitatively affect the conclusions about lead-time skill and model performance.
evidence_items.title: Multi-Horizon SPI Drought Forecast Skill under Alternative Accumulation Protocols: A Rolling-Origin Benchmark for Bangladesh
