evidence_items.summary: Polyol sweeteners in sugar-free beverages can cause osmotic diarrhea after acute bolus intake. Reference points, mostly no-observed-adverse-effect levels, depend on tested doses and lack uncertainty intervals. A systematic search yielded eight datasets covering six polyols; six datasets (five polyols) formed the primary analysis, with dose-escalation sorbitol data analyzed exploratorily. Bayesian model averaging at 10% extra risk yielded adult lower credible bounds on benchmark doses (BMDLs) of 0.400, 0.358, 0.162, 0.132, and 0.087 g/kg body weight for erythritol, maltitol, xylitol, isomalt, and lactitol, respectively; the pediatric erythritol BMDL was 0.552 g/kg body weight. Lowering the benchmark response to 5% reduced BMDLs by 44.4–53.7% without changing adult rankings. Using consumption and body-weight data, BMDLs were converted into concentrations. For a 20 kg child consuming 0.9 L once (uncertainty factor 1), reference concentrations were 1.9–12.2 g/L, inversely proportional to volume. Differences in matrices, endpoints, background incidences, and dose designs preclude definitive intrinsic potency ranking. Most estimates required low-dose extrapolation; except for erythritol, child scenarios used adult data without pediatric dose–response evidence. These concentrations are not safety or regulatory limits, formulation recommendations, individual no-effect thresholds, or concentrations validated to protect all children. Values derived from solid matrices require validation in beverages.
evidence_items.title: Reassessment of the Laxative Effects of Polyol Sweeteners Using Benchmark Dose Modeling, with an Analysis of Beverage Consumption Scenarios

evidence_items.summary: Abstract De novo drug design must balance global drug properties with local structural determinants of target specificity. However, existing methods often reduce both objectives to local geometric optimization, relying on blind, reward-driven perturbations that can disrupt essential scaffolds and compromise overall drug-likeness. To resolve this destructive optimization trap, we propose CadreAI, a semantically decoupled agentic de novo drug design framework. CadreAI explicitly decomposes the entire drug design process into two independent subtasks: target-oriented semantic planning and plan-conditioned molecular generation. This strict separation mitigates potential task interference, allowing each module to focus exclusively on its dedicated objective without mutual disruption. Crucially, the strategic logic of how to formulate these target-oriented plans is driven by Simulation-Guided Insight Consolidation (SGIC). To eliminate trial-and-error guessing, this persistent memory mechanism translates transient numerical docking feedback into reusable textual heuristics, allowing the agent to continuously learn and logically deduce subsequent structural edits. Evaluated on the CrossDocked2020 and DrugGen benchmarks, molecules generated by CadreAI achieve superior docking performance with suitable drug-likeness and synthetic accessibility. Additional Boltz-2 evaluations provide orthogonal computational validation of predicted structural plausibility and binding affinity. These results demonstrate that semantically decoupled reasoning offers a highly controllable and practical route for in silico therapeutic design.
evidence_items.title:
CadreAI: Agentic
AI for Semantically Decoupled Protein–Drug
Design and Optimization

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Public sector agencies increasingly seek to use artificial intelligence in complex administrative workflows, yet guidance on process architecture for AI integration remains limited. We present an action design research study of an AI-augmented grant evaluation process in a Singapore enterprise development agency. Across three architectural iterations, we moved from an agentic AI approach, through a layered extraction-evaluation pipeline, to a workflow-based design that models grant evaluation as a directed acyclic graph of typed process nodes (data ingestion, AI processing, and deterministic computation) with mandatory human review checkpoints. Across the iterations, we observed improvements in consistency, debuggability, and governance compatibility. In a three-month pilot with 11 officers and 123 cases, 80 of the 103 outputs produced were accepted (77.7%), and five officers self-reported a 21% reduction in processing time per application. Seven months later, a census of the nine remaining officers found reported routine use and the lowest ratings for judgement-adjacent outputs; none of the six officers who answered both surveys lowered any of four repeated ratings, and officers reported adapting their practices in different ways (process co-evolution). We derive three design principles for AI-augmented business processes: (1) decompose complex processes into typed, bounded workflow nodes rather than delegating end-to-end reasoning to AI agents; (2) separate AI-suitable tasks from deterministic computation and human judgment within the process model; and (3) design conservative failure modes that route exceptions to human handlers. We also argue that research on structured language-model agents supports, rather than refutes, explicit process structure.
evidence_items.title: From Agentic AI to Structured Workflows: Designing Process Architectures for AI-Augmented Administrative Decision Support

evidence_items.summary: Large language models routinely hedge on contested questions, but the surface uniformity of such hedging conceals a heterogeneous mixture of underlying latent drivers. We distinguish four latent drivers: epistemic uncertainty, hermeneutic openness, alignment-induced policy effects (which can suppress or amplify evaluative stance), and cross-context interpretive divergence. We argue that verbalised output is best understood as a measurement-and-identification problem in which these heterogeneous latent drivers of uncertainty and stance are compressed into a single output channel by a noninjective verbalisation map: similar hedging or balancing language may reflect genuine uncertainty or instead policy and contextual effects, and a user cannot reliably distinguish these drivers from a single output. We formalise this compression, characterise the decision-theoretic regret of conflating drivers whose appropriate downstream interventions differ, and observe that this regret does not vanish under additional factual evidence when the dominant driver is non-epistemic. Empirical claims are anchored in a pre-specified replication study. We then introduce four families of identifying probes, namely factual-evidence augmentation, counterfactual rephrasing, standpoint-conditioned elicitation, and cross-lingual consistency, which provide directional identification of the dominant latent driver of an observed hedge. We close with implications for professional practice in journalism, policy analysis, and comparative research; design principles for uncertainty-disclosure interfaces; and a benchmark proposal for driver-stratified evaluation of LLM uncertainty.
evidence_items.title: When Hedging Hides Heterogeneity: A Measurement and Identification Framework for Uncertainty in Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Body-composition measurements are often recorded in the free text of electronic health record (EHR) notes, limiting large-scale assessment of the composition of weight change. We evaluated a large language model (LLM)-based pipeline for extracting and harmonizing these measurements and characterizing the lean-mass proportion of weight change. Among 670,422 adults initiating semaglutide or tirzepatide, the pipeline yielded 158,573 harmonized lean body mass (LBM) measurements for 29,154 patients; 7,965 had baseline and follow-up measurements. Manual review of a sample of 53 notes found correct values and units in all 32 notes with extracted LBM values and correct dates in 93.8%, with no missed values in 21 screened negatives. Repeat extraction showed 95%–97% agreement for values, units, and dates. Across a wider clinical-note corpus, analyses of 1,907 weight-loss-associated medications, procedures, and conditions distinguished relatively lean-sparing loss with bariatric surgery (lean-mass proportion, 0.24), semaglutide (0.27), and tirzepatide (0.26) from lean-depleting loss with catabolic illness (0.70–0.74). Analyses of 427 weight-gain-associated entities distinguished fat-predominant from lean- or fluid-predominant gain. Matched comparisons generally placed incretin therapies between lifestyle counseling and bariatric surgery in weight and LBM loss. Comparing tirzepatide with semaglutide, the covariate-adjusted 12-month difference in LBM change was −1.9 percentage points (95% CI, −3.6 to − 0.3), attenuating to − 0.1 (95% CI, −1.6 to 1.4) after adjustment for concurrent weight change. Among 465 matched pairs, the 12-month lean-mass proportion of weight lost did not differ significantly (0.24 vs 0.22; difference, 0.02; 95% CI, −0.04 to 0.09). These observational findings support scalable assessment of body composition from routine EHR notes and suggest that tirzepatide’s greater LBM loss accompanies greater weight loss.
evidence_items.title: Large-scale data extraction from clinical notes reveals the lean-mass fraction of weight-loss in patients treated with GLP-1 medicines

evidence_items.summary:
This study investigates the evolution and future trajectory of artificial intelligence (AI) in advancing environmental sustainability in Egypt and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) from 2015 to 2030. It analyzes how these distinct governance models, centralized policy capacity vs rapid technology-led implementation leverage AI to bridge the “Policy-to-Action” gap regarding resource scarcity and long-term climate resilience.
 
 
 
 The research employs a longitudinal comparative case study methodology utilizing qualitative document analysis and thematic process tracing to systematically evaluate national AI strategies and legislative frameworks from 2015 through to 2030 strategic targets. It utilizes 2026 benchmarks, including the Government AI Readiness Index 2025 (Oxford Insights, 2026), to assess AI efficacy in water management, energy systems, and urban planning.
 
 
 
 The analysis reveals a significant policy divergence: the UAE has transitioned to mandatory AI-driven climate reporting via Federal Decree-Law No. 11 (2024a), while Egypt has established global leadership in “Policy Capacity,” achieving a perfect score of 100/100 and ranking 1st in Africa in the 2025 AI Readiness Index. Both nations successfully deploy AI for water management; however, the UAE leads in urban “Net Zero” integration and operational efficiency (e.g. 95% water savings in AI-managed agriculture), while Egypt excels in localized strategic alignment and “Sovereign AI” infrastructure. Findings reveal that while the UAE's Implementation-First model drives faster infrastructure deployment, Egypt's Policy-First approach fosters deeper institutional ownership, though both face a critical energy-water-AI paradox that threatens 2030 sustainability targets.
 
 
 
 This paper provides an original comparative treatment of Arab AI governance by incorporating 2025–2026 strategic updates, including the UAE's January 2026 integration of the National AI System as a Cabinet advisory member. It introduces a novel framework the Policy-to-Action Bridge, highlighting AI as a central pillar of modern environmental legislation and procedural justice rather than merely a technical instrument.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence and environmental sustainability in Egypt and the UAE: a comparative study of policy maturity and future roadmaps (2015–2030)

evidence_items.summary: Malaria is currently a challenge in Africa, where transmission is shaped by interacting climatic, demographic and socioeconomic conditions. Improved prediction could support earlier identification of high-risk settings and more targeted use of control resources. This study evaluated multiple machine-learning approaches for malaria-risk prediction across Africa and examined the variables driving model predictions. Malaria burden data for 2000–2024 from the Malaria Atlas Project (MAP) were combined with climate indicators from NASA POWER and demographic, socioeconomic and health indicators from the World Bank. Descriptive analyses covered 47 African countries, while the harmonised machine-learning dataset comprised 1,056 country-year observations from 44 countries. Six classification algorithms were used including, logistic regression, decision tree, Random Forest, support vector machine (SVM), gradient boosting machine (GBM) and XGBoost. Model development used leakage-free expanding-window temporal cross-validation, while 2021–2024 was retained as an independent out-of-time test period. Uncertainty was assessed with country-cluster bootstrap confidence intervals model calibration and internal grouped-country performance were also examined. Performance was assessed using accuracy, balanced accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, F1-score, Receiver Operator Curves (ROC)-Area Under Cureve (AUC), PR-AUC and Brier score. Across 2000–2024, the dataset contained 5.63 billion reported clinical malaria cases and 17.78 million malaria deaths. Cases increased from 204.3 million in 2000 to 244.7 million in 2024, while deaths declined from their early-period peak. Random Forest had the largest mean temporal cross-validated ROC-AUC (0.968). In the independent test period, the four principal machine-learning models showed similar discrimination: ROC-AUC was 0.955 for SVM, 0.950 for Random Forest, 0.949 for GBM and 0.943 for XGBoost, and pairwise confidence intervals for their ROC-AUC differences included zero. Random Forest achieved 0.903 accuracy and 0.902 balanced accuracy. Performance was lower when entire countries were held out, with pooled ROC-AUCs of 0.874 for Random Forest and 0.870 for XGBoost. Model interpretation showed that climatic and socioeconomic variables contributed jointly to predictions, with wind speed, lagged temperature, life expectancy, age dependency and unemployment among the leading predictors. Machine-learning models may provide useful malaria risk prediction from routinely available climate and socioeconomic indicators. However, geographic transferability is less certain than temporal prediction within represented countries. Further work should use finer spatial and temporal data, external validation and locally relevant intervention indicators before operational use.
evidence_items.title: Spatiotemporal patterns and machine-learning prediction of malaria risk across Africa, 2000–2024

evidence_items.summary: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder whose early diagnosis remains challenging in distributed healthcare settings where direct sharing of patient data may be restricted. Federated learning enables collaborative model development while retaining raw data at local participants; however, its reliability can deteriorate under statistical heterogeneity and Byzantine clients that transmit malicious model updates. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a Trust-Gated Median Hybrid (TGMH) aggregation framework that integrates adaptive trust estimation, hard trust gating, coordinate-wise median protection, and adaptive hybrid fusion. The principal contribution lies in the server-side aggregation strategy for improving resilience to adversarial updates rather than in the development of a new diagnostic classifier. The framework is evaluated on 65 subjects from the OpenNeuro ds004504 EEG dataset using subject-independent five-fold outer cross-validation and simulated federated clients. TGMH is compared with FedAvg, FedProx, FedNova, FedAdam, SCAFFOLD, Coordinate Median, Trimmed Mean, Krum where theoretically feasible, and the Original Hybrid Trust–Trimmed framework. Robustness is evaluated under Sign Flip, Gaussian Poisoning, and Model Replacement attacks at 0, 20, and 40% Byzantine participation, together with an additional adaptive stealth stress test. Under the high-intensity 40% Model Replacement attack, TGMH substantially improves predictive performance relative to the Original Hybrid framework. Paired subject-level analysis further identifies six of 27 Byzantine-condition comparisons that remain significant after Holm correction, with large rank-biserial effects observed in several Model Replacement and Sign Flip comparisons. Subject-level bootstrap confidence intervals, component-wise ablation, trust-parameter sensitivity analysis, and scalability experiments provide complementary evidence regarding performance variability and the operating characteristics of the framework. Importantly, the adaptive stealth experiment shows that norm- and direction-constrained malicious updates can satisfy the current trust-gating criterion, indicating that the proposed defense does not provide universal robustness against adaptive adversaries. Scalability experiments with 5, 10, and 20 simulated clients further show that 50% partial participation reduces measured communication overhead by approximately 46–50% while producing only small within-configuration changes in mean Balanced Accuracy. Overall, the results demonstrate that TGMH provides a reproducible Byzantine-resilient aggregation framework with condition-dependent robustness advantages for federated EEG-based Alzheimer’s disease classification, while retaining raw subject data locally and without implying formal privacy guarantees.
evidence_items.title: Trust-gated median hybrid aggregation for byzantine-resilient federated learning on distributed EEG biomarkers for Alzheimer’s disease classification

evidence_items.summary:
BACKGROUND AND AIMS
Patients who previously had a normal colonoscopy may subsequently undergo colorectal cancer (CRC) screening with multitarget stool DNA (mt-sDNA) testing. The yield of advanced neoplasia following a positive mt-sDNA test in this subgroup is not well defined. We compared colonoscopy outcomes after positive mt-sDNA tests in patients with and without a prior normal colonoscopy.


METHODS
We conducted a registry-based analysis using data from the population-based New Hampshire Colonoscopy Registry (NHCR). The primary outcome was an ordered four-level categorical variable reflecting colonoscopy findings: CRC, advanced colorectal neoplasia, non-advanced colorectal neoplasia, and no neoplasia. Ordinal logistic regression models were used to evaluate the association between prior normal colonoscopy and severity of findings.


RESULTS
Patients with a prior normal colonoscopy (n=739) were approximately half as likely to have more advanced findings compared with patients without a prior colonoscopy (n=994); prior normal colonoscopy was associated with lower odds of more advanced versus less advanced outcomes (OR 0.51; 95% CI 0.41-0.62; P < 0.001). However, the absolute prevalence of advanced colorectal neoplasia among patients with a previous colonoscopy remained substantial (19.1%; 95% CI 16.3-22.1%).


CONCLUSIONS
Although prior normal colonoscopy is associated with lower odds of advanced findings after a positive mt-sDNA test, the residual prevalence of advanced neoplasia remains clinically meaningful. Regardless of prior screening history, there is a high yield of neoplasia, which could be attributed in part due to missed lesions on the prior colonoscopy. Our data provide potential benchmarks for expected lesion yield in this population.
evidence_items.title: Colonoscopy outcomes after positive multi-target stool DNA testing in patients with and without a prior normal colonoscopy: Data from the New Hampshire Colonoscopy Registry.

evidence_items.summary: Accurate temporal monitoring of power-system operating states is increasingly important in renewable-rich and measurement-intensive grids. This paper presents an interpretable Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT)-based framework for multivariate power-system state prediction from sequential measurements. The framework combines variable selection, gated residual processing, recurrent temporal encoding, multi-head attention, and post-hoc feature-attribution analysis. The learning task is explicitly formulated as temporal state prediction: a fixed window of historical measurements is mapped to a future state vector, rather than reconstructing the instantaneous state through a conventional static estimator. The method is evaluated on Monte Carlo operating scenarios generated for the IEEE 118-bus benchmark. In response to robustness and reproducibility requirements, the revised study includes five independent random-seed trials, paired significance testing, component ablation, Gaussian-noise and missing-data experiments, hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, and computational-complexity measurements. Across five seeds, the proposed TFT obtains an RMSE of \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$0.03486\pm0.04756$$\end{document} and MAE of \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$0.01988\pm0.02692$$\end{document}, compared with RMSE values of \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$0.12508$$\end{document}, \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$0.13178$$\end{document}, and \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$0.22107$$\end{document} for GRU, LSTM, and Transformer baselines, respectively. evidence_items.title: An interpretable hybrid deep learning framework for power system state monitoring using temporal fusion transformers

evidence_items.summary: Risk assessment of agrochemicals has traditionally relied on animal studies to derive points of departure (PODs) for the establishment of regulatory guidance values. More recently, new approach methodologies (NAMs) have been explored as a means to estimate protective exposure levels without generating new animal data. In the present case study, we evaluated whether a transcriptomics-based NAM workflow combined with physiologically-based kinetic (PBK) modeling can provide biologically plausible estimates of systemic toxicity thresholds for pendimethalin (PDM), an agrochemical with extensive toxicological and kinetic reference data. We compared two in vitro liver models and transcriptomic approaches: targeted TempO-Seq in HepG2 cells and untargeted RNA sequencing in HepaRG cells. After 48 h exposure to PDM in concentration ranges of 0.07-202 µM (HepaRG) and 0.8-56 µM (HepG2), gene expression changes were analyzed using benchmark-dose modeling in BMDExpress 3.0. Transcriptomic PODs (tPODs) were derived using gene- and distribution-based approaches and subsequently translated to external doses by in vitro-to-in vivo extrapolation (IVIVE) employing three rat PBK models. The resulting PODs were compared with regulatory in vivo PODs reported for PDM. In addition, a human population-based PBK model was used to derive an oral equivalent dose (OED) from the most sensitive transcriptomic POD. Across transcriptomic platforms, tPOD derivation methods, and PBK models, the resulting IVIVE-derived PODs generally fell within the range of regulatory in vivo PODs reported for PDM. The most sensitive prediction yielded a POD of 6.0 mg/kg bw/day for the rat, while human population-based modeling resulted in a 5th-percentile OED of 0.068 mg/kg bw/day, close to currently established regulatory guidance values. Notably, the variability introduced by the choice of toxicokinetic model was of a similar magnitude as the variability associated with transcriptomic POD derivation, indicating that uncertainty in IVIVE contributes at least as much to the final prediction as uncertainty in transcriptomic data analysis. Overall, this study supports the feasibility of combining in vitro transcriptomics with IVIVE to estimate systemic toxicity thresholds for an agrochemical compound. The results encourage further evaluation of transcriptomics-based NAM workflows and next-generation risk assessment of agrochemicals. Assessment of a broader range of agrochemicals, together with continued refinement of toxicokinetic modeling and in vitro dosimetry, will be required to establish their predictive performance and future regulatory applicability.
evidence_items.title: How robust are transcriptomics-based points of departure when translated to in vivo doses by kinetic-modeling? A case study with the herbicide pendimethalin using HepG2 and HepaRG cells.

evidence_items.summary:
This study aims to improve the dynamic modelling accuracy of small unmanned helicopters with multi-input multi-output behaviour, strong coupling, and nonlinear flight characteristics. Existing linear identification methods can capture dominant dynamics but have limited ability to represent nonlinear residual effects caused by aerodynamic coupling and unmodelled disturbances.
 
 
 
 A three-stage numerical algorithms for subspace state space system identification–prediction error method–gradient boosting decision tree (N4SID-PEM-GBDT) hybrid identification framework is proposed. First, N4SID is used to establish a linear state-space model and extract the dominant system dynamics. Next, prediction error method (PEM) is applied to refine the linear model parameters, thereby obtaining an improved benchmark model. Finally, causal time-series features are constructed from the optimized residuals, and gradient boosting decision tree (GBDT) is employed to learn nonlinear residual compensation for the pitch-rate and roll-rate channels.
 
 
 
 Time-domain validation using an independent dataset demonstrated that the proposed N4SID-PEM-GBDT framework achieved an R2 of 0.9112 and a root mean square error (RMSE) of 3.4518. Compared with N4SID and N4SID-PEM, the proposed method increased the average R2 by 13.17 and 8.15 percentage points, respectively, while reducing the average RMSE by 33.61% and 26.37%, respectively. Furthermore, compared with N4SID-PEM-RNN, N4SID-PEM-extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) and N4SID-PEM- Gaussian Process (GP), the proposed method reduced the average RMSE by 4.71%, 6.57% and 8.19%, respectively. These results demonstrate that the proposed method further reduces prediction errors on independent test data while retaining the ability of the linear state-space model to capture the dominant system dynamics.
 
 
 
 This study integrates subspace identification, prediction error optimization, and GBDT-based residual learning into a unified hybrid framework, providing an effective approach for high-precision modelling of strongly coupled small unmanned helicopter systems.
evidence_items.title: Hybrid N4SID-PEM-GBDT identification for small unmanned helicopter modeling

evidence_items.summary: Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infection is a primary driver of upper gastrointestinal morbidity among children in developing nations. This study aims to evaluate the clinical presentations, associated secondary complications, and therapeutic eradication outcomes of pediatric H. pylori cases within the municipality of Gharyan, Libya. A retrospective, cross-sectional cohort study was conducted on 100 consecutive pediatric patients (aged 1–15 years) diagnosed with H. pylori infection in Gharyan, Libya, over a period spanning from January 2023 to December 2024. Comprehensive clinical records were analysed to extract data on demographics, primary gastrointestinal complaints, risk factors, compliance diaries, and definitive post-treatment eradication success, verified by monoclonal stool antigen testing performed 4–8 weeks after treatment cessation. The study cohort comprised 55% females and 45% males. The predominant age demographic was school-age children (6–11 years) at 48%, followed by adolescents (12–15 years) at 30%, and toddlers (1–5 years) at 22%. Non-invasive monoclonal stool antigen testing served as the primary clinical diagnostic modality (94%). Epigastric pain was identified as the most prevalent primary complaint (66%), followed by chronic vomiting (21%) and growth failure (13%). Notably, 37% of the infected children suffered from documented iron deficiency anaemia (IDA), which demonstrated a statistically significant correlation with a symptom duration exceeding 6 months. Following empiric first-line standard triple therapy, the final eradication success rate was 76.0%, revealing a substantial treatment failure rate of 24.0%. The findings demonstrate a high therapeutic failure rate (24%) for standard empiric triple therapy in Gharyan, dropping significantly below the globally accepted 90% eradication benchmark. The high prevalence of extra-gastric complications, such as iron deficiency anaemia, emphasises the critical need for early non-invasive screening. Pediatric clinicians practising in western Libya should transition from empiric standard triple therapy to bismuth-containing quadruple regimens to counteract regional resistance.
evidence_items.title: Clinical Profile, Risk Factors, and Eradication Outcomes of Pediatric Helicobacter pylori Infection in Gharyan, Libya: A 2-Year Retrospective Study of 100 Cases

evidence_items.summary: Active colloidal matter provides a rich setting for the emergence of nonequilibrium patterns, dynamic aggregates, and self-assembled structures. Understanding how such organization arises from microscopic interactions, fluctuations, and sustained external driving remains a central challenge in soft-matter physics. This is largely because traditional theoretical and computational approaches often struggle with nonlinear dynamics, multiscale behavior, and high-dimensional parameter spaces. In this context, machine learning (ML) is increasingly used to identify relevant order parameters, classify dynamical regimes, predict emergent structures, infer assembly pathways, and guide the design and control of target states. This review examines how ML methods are incorporated into the study of pattern formation and self-assembly across both equilibrium and active colloidal systems. The discussion is organized around the analysis and representation of data pertaining to complex nonequilibrium systems, the prediction of dynamical and structural outcomes, the inference of latent variables and assembly pathways, and the design or control of target states through generative models and reinforcement learning strategies. We also discuss hybrid approaches that incorporate physical constraints to improve interpretability, robustness, and generalization. By focusing on the interplay between machine learning and nonequilibrium soft-matter physics, we highlight both the opportunities and the open challenges of the field, including the connection between learned representations and physical variables, limited extrapolation capability across state space, and the need for reproducible benchmarks and high-quality datasets. Overall, we argue that ML is emerging as an important complement to theory and simulation in the study of active colloidal self-assembly, not as a replacement for physical modeling, but as a means to accelerate discovery and deepen understanding of emergent nonequilibrium organization.
evidence_items.title: Machine learning techniques for understanding pattern formation and self-assembly in active colloidal systems.

evidence_items.summary: The European Ground Motion Service (EGMS) constitutes a part of the European Union’s Copernicus program, providing a continental-scale and open-access dataset of ground surface displacement. The EGMS data are derived from multi-temporal Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (MT-InSAR) processing of the Sentinel-1 SAR satellite imagery, collected from 2015, across the European territory. The paper introduces the EGMS-PCA tool, a Python-based graphical user interface (GUI) application that employs the Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to facilitate the temporal analysis of EGMS time series. The tool provides an efficient workflow that enables users to analyse MT-InSAR displacement components (i.e. ascending, descending, east-west, vertical) and distinguish between different displacement patterns. The EGMS-PCA tool has the capacity to automatically manage the EGMS data, merge and interpolate the time series, clip on a Region of Interest (ROI) provided by the user, apply the PCA analysis, generate a plot of each cluster and provide the output in a Geographic Information System (GIS)-ready format for further analysis. The practical utility of the tool is demonstrated through a country-scale benchmark application in Northern Ireland, where the complete workflow ingests almost one million measurement points and analyses over 380,000 of them within the region of interest in approximately 24 min. The resulting classification identifies a set of subsiding clusters whose spatial distribution shows a quantified agreement with independently mapped peatland areas, illustrating the scalability of the software and its suitability for the preliminary exploration of large-scale ground deformation datasets.
evidence_items.title: EGMS-PCA: a Python GUI tool for temporal analysis of EGMS time series

evidence_items.summary: Acute exposure to organophosphate (OP) nerve agents and pesticides induces status epilepticus (SE), nitrooxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and long-term neurological dysfunction. Although rodent models are widely used to study OP-induced neurotoxicity, the guinea pig offers important translational advantages due to its closer similarity to humans in cholinergic physiology and brain organization. The present study aimed to establish and characterize a guinea pig model of diisopropylfluorophosphate (DFP)-induced neurotoxicity suitable for therapeutic evaluation. Unlike the rat model, acute lower doses of DFP (3 or 4mg/kg, s.c.) did not induce behavioral toxicity signs or seizures, while 6mg/kg induced non-convulsive seizures with occasional convulsive seizures. However, 8mg/kg, reliably induced severe and sustained SE (>40min) without mortality. DFP-exposed animals (8mg/kg) transiently lost body weight (~10%) followed by recovery to control levels within three days post-exposure. During the 8 weeks of post-exposure, serum analysis revealed persistent nitro-oxidative stress characterized by elevated nitrite and reactive oxygen species levels, reduced glutathione concentrations, and a decreased GSH/GSSG ratio. DFP exposure (8mg/kg) significantly increased inflammatory cytokines and chemokines in both serum and cerebrospinal fluid, including TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1α, IL-1β, IL-17A, IL-18, and MCP-1 compared to control. Histological analyses revealed increased microgliosis, astrogliosis, and evidence of neurodegeneration in the amygdala, cortex, hippocampus, and thalamus at eight weeks post-DFP exposure (8mg/kg). These findings identify 8mg/kg DFP as the optimal dose for inducing robust status epilepticus (SE), neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, and neurodegeneration without mortality. Collectively, these results support the guinea pig as a clinically relevant higher-order preclinical model for evaluating novel medical countermeasures against organophosphate (OP)-induced neurotoxicity.
evidence_items.title: Optimization and Characterization of a Guinea Pig Model of Diisopropylfluorophosphate-Induced Status Epilepticus, Nitrooxidative Stress, and Neuroinflammation for Therapeutic Evaluation.

evidence_items.summary: Glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK-3β) is a multifunctional serine/threonine kinase implicated in neurodegeneration, cancer, metabolic disorders, and inflammatory diseases. The discovery of structurally novel GSK-3β inhibitors remains important for developing new chemical probes and therapeutic starting points. In this study, we established a machine learning-assisted computational screening workflow for the identification of potential GSK-3β inhibitors. A Random Forest (RF) classification model was trained using a curated dataset of reported GSK-3β-related compounds collected from 2016 to 2024. The optimized RF model showed good predictive performance, with an accuracy of 0.89 and an AUC-ROC of 0.91 ± 0.02, supporting its use as an initial prioritization tool for virtual screening. The trained classifier was applied to the Asinex compound library, and prioritized compounds were further evaluated through physicochemical and ADMET filtering, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics simulations. This integrated workflow led to the selection of two representative candidates, RF03 and RF05, for experimental validation. In vitro enzymatic assays confirmed moderate GSK-3β inhibitory activity, with IC₅₀ values of 85.04 µM for RF03 and 58.73 µM for RF05. Among them, RF05, which contains a non-classical and sterically hindered aromatic ester scaffold, also reduced the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including TNF-α and IL-6, while maintaining low cytotoxicity under the tested conditions. Overall, this study demonstrates the feasibility of combining machine learning-based prioritization with structure-based modeling and biological evaluation to identify previously underexplored GSK-3β inhibitory scaffolds. Although RF05 requires further optimization to improve potency, selectivity, and pharmacological properties, it provides a useful starting point for the development of next-generation GSK-3β-targeted anti-inflammatory agents.
evidence_items.title: Machine learning-guided discovery and preliminary biological evaluation of novel GSK-3β inhibitory scaffolds with anti-inflammatory potential

evidence_items.summary: Let Sym n denote the space of complex symmetric n×n matrices with the Hilbert–Schmidt inner product. Girard, Leung, Levick, Li, Paulsen, Poon and Watrous showed that the symmetric Werner–Holevo channel on M n has minimal mixed-unitary rank binom(n+1,2) if and only if Sym n admits an orthogonal basis consisting of unitary matrices. They established this for even n and for n=3, and conjectured it for all odd n; Levick and Rahaman settled the case of primes n≡7 (mod 8). We introduce a family of symmetric unitaries ("chirped circulants") for odd n and prove that, for this family, the pairwise orthogonality conditions reduce exactly to a square system of (n^2-1)/4 real equations in as many unknown phases. Using this reduction we give (i) a fully explicit basis for n=5, with all entries in an explicit degree-8 number field and an exact-arithmetic verification, and (ii) a computer-assisted proof, based on the Krawczyk operator evaluated in Arb ball arithmetic, that a symmetric unitary orthogonal basis exists for every odd n with 3≤n≤67. Consequently the conjecture of Girard et al. holds for all n≤68. We also record several obstructions to natural approaches for general odd n, and a further reduction for prime n.
evidence_items.title: Orthogonal bases of symmetric unitary matrices in odd dimensions and the mixed-unitary rank of the symmetric Werner–Holevo channel

evidence_items.summary: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into modern robotics is changing robots from systems that primarily execute predefined instructions into systems capable of interpreting complex environments, learning from experience, adapting their behaviour, and making decisions under uncertainty. This article examines the theoretical foundations and principal technological mechanisms that enable this transition. A narrative analytical review approach is used to synthesise selected peer-reviewed research on machine learning, deep learning, reinforcement learning, robot perception, autonomous planning, adaptive control, and human–robot interaction, together with relevant industrial safety standards. The analysis organises AI-enabled robotics around an integrated perception–learning–decision–control architecture and compares the contributions and limitations of major AI paradigms. The synthesis indicates that adaptive robotic capability does not arise from a single algorithm; it depends on the coordinated operation of sensing, state estimation, task and motion planning, control, feedback, and safety supervision. Learning-based methods can improve perception and adaptation, while model-based reasoning and conventional control remain important for stability, constraint handling, and predictable execution. Persistent barriers include limited transferability across embodiments and environments, data and computational demands, uncertain behaviour, explainability, cybersecurity, and the validation of safety in physical settings. The article proposes a set of design principles for developing more dependable autonomous robotic systems, emphasising hybrid intelligence, continuous evaluation, human oversight, and safety-by-design. The work provides a conceptual framework for researchers and developers examining the responsible integration of AI into next-generation robotics.
evidence_items.title: THE INTEGRATION OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE INTO MODERN ROBOTICS: THEORETICAL FOUNDATIONS, ADAPTIVE INTELLIGENCE, AND AUTONOMOUS SYSTEM DEVELOPMENT

evidence_items.summary: The Origins of 360° MDL preserves the starting point of the 360° MDL — Multidimensional Literature Review Model. In July 2023 the author sketched a literature review "resilient methodology" in four slides and applied it, a few days later, to a review of smart cities. This document redraws those original sketches in a modern form, explains the criteria behind every source stream, and traces each idea to 360° MDL Version 2026 (doi:10.5281/zenodo.23724393). Contents (14 pages). A foreword and a timeline from the first sketch (15 July 2023) to Version 2026; Approach A (Holistic) and Approach B (Influencers), redrawn, with the criteria of each stream and their Version 2026 equivalents; the simplified influencer rule (one most-cited and one most-recent paper); selection by Complementarity, Coverage and Diversity with a target of at most 50 items; the six original analyses, including the General Matrix and the Keywords Matrix; the 2023 smart cities review tables, with one paper coded across all four tables and the "Value Based Framework MDL" column that became the method's interpretive layer; a table mapping every 2023 element to Version 2026; and an afterword. It shows that the method's philosophy — multiple streams, portfolio selection, a 50-item corpus, matrices instead of summaries and a value-based framework at the end — dates from 2023, and that Version 2026 turned each intuition into an explicit rule, a tool and a test. Part of the 360° MDL ecosystem. evidence_items.summary: # Localizing and repairing structural deficits of a conceptual hydrological model with multi-source observations: data and code   ## Overview   This package contains the code and data needed to reproduce the analysis of structural deficits in the conceptual rainfall-runoff model SIMHYD. The method works as follows:   - A differentiable version of SIMHYD carries correction slots of identical structure and capacity on eight fluxes (S1–S8). - Forcing errors and observation errors are modeled separately from structural errors. - A deficit is localized by comparing competing single-slot hypotheses with a significance test. The comparison uses streamflow and, where available, soil moisture, evapotranspiration (ET) and snow water equivalent (SWE). - After localization, only the localized slots are repaired, and the repair is evaluated with variables not used in training.   The package covers two applications:   1. Synthetic experiments. Ten types of implanted structural deficits (D1–D9) and compound deficits (C1–C3) are tested, together with a no-deficit control (D0). Two independently generated truth sets are used (realizations r0 and r1), with eight observation combinations, two observation-quality levels and three types of input error. 2. Application to 156 CAMELS basins in the conterminous United States. Training uses streamflow, ESA CCI soil moisture, ERA5-Land or GLEAM evaporation, and UA SWE. Independent evaluation uses FLUXCOM-X-BASE ET and MODIS NDVI.   All results shown in the figures and tables of the associated article can be recomputed from the files in data/results/ . The 12 figure scripts in code/figs/ reproduce the article figures pixel for pixel from this package.
evidence_items.title: Localizing and repairing structural deficits of a conceptual hydrological model with multi-source observations: data and code

evidence_items.summary: Federated Learning (FL) with Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) enables efficient adaptation of Large Language Models (LLMs), yet its energy and carbon costs across hardware remain poorly understood. We evaluated federated Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning on NVIDIA A40, RTX 6000 Ada, and A100 GPUs using a 22 full factorial design that varied model size and local optimization steps. Power, energy consumption, and CO2-equivalent emissions were monitored throughout training. Factorial analysis of variance (ANOVA) attributed 84.8–91.2% of the variance in energy and emissions to local optimization steps, while model size explained less than 10%. Configurations with fewer steps achieved comparable accuracy with 6–8-fold lower energy consumption and higher accuracy per kWh. These findings identify local optimization intensity as the dominant driver of the training footprint and support configuration choices that balance predictive performance with energy efficiency.
evidence_items.title: Sustainable Federated Fine-Tuning with LoRA: Environmental Impact and Performance Footprint

evidence_items.summary: For fixed positive vertex activities, we maximize the independent-set partition function over labelled graphs with a prescribed number of edges. After ordering the activities, a weighted Kelmans identity reduces the optimization to graphs obtained by deleting a smallest universal vertex or a largest isolated vertex. An interval dynamic program computes the optimum for every edge budget using O(m^4) arithmetic operations on m vertices. Exact equality conditions for each compression and maximizing paths in the dynamic program give a polynomial criterion recognizing every optimal graph. The result determines the complete generalized Hamming weight hierarchy of homogeneous square-free quadratic evaluation codes on Cartesian sets containing zero with two alphabet sizes, and characterizes all optimal monomial subspaces.

evidence_items.summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a Structured PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/24244231 . Does the introduction explain the objective of the research presented in the preprint? Yes The introduction explains the objective clearly and in a logical order. 1. It first describes the background and the fact that fraud detection has moved from statistical models to machine learning, explainable AI (XAI), and decision-oriented evaluation (pp. 1–2). 2. It then names the problem. A fraud score with an explanation does not tell the auditor what to do next. The paper calls this the "prediction–decision–governance gap" (p. 2). 3. It states the aim directly, which is to develop a Human–AI Decision Governance Framework for fraud risk assessment. 4. It lists three research questions and four contributions. Are the methods well-suited for this research? Neither appropriate nor inappropriate This is a conceptual paper, so the methods section draws from existing literature and no data, sample, or statistical analysis is involved. What works well: 1. A conceptual design fits the aim of the paper, which is to connect several separate research areas and to propose ideas for later testing. 2. The paper follows a recognized approach for conceptual articles as recommended by Jaakkola (2020). 3. The author states openly that the literature was selected for a specific purpose and that the paper is not a systematic review. This honesty is good practice. 4. The author explicitly states boundary conditions, so readers know where the framework applies. What to Improve: 1. The steps from the literature to the six layers are described only briefly. The paper does not explain why there are six layers, why they are in this order, or what other designs were considered. 2. The equations do not match the framework.
evidence_items.title: Structured PREreview of "From Fraud Signals to Audit Response: A Human–AI Decision Governance Framework for Explainable Financial Statement Fraud Risk Assessment"

evidence_items.summary: Complete removable dentures frequently lose functional stability, occlusal balance, and mucosal adaptation due to polymerization shrinkage during laboratory processing, progressive residual ridge resorption, and gradual wear of artificial occlusal surfaces. Secondary modeling—encompassing split-cast laboratory remounting, clinical remounting in centric relation, functional base re-contouring, and selective occlusal equilibration—offers a systematic extraoral method to restore biomechanical harmony without fabricating an entirely new prosthesis. This clinical study evaluated the functional and occlusal outcomes of secondary modeling in 14 completely edentulous patients treated at the Department of Orthopedic Dentistry and Orthodontics of Andijan State Medical Institute. Each patient's maxillary and mandibular complete dentures underwent extraoral remounting on a semi-adjustable articulator using passive centric relation interocclusal records, followed by targeted selective grinding and functional border re-contouring. Quantitative assessment revealed that mean incisal pin opening decreased from 0.68 ± 0.19 mm before equilibration to 0.03 ± 0.02 mm after secondary modeling (p < 0.001). Simultaneous bilateral posterior occlusal contact symmetry increased from 28.6% (4 of 14 patients) at baseline to 92.9% (13 of 14 patients) post-remodeling (p < 0.001). Mean masticatory efficiency, assessed via standardized test-food breakdown, improved from 54.2 ± 8.4% to 81.6 ± 6.9% (p < 0.001), while unscheduled mucosal sore-spot recalls over 30 days were limited to 1 of 14 patients (7.1%). Secondary modeling reliably restores occlusal equilibrium and functional longevity in complete removable denture therapy.
evidence_items.title: SECONDARY MODELING OF COMPLETE REMOVABLE DENTURES

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly becoming core components of IT infrastructure, tasked with processing user data according to predefined instructions. However, LLMs remain vulnerable to prompt injection attacks, where malicious users inject directive tokens within the data to manipulate model behavior. The current defense strategies attempt to train LLMs to semantically distinguish between data and instruction tokens. Nevertheless, these approaches still face two key challenges: (1) the balance between security and utility, especially when interpreting the instruction-like tokens in the data section, and (2) the robustness against adaptive adversarial samples. In this work, we propose DRIP which aims to (1) achieve a new security-utility balance by ''de-instructionalization'', i.e., precisely removing the instruction semantics from the tokens in the data section while preserving their data semantics and (2) robustly maintain the effectiveness of the intended instruction, even against strong adversarial content. As for ''de-instructionalize'' tokens in the data section, we propose a training paradigm across data curation, model architecture, and loss design. It introduces a lightweight representation-editing module, which is trained to edit the embedding of instruction-like tokens in the data section, enhancing the model's security without compromising utility. As for preserving the intended instruction against unseen adversarial content, we improve the model architecture by introducing a lightweight residual module in LLM, largely reducing the overwriting possibility of adversarial content. We extensively compare DRIP with state-of-the-art techniques, including StruQ, SecAlign, ISE, and PFT on LLaMA-8B and Mistral-7B across three prompt injection benchmarks (SEP, AlpacaFarm, and InjecAgent). The results show that DRIP (1) improves role separation score by 44–64% and reduces attack success rate by over 68% for adaptive attacks and (2) achieves utility on par with the undefended model, indicating a new state-of-the-art against prompt injection attacks.
evidence_items.title: DRIP: Defending Prompt Injection via Token-wise Representation Editing and Residual Fusion

evidence_items.summary: The growing deployment of large language models (LLMs) in privacy-sensitive settings demands inference mechanisms that preserve data confidentiality. Homomorphic encryption (HE) offers a principled solution by enabling computation directly on encrypted data; however, existing solutions struggle to scale to full LLMs. We present Tricycle, a system for efficient private transformer inference. At its core, Tricycle introduces tricyclic encodings, a novel packing scheme that enables batch matrix multiplications with optimal multiplicative depth while naturally supporting multi-head attention. We demonstrate that Tricycle's matrix multiplications are particularly amenable for integration with other optimizations including Baby-Step Giant-Step optimizations, optimized block matrix multiplications, lazy relinearization, and complexification, which significantly improve performance. We further introduce statistical max estimation, a lightweight method for stabilizing softmax under HE. We implement Tricycle end-to-end on a GPU-accelerated CKKS pipeline and evaluate it on BERT models. For BERT-Base with 128 tokens, Tricycle achieves 100.5 seconds latency on a single GPU, yielding 6× and 3.4× speedups over prior state-of-the-art systems, Thor and Powerformer, respectively. These results demonstrate that careful design of packing, algorithms, and optimizations can significantly reduce the cost of private LLM inference, bringing practical deployment closer to reality.
evidence_items.title: Tricycle: Private Transformer Inference with Tricyclic Encodings

evidence_items.summary: Objectives: Pharmacotherapy during pregnancy is considered risky and continues to be a relevant issue. This study aimed to determine how pharmacotherapy in pregnant patients influences pregnancy outcomes in clinical practice and to investigate complex and hypothetical protective factors that contribute to pregnancy outcomes. Material and methods: A retrospective observational study of pregnant patients ( n = 112) was conducted at the Department of Internal Medicine, Teaching Hospital Nitra, in Nitra, Slovak Republic, over a period of 12 years. Clinical outcomes, including the stage of pregnancy, exposure of the embryo/foetus to therapeutic agents, and pregnancy outcomes, were assessed. Results: Among the assessed patients, 82 (73%) used therapeutic agents in the first trimester; the most common use was that of a single therapeutic agent ( n = 44, 39%). Patients most frequently used therapeutic agents from group N: Nervous system ( n = 80 therapeutic agents, 25%). Notably, although half of the patients ( n = 54) used therapeutic agents during the high-risk period for malformation, more than half had healthy newborns ( n = 74, 66%). From a risk perspective, therapeutic agents classified as having no teratogenic potential but that can lead to adverse development of the embryo/foetus were predominant ( n = 92 therapeutic agents, 29%). The presence of hypothetical protective factors capable of weakening and reducing the transfer of substances, therapeutic agents, or metabolites to the embryo/foetus and lowering the potential embryotoxic/foetotoxic effects was observed in 17% of patients in the studied sample who delivered healthy neonates ( n = 76). Conclusion: Pharmacotherapy during pregnancy must be carefully considered and follow the principles of rational pharmacotherapy. Even after exposure to risky pharmacotherapy, more than half of the pregnancies resulted in healthy neonatal outcomes.
evidence_items.title: Evaluation of pharmacotherapy in pregnant patients with a focus on its risks and hypothetical protective factors

evidence_items.summary: Multi-tenant LLM services can reduce serving costs by sharing a full-precision base model and storing compressed fine-tuning updates. Uploaded fine-tuning data can weaken alignment or implant harmful and targeted backdoors, but prior security studies quantize entire checkpoints. We evaluate BitDelta after full-parameter fine-tuning on four open-source models under static attacks, measuring factual utility separately. One-bit delta compression reduces malicious behavior in many tests relative to the full-precision attacked checkpoint. On Llama-2-7b-chat, mean harmfulness Score changes from 3.34 to 1.13 under red teaming and from 2.87 to 1.02 in a harmful-backdoor setting. In a targeted-backdoor setting, triggered ASR falls from 95% to 9%, while untriggered target insertion falls from 54% to 11%. By comparison, full-model GPTQ and int8 leave attack behavior close to the full-precision attacked checkpoint. Across 12 fine-tuning conditions, TriviaQA accuracy decreases by 5.35% on average, with substantial cross-model variation. A preliminary LogitLens analysis links the recovered safety behavior to refusal-token predictions in deeper layers. These findings apply to the tested models and BitDelta configurations; the comparison does not independently separate compression location from compression severity.
evidence_items.title: Delta-Weight Quantization Preserves Alignment in Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Malware sandboxes produce rich behavioral reports, yet these reports are lengthy, deeply nested JSON documents that defy direct analysis. In this paper, we address how general-purpose Large Language Models (LLMs) can reconstruct coherent behavioral chains of malware from such reports, and propose LHPD, a detection framework that bridges the cognitive reasoning gap between generic LLMs and expert analysis. LHPD introduces Semantics-Driven Feature Reconstruction (SDFR) to reorganize raw JSON reports into four complementary semantic dimensions—signatures, PE metadata, the import address table, and time-ordered API sequences—reducing structural noise while preserving causal links between high-level alerts and low-level traces. A Heuristic-Based Fine-Tuning Strategy (HBFS) then progressively aligns models with curated security heuristics before refining them on the reconstructed corpus. On a CAPE-based dataset of 13,623 reports, the LHPD-tuned Qwen3-32B attains 94.87% accuracy, surpassing both dedicated detectors and generic LLMs, and remains robust under few-shot settings.
evidence_items.title: POSTER: LHPD: LLM-Based Heuristic Pre-Training for Malware Detection

evidence_items.summary: When triaging unknown binaries, security analysts must quickly decide which samples to clear as benign, flag as malicious, or escalate for deeper analysis. Large Language Models (LLMs) could support these decisions by interpreting decompiled code, but a binary can contain hundreds or thousands of functions, making exhaustive LLM analysis impractical. We study how current LLMs behave when static triage is formulated as budgeted evidence acquisition: which functions they inspect and how they trade off benign clearance, malware detection, and escalation. To enable a controlled comparison, we implement TRIAGE-CPG, a fixed pipeline over a code property graph (CPG) of a decompiled binary. An LLM-free heuristic selects seed functions, an agent expands the resulting evidence dossier under a fixed budget, and a reporting stage produces a benign, suspicious, or malicious verdict together with a behavioral report. We evaluate eight closed-source and open-weight models on 1,000 Windows PE binaries, using a 600-sample test split and the same zero-shot protocol for every model. We assess the ternary verdicts under both a strict binary reading and triage balanced accuracy (tBA), which credits malware that is flagged or escalated and benign samples only when cleared. After analyzing about 40 of a mean 1,000 functions per binary, the highest-scoring model reaches a strict balanced accuracy of 0.805 and a tBA of 0.855, flagging 65% of malware, escalating another 12%, and clearing 94% of benign samples. The models implement different triage policies: high-specificity models produce small, malware-rich escalation queues, whereas recall-oriented models escalate or flag much more broadly. Both closed-source and open-weight models appear across this spectrum. Our results identify no universal deployment configuration: model choice itself determines the clear/flag/escalate trade-off under limited static evidence.
evidence_items.title: TRIAGE-CPG: A Cross-Model Study of Budgeted Static Malware Triage with Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Publicly accessible cloud object-storage buckets (e.g., Amazon S3 and Google Cloud Storage) pose a significant security risk to organizations by unintentionally exposing sensitive documents. Automated file classification is essential for detecting such leaks; however, accurate risk evaluation requires semantic understanding beyond keyword matching and metadata analysis. Although large language models (LLMs) can interpret document content and identify sensitive information, their adoption is often limited by the privacy risks of sending exposed data to third-party APIs. In this paper, we evaluate locally deployed open-source LLMs for automated severity classification of files found in public buckets, using model quantizations that balance accuracy and inference speed. Our experiments demonstrate that resource-efficient LLMs can support practical leak-detection workflows, enabling organizations to discover and remediate exposed sensitive information.
evidence_items.title: POSTER: Assessing Open-Source Large Language Models for Leaked File Classification

evidence_items.summary: Despite the considerable advantages of open-source large language models (LLMs) in terms of interpretability and customizability, the full-access sharing paradigm inevitably exposes them to a severe security threat, i.e., malware embedding attacks (MEAs), where adversaries embed malware binaries (i.e., payloads) into model parameters for subsequent execution. While existing sanitization defenses have been explored to eliminate payloads within parameters, they exhibit limited generalization against emerging MEAs and lack theoretical guarantees for model utility preservation. In this paper, we propose SymSan, an effective LLM sanitization method grounded in parameter space symmetry theory. SymSan leverages rigorously designed permutation and scaling symmetries, systematically transforming parameter matrices across complementary component pairs, thereby eliminating embedded payloads while ensuring mathematical functional equivalence. Experiments across diverse LLMs against a wide spectrum of MEAs demonstrate that SymSan achieves at least 0.47 BER against all evaluated existing MEAs while maintaining equivalent model performance on both foundational and downstream tasks, significantly outperforming all baselines.
evidence_items.title: SymSan: Mitigating Malware Embedding in Large Language Models via Parameter Space Symmetry

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are well-known for their natural language generation abilities, but their performance in domain-specific text comprehension, particularly for Classical Chinese and English, has been less explored. This study focuses on bilingual data from Zizhi Tongjian in Classical Chinese and English. We construct an entity extraction instruction dataset by manually annotating official titles in fifteen volumes of Zizhi Tongjian. The annotations are verified using a BERT-based model. Based on this, we build an instruction dataset for entity extraction to fine-tune LLMs. The study involves fine-tuning two types of LLMs: the Xunzi series (domain-specific models for ancient texts) and general open-source LLMs using the LoRA framework. We experiment with different prompt formats to assess their impact on performance. Results show that, under identical conditions, the Xunzi-Qwen2-7B model outperforms other models. The best results were achieved by constructing instruction data from annotated original text, with entity-only instruction data also showing improvements. After fine-tuning with 5,000 samples, the Xunzi-Qwen2-7B model achieved an accuracy of 85.90 per cent, recall of 86.75 per cent, and F1 score of 86.32 per cent for official title extraction in Zizhi Tongjian.
evidence_items.title: Research on ancient text entity extraction based on domain-specific large language models

organizations: University of Massachusetts Amherst, Amherst, Massachusetts, USA

evidence_items.summary: Discovering new censorship evasion strategies remains a predominantly slow and manual process. Prior systems that automate evasion discovery are restricted to packet headers and unencrypted protocols by the limited expressiveness of their domain-specific grammars, leaving more complex and widely-used encrypted protocols like TLS and QUIC out of reach. To address this, we present CircumVolve, a system that formulates censorship evasion as LLM-guided program synthesis within an evolutionary optimization loop. Candidate evasion strategies are expressed as executable Python programs that can encode arbitrary protocol manipulations, including cryptographic operations, and are iteratively refined by an LLM that proposes semantically informed mutations based on empirical feedback. This programmatic representation enables automated discovery of evasion strategies across the full network stack. We evaluate CircumVolve on five major network protocols subject to censorship (TCP/IP, DNS, HTTP, TLS, and QUIC) in both simulated and real-world environments. Against real-world censors in China, Iran, Pakistan, and Kazakhstan, the system successfully identifies effective evasion techniques spanning all protocol layers, from variants of previously known methods to entirely novel strategies.
evidence_items.title:
<scp>CircumVolve:</scp>
                    Automated Discovery of Censorship Evasion Strategies Using Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Road infrastructure is a long-lived public investment exposed to uncertainty in terrain, design, procurement, traffic management, climate, materials, stakeholder interfaces and contract administration. The resulting project records offer an opportunity to complement conventional management with evidence-based forecasting, provided the data are documented and the models are evaluated responsibly. This textbook has been structured for engineering students, site and planning engineers, construction managers, public-sector road authorities and researchers. It begins with conventional management concepts and data architecture, progresses to machine learning and integrated prediction, and concludes with a realistic case-study methodology and practical pathways for implementation in Iraq. The emphasis is on human-supervised decision support rather than automated contractual decisions. Baselines, contemporary project updates, measurement standards, professional judgment and defensible documentation remain essential. Throughout the volume, the reader should distinguish analytical demonstration from field-validated causal or predictive evidence.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Road Project Management

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence promises to reduce the uncertainty that surrounds entrepreneurial decisions by predicting demand, scanning environments, and evaluating strategic alternatives at negligible cost. We argue that this promise is conditional on the type of uncertainty a decision involves. Drawing on real options reasoning and research distinguishing risk from Knightian uncertainty, we theorize that AI reduces uncertainty that can be resolved through information but cannot resolve uncertainty that is revealed only through action. When decision makers fail to distinguish the two, AI produces uncertainty compression, a condition in which perceived uncertainty falls faster than actual uncertainty, leading entrepreneurs to abandon flexibility and commit prematurely to irreversible investments. We contrast two modes of AI use. In oracle mode, AI is used to resolve uncertainty and select a single course of action. In generator mode, AI is used to expand, stage, and monitor a portfolio of real options. We develop propositions specifying when each mode improves decisions and how entrepreneurial theorizing and competitive diffusion of AI condition these effects. The framework reframes AI not as a substitute for entrepreneurial judgment under uncertainty but as a technology that changes the economics of flexibility.
evidence_items.title: Computing The Incomputable? Artificial Intelligence and Entrepreneurial Decision Making Under Uncertainty
