evidence_items.summary: Soil arsenic contamination threatens vegetable production in South Asia, yet the dose-dependent response of brinjal (Solanum melongena L.) to elevated soil arsenate [As(V)] remains insufficiently quantified. A pot experiment was conducted at Sher-e-Bangla Agricultural University, Dhaka, Bangladesh, using a Completely Randomized Design with four replications to evaluate the effects of sodium arsenate (T₁:0, T2:25, T3:50, and T4:75 mg As kg⁻¹ soil) on S. melongena cv. BARI Brinjal 5. Arsenate exposure progressively inhibited vegetative growth, root development, biomass accumulation, and reproductive yield, with peak phytotoxicity observed at 75 mg As kg⁻¹ soil. Compared with the control, the 75 mg As kg⁻¹ treatment significantly reduced root length by 61.7%, root dry weight by 54.2%, plant height by 39.6%, leaf number by 29.2%, and stem diameter by 27.8%, alongside a 32.9% decline in shoot dry weight. Reproductive traits were similarly impaired, reducing individual fruit weight by 34.6% and total fruit yield per plant from ~1.4 kg to ~0.3 kg. These findings demonstrate that soil arsenate severely compromises brinjal productivity; thus, proper soil management and suitable cultivation practices need to be adopted for sustainable vegetable production in arsenic affected areas.
evidence_items.title: Growth and Yield Responses of Brinjal (Solanum melongena L.) to Increasing Levels of Soil Arsenic Contamination

evidence_items.summary: Practitioners routinely swap one large language model (LLM) for another as new releases appear, tacitly assuming the surrounding strategy is unaffected. We test that assumption. Starting from the open-source TradingAgents framework [20], a multi-agent workflow emits return views and confidence scores for a 14-instrument 60/40 proxy, mapped into a Black–Litterman model. Holding universe, pipeline, optimizer, and 2019–2024 backtest fixed, we replace an open 32B model (GLM-4-32B) with a tiered frontier stack (GPT-5.4 with GPT-5-nano); the passive benchmark and a non-LLM control are bit-identical across runs. One result is unambiguous and invariant to the swap: both suites destroy value. Averaged over 16 configurations, each loses \(3.5\%\)/yr to passive and \(4.7\%\)/yr to a control built from four rule-based heuristics on the same universe and optimizer (p ≤ 0.021 throughout). Forecasting skill is absent under both stacks, and a 200-permutation test, checked against an oracle that it rejects decisively, places the published confidence-to-Ω map inside its own null. Substitution changes what the system says: across more than 15, 000 views per run, the frontier stack’s mean 30-day view is 1.33pp lower, far beyond within-run noise, though with one run per stack we cannot compare this gap with that between two runs of one stack. Its effect on what the portfolio earns is unresolved: no comparison at our 10bps baseline is significant; at 50bps the paired difference turns significant against the open stack’s higher turnover, so the sign follows the cost assumption, not the backbone; and detecting the gap we observe at 80% power would take 12.5 years of data against the 5.25 available. One backtest per candidate model can reject a strategy but cannot validate a swap.
evidence_items.title: One Backtest Can Reject a Strategy but Cannot Validate a Model Swap: LLM-Stack Sensitivity in Multi-Agent Black–Litterman Asset Allocation

evidence_items.summary: Fundamental investors reason from cognitive frameworks, and large language model investment agents inherit the same idea, using such a framework as their reasoning backbone. A real market is not stationary. The market shifts, and a thesis that once held can fail after a paradigm shift. Existing financial agents treat the framework as a fixed input and cannot track such a shift. We ask two questions. Can an agent detect that its own framework is being disrupted? Can it revise that framework in time? We consider two natural mechanisms for keeping pace: a memory of incoming evidence, and self-evolution of the framework itself. Our benchmark is a 61-day stream of 1,126 real news clusters over an accumulating investment paradigm shift. Investment experts hindsight-label each cluster as reinforce, disrupt, or noise. The expert framework is recovered at the start and end of the window. We ablate four memory architectures and seven self-evolution architectures against these labels. A precise structured memory yields a modest accuracy gain, while an imprecise memory is harmful. More importantly, no memory design halts the temporal decay of disrupt recall. Self-evolution of the framework recovers it, lifting late-window disrupt recall from \(27.6\%\) to \(43.4\%\) at no accuracy cost. The two self-evolution families expose a recall-versus-abstraction trade-off. Anchored patches recover recall but barely move the thesis. Full rewrites move closer to the expert at a cost in stability. In our setup, memory and self-evolution act as partial substitutes rather than complements. Stacking them yields no compounding benefit.
evidence_items.title: Memory × Self-Evolution: When Agents with Cognitive Frameworks Meet Market Paradigm Shifts in Investment

evidence_items.summary: Resolved records can inform forecast assessment, but access does not ensure that a language-model financial agent uses them. We study this reconstruction–use gap in 30,360 A-share firm-years with 27,772 resolved annual earnings-forecast claims, using blinded interventions that hold the current disclosure fixed while changing the resolved record. In a three-checkpoint primary panel, authoritative resolution content alone raises the high-minus-low fulfillment-probability gap (record sensitivity) slightly (+ 0.048), whereas correct claim–resolution relations (+ 0.246) and temporal alignment (+ 0.199) have larger effects. Issuer-specific attribution is unsupported. Across five fixed checkpoints, models match claims to resolutions by pseudo-year almost perfectly when asked, yet weakly deploy that relation in direct predictions. Reconstruct-Then-Predict (RTP) increases record sensitivity in all five (descriptive mean + 0.404). Component contrasts support explicit labeling and compact record states, but do not isolate reconstruction from computation, length, or salience. A shorter current-claim-only scaffold does not increase record sensitivity. In a separate three-checkpoint evaluation on 2,471 FY2025 events, resolved-record memory with FY2024-fitted calibration lowers Brier scores and reduces the failure rate among the highest-scored 20% by 8.62–12.59 percentage points. A structured logistic reference remains stronger on this endpoint. The contribution is a diagnosis of record-conditioned information use and an interface workflow. Fresh local validation supports directional stability under repeated generation and mild wording changes; a post-hoc score-combination analysis finds a small incremental Brier gain for GLM.
evidence_items.title: Access Is Not Use: The Reconstruction–Use Gap in Language-Model Financial Agents

evidence_items.summary: Large vision language models (LVLMs) increasingly exhibit implicit geolocation inference capabilities, which raises concerns that publicly shared images can leak sensitive location information even without explicit metadata. To systematically quantify this privacy leakage, we present a large-scale empirical evaluation of 19 state-of-the-art LVLMs from 9 commercial LVLM providers, including models such as Claude-Opus-4.8, Gemini-3.1-Pro, GPT-5.5, Grok-4.6, Llama-4-Maverick, Qwen-3.5, MiniMax-M3, and Kimi-K2.7, etc. The evaluation spans 10,620 geotagged social images covering six continents and over 180 countries across diverse visual categories, under a no-fine-tuning setup with two prompting strategies, including zero-shot and Chain-of-Thought reasoning. Furthermore, our framework conducts a fine-grained category-level analysis to explore when LVLM geolocation inference is reliable and when it degrades, and further illustrates regional biases and the calibration of safety filters against privacy-sensitive queries. Our findings reveal that top-tier commercial LVLMs exhibit exceptionally strong capabilities under both prompting strategies. In addition, performance varies systematically with visual content, while regional disparities and inconsistent safety-filter calibrations further amplify the privacy risk. Overall, our study provides a comprehensive framework for evaluating LVLMs geolocation inference and its privacy impacts, demonstrating that LVLMs pose a concrete and substantial threat of geolocation privacy leakage in real-world settings.
evidence_items.title: From Snapshot to Snooping: An Empirical Study on Geolocation Privacy Leakage in Large Vision Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA)-based embodied agents combine large AI models with physical perception and actuation, creating safety and security risks when unauthorized actions lead to physical hazards. These systems therefore require context-based access control that accounts for runtime conditions while meeting latency constraints. However, existing work has focused primarily on access policies, leaving the system-level implications of alternative access-control designs underexplored. This short paper implements a context-based authorization framework for VLA-based embodied agents and evaluates motion thresholds, session key validity periods, and centralized versus decentralized authorization deployments. Our results quantify how these design choices affect authorization frequency and end-to-end latency and show that decentralized authorization substantially reduces latency and variability.
evidence_items.title: Design Exploration for Context-Based Access Control of Vision-Language-Action Model-Based Embodied Agents

evidence_items.summary: Aligned large language models (LLMs) often refuse harmful requests under direct prompting, motivating decomposition-based jailbreak attacks that split an unsafe task into multiple narrower sub-questions. Although such attacks can reduce refusal, existing methods typically rely on static or heuristic decomposition strategies and lack principled mechanisms for improving decomposition quality or selecting among decompositions of different granularities. In this work, we propose a unified decomposition-based jailbreak framework that combines reinforcement-learning-based policy improvement with neuron-guided adaptive selection. We first train a weak decomposer using online reward-based optimization, where generated sub-questions are evaluated by downstream refusal behavior and helpfulness. We then construct a neuron-based risk score based on internal activations of a strong model and use it at inference time to rank candidate decompositions and select the lowest-risk candidate for execution. The trained decomposer and reference-model scorer are reused across target models without target-specific training. Tested on multiple aligned strong models, the proposed pipeline consistently reduces refusal while maintaining helpfulness. Compared with representative automatic jailbreak baselines, it achieves stronger attack performance with substantially lower refusal exposure, which is particularly important in commercial API settings where repeated refusals may increase the risk of monitoring, throttling, or access restrictions. Our mechanistic analyses further suggest an activation dilution effect: when a harmful request is decomposed into separately executed sub-questions, safety-relevant signals are dispersed across queries, whereas recombining them into a single batched prompt partially restores risk. These results show that effective decomposition-based jailbreaks depend not only on whether a task is decomposed, but also on how the decomposition policy is learned and how decomposition granularity is controlled at inference time.
evidence_items.title: Jailbreaking via Activation Dilution: Neuron-Guided Adaptive Decomposition of Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Organizations increasingly host open-weight large language models (LLMs) on dedicated cloud instances to avoid the opaque data control imposed by closed-source APIs and the burden of costly local infrastructure. However, this deployment paradigm inadvertently exposes sensitive tenant prompts and outputs to service providers. Existing protection routes do not fit this setting well in practice: cryptographic inference incurs prohibitive overheads; Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) rely on specialized hardware that is difficult to deploy consistently across heterogeneous legacy accelerators; and traditional data-only obfuscation methods, such as token replacement, require substantial perturbation to achieve meaningful privacy, often causing severe utility degradation. To address this gap, we present TWIST, a practical system for private open-weight LLM serving on dedicated cloud instances. Rather than perturbing input tokens alone, TWIST applies a shared, structure-preserving transformation to both the model weights and input tokens. This coupled design extends protection beyond data-only obfuscation and addresses the traditional utility bottleneck. We analyze leakage to an honest-but-curious provider using Rényi-metric differential privacy (RmDP), and show a smaller privacy budget than a data-only baseline with the same online mechanism. Practically, we implement TWIST for modern dense and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures, including attention, FFN, and MoE routing modules, without disrupting standard serving pipelines. Evaluations on the 671B-parameter DeepSeek-V3.1-Terminus model show that TWIST reduces token recovery rate to under 5% against advanced inversion attacks, while incurring only 0.0% - 3.5% accuracy loss and <10% inference speed loss, offering a practical solution for private tenant-dedicated LLM serving.
evidence_items.title: TWIST: Private Tenant-Dedicated LLM Serving via Joint Model-Token Transformation

evidence_items.summary: Financial causal claims carry modality, commitment, and institutional agency that cause–effect spans discard. We formalize these as a Modal Causal Frame (MCF) and audit an open extraction pipeline whose labels largely conform to its schema and were evaluated using a large language model (LLM) judge and span-overlap scores, yet rarely quote their source. Null-baseline audits expose weaknesses in the reported evaluation: a whole-passage baseline outperforms both extractors under the evaluated FinCausal token-overlap score. We repair this with a provenance-aware protocol that verifies every span against its source before release, without losing structured output. The verified student exceeds its base-model reference in exact span grounding and several fields on a controlled challenge. A three-seed replication does not reproduce the apparent grounding–modality trade-off in the mean results. The tested modular extraction-and-field-prediction pipeline achieves higher modal accuracy than the corresponding single-stage student. Under institutional, temporal, and genre splits, raw student grounding remains high in most cases, while modal accuracy on the shared diagnostic suite varies with training composition. The verified release is more useful downstream only in a narrow setting: it improves prediction of the next observed rate direction under retrospective institution transfer, exceeding the strongest non-MCF text baseline by about 0.22 macro-F1, but yields no consistent benefit on the two shorter-horizon targets. The results support source-verifiable supervision, null-baseline evaluation, and modular span extraction and MCF field prediction for financial text.
evidence_items.title: Auditing and Repairing Modal Causal Extraction in Financial Text

evidence_items.summary: A shadow rating provides an indicative credit assessment for unrated debt. We study the post-pricing task of predicting a municipal reference rating at the time of issue, from issuance spread, deal structure, and prior market evidence. The evidence available differs by issuer history: a no-history issuer has no prior issuance in the data and must be rated from comparable bonds, whereas an established issuer draws on its own prior spreads and structures in addition to comparable bonds. We evaluate a deterministic two-regime policy that routes each bond by a fixed rule on prior issuance: no-history issuers to a retrieval-grounded large language model (LLM), established issuers to a history-aware gradient-boosted tree. On a frozen out-of-sample test of U.S. municipal bonds against issue-date reference ratings, the LLM improved accuracy over an information-matched non-LLM model for no-history issuers but not for established ones, where the tree models did as well as or better than the LLM. Because the benefit is confined to the no-history regime, routing on issuer history gives the lowest overall error of the policies tested and calls the LLM on 23.4% of bonds.
evidence_items.title: History-Conditioned Routing for Shadow Ratings: Evidence from Municipal Bonds

evidence_items.summary: Large language models embedded in financial workflows fail most dangerously by emitting confident, well-formatted but wrong numbers with no signal distinguishing them from correct ones. We argue that the central deployment problem is governability: a system must determine when a question supports a numeric answer and when it should instead clarify, intercept, or refuse. We present VerifiQuant, a governance-by-execution framework that packages financial logic into inference contracts and evaluates each query through an executable diagnostic funnel before deterministic computation. This separation makes computation, clarification, and refusal structured and auditable while keeping financial arithmetic outside the language model. Against matched retrieval-and-execution baselines, and within a declared contract library, the principal benefit is not higher accuracy on well-posed questions but safer behavior when an input does not justify a number. When it finds no applicable contract, it says so instead of guessing. Coverage sweeps and failure analysis put a price on this boundary: safety is bought with coverage rather than with accuracy, and residual failures remain attributable to specific runtime frontiers.
evidence_items.title: VerifiQuant: Governance-by-Execution for Financial LLM Workflows

evidence_items.summary: Commodity markets react rapidly to evolving geopolitical, macroeconomic, and supply-chain narratives, yet traditional volatility forecasting frameworks often fail to capture the semantic structure of financial news. This paper proposes NarrativeRL, an interpretable generative-AI framework for commodity market risk forecasting and adaptive hedging. Using more than 645,000 Reuters oil-market headlines from 2014–2024, we construct a Narrative Signal Index (NSI) combining attention intensity, tone imbalance, semantic novelty, narrative disagreement, geopolitical risk, and supply-shock signals extracted via sentence-transformer embeddings, topic-aware decomposition, and a large language model interpretation layer, and embed these representations into a reinforcement-learning-based hedging module that adapts hedge ratios under transaction costs and changing market regimes. Empirical results show that narrative-aware representations improve realised volatility forecasting relative to HAR-based benchmarks, most clearly at the 22-day horizon (Diebold–Mariano p = 0.039), with narrative effects becoming larger in high-volatility regimes. In out-of-sample hedging experiments, NarrativeRL attains the highest Sharpe ratio, narrowly ahead of volatility targeting, and reduces CVaR95 by 41% relative to the unhedged position, while volatility-targeting and HAR-based hedges attain lower tail risk at the cost of lower returns. NarrativeRL remains ahead of the unhedged benchmark across all tested transaction-cost settings. These findings suggest that interpretable generative AI can support adaptive financial decision systems by transforming evolving market narratives into deployable risk-monitoring and hedging signals.
evidence_items.title: NarrativeRL: Narrative-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning for Anticipatory Commodity Hedging

evidence_items.summary: Today, platforms of Model-as-a-Service (MaaS) provides access to various foundation models to users. Users trust that the platform indeed provides the exact service as requested. However, this trust may be misplaced for benign or malicious intentions, where results from providers are not exactly the same as what the user requested. To detect such violations, this paper introduces Espeon, a large language model (LLM) inference verification framework. It enables reproducible deterministic inference through batch-invariant kernels and includes different verification variants for flexible computation and storage budgets of verification. We evaluated Espeon with single-point manipulation cases and Espeon's performance of serving and verification. Espeon can detect such cases, and under the full verification mode it can achieve a speed-up of 4.56X compared to serving time.
evidence_items.title: ESPEON: Verifying the Predestined Execution of Deterministic LLM Inference

evidence_items.summary: Large language model assistants have become a popular way to learn about software vulnerabilities, yet whether they effectively support this process remains unclear. We present a controlled within-subject study with 70 participants comparing LLM-based assistance with web search across five dimensions of vulnerability understanding. We find that LLM-based assistance is associated with smaller measured learning gains than web search, with the disadvantage concentrated in reasoning-oriented dimensions such as understanding causes, runtime behavior, and security consequences. Process analysis reveals that LLM sessions involve broader but faster-shifting queries, earlier movement toward solution-seeking, and reduced sustained engagement with explanatory content. Despite these smaller measured gains, participants consistently perceive LLM assistance as more helpful, clearer, and more efficient, yet report comparable workload to web search. These findings reveal a gap between perceived support and measured learning gains. Motivated by this gap, we design VulnScaffold, a scaffolded LLM-based learning system that restructures query formulation, response organization, and reflective practice. A preliminary evaluation suggests promising improvements in both learning outcomes and user experience, helping address the gap identified in LLM-based learning.
evidence_items.title: Learning Less While Asking More: How LLM-Based Assistance Shapes Vulnerability Learning

evidence_items.summary: Session Replay (SR) is a powerful tool that reconstructs a user's in-app session from fine-grained UI states and interaction events collected over time. Although SR is legitimately used by app developers, it may introduce significant security and privacy risks by recording sensitive on-screen interactions. While these risks have been studied on the web, their prevalence and nature in the mobile ecosystem remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we present the first large-scale, systematic dissection of SR in Android apps. To enable the study, we developed TapSpy, a novel auditing framework that synergistically combines program analysis with schema-guided, evidence-grounded large language model reasoning to perform a deep semantic audit of SR usage. Using TapSpy, we conducted a measurement study on 47,855 high-impact Android apps. Our findings reveal a systemic failure in the mobile ecosystem's approach to SR security and privacy. Transparency is the first casualty: the vast majority of apps using SR fail to disclose this data collection in their Data Safety sections, creating a significant gap between their declared and actual privacy practices. We uncover a stark asymmetry in developer effort, where developers meticulously enrich session data with user identifiers and custom events for analytics but overwhelmingly rely on coarse, default masking for privacy. Consequently, risks rarely occur in isolation but instead form dangerous bundles, such as failure in redacting sensitive UI content (i.e., masking), logging sensitive information, linking it to a user's identity, and failing to disclose any of it. Our work provides the first large-scale empirical study of SR risks of these widespread issues in mobile apps and offers actionable insights for developers, SR vendors, and platform operators to mitigate the risks associated with this powerful technology. In line with responsible disclosure, we reported high-severity risks to the developers of affected apps.
evidence_items.title: TapSpy: Semantic Usage Analysis and Triangulated Risk Assessment of Session Replay in Mobile Apps

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) reportedly ‘reason’ with increasing sophistication, but whether they ‘know’ when they are wrong remains poorly understood. We study epistemic calibration, the alignment between expressed confidence and empirical correctness, across approximately 30 contemporary models and configurable reasoning-effort budgets, using XFinBench (graduate-level financial reasoning) and SQuAD v2 (answerable and unanswerable questions). Reported confidence stays high relative to accuracy, with weak discrimination between correct and incorrect or unsupported answers. Miscalibration follows a Dunning–Kruger–like pattern: weaker models are often strongly overconfident, while frontier models are mildly underconfident. Reasoning effort significantly improves accuracy but has no detectable effect on the confidence–accuracy gap or ECE; stable between-model differences explain over 96% of calibration variance, versus a negligible effort effect. Calibration deteriorates most on scenario planning and numerical modeling. On SQuAD v2, models answer four in five unanswerable questions and remain near-maximally confident even when no answer is supported; higher reasoning effort yields no robust gain in calibration or abstention after multiplicity correction. We discuss implications for evaluation, deployment, and the design of calibration-aware, boundary-aware financial reasoning systems.
evidence_items.title: Reasoning More, Knowing No Better? Epistemic Calibration in Financial Reasoning Tasks

evidence_items.summary: Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) traditionally employ a ''measure-then-launch'' model, attesting all code and data before execution begins. While this provides strong integrity guarantees, it imposes a startup latency proportional to the total program size, which is a significant bottleneck for large-scale applications like Large Language Models (LLMs) or databases that may only access a fraction of their footprint. We propose a lazy-verification architecture that decouples holistic attestation from per-block verification. At launch, the design performs an attestation of compact metadata representing the entire program state. Integrity is enforced through incremental verification of requested code and data blocks during runtime loading, before their first architecturally visible use. We formally model enclave execution under lazy verification and prove that our design preserves the same security properties and accepted execution traces as conventional whole-program attestation. We implement our design on both Intel SGX and AMD SEV-SNP. Evaluation across network services, database workloads, and LLM inference shows that our approach significantly reduces startup overhead and improves end-to-end performance, particularly for data-intensive applications with sparse access patterns.
evidence_items.title: Attest the Whole, Verify Incrementally: Whole-Program Integrity via Lazy Verification in Trusted Execution Environments

evidence_items.summary: The inception of large language models (LLMs) is expected to revolutionize the software security analysis pipeline. However, is it possible to use state-of-the-art LLMs for detecting and reasoning about the attack vector of real-world wireless attacks? In this paper, we propose, design and evaluate AirVScan– a generic workflow to study the current capabilities of LLMs in light of analyzing wireless attacks. AirVScan takes a packet sequence, possibly containing an attack, as input and as an output, it produces the attack vector (e.g., abnormal packet field) with reasoning if the attack is detected. AirVScan differs from works that investigate LLMs to understand the security of source code, as our approach merely takes the packet sequence as an input. We implement the workflow of AirVScan and evaluate it with state-of-the-art LLMs (o3, grok-4, gemini-2. 5-pro) against 40 benign test cases and 128 attack test cases. Among them, 80 attack test cases exploit real-world implementation vulnerabilities in two widely used wireless protocols (Bluetooth and 5G NR). Our evaluation reveals that AirVScan correctly reasons about the root cause of wireless attacks with a rate of 60.7% for Bluetooth but with only 7.7% for 5G NR, highlighting the limitations of current LLMs to reason about attacks on complex protocol implementations. We also evaluated AirVScan to study the effectiveness of LLMs for an unfamiliar protocol that we created by obfuscating Modbus. For such an unfamiliar protocol, AirVScan was mostly ineffective at reasoning about complex, synthesized attacks. However, the inclusion of context improved the attack vector identification to over 82.1%. Finally, we compare AirVScan with AirBugCatcher-a competitive and customized tool for analyzing attack vector of wireless attacks. Our results shed light on the LLMs' current capabilities and required future research for detecting wireless attacks.
evidence_items.title: AirVScan: Are LLMs Capable of Detecting and Reasoning about Wireless Attacks?

evidence_items.summary: Memory safety vulnerabilities account for approximately 70% of reported security bugs, prompting the adoption of Rust, a systems programming language designed to prevent such issues through compile-time checks. While Rust categorizes code into safe and unsafe regions, we identify a previously understudied class of vulnerabilities: modular unsafe functions (MUF) in Rust code. These functions appear safe to the compiler but are, in fact, unsafe within the whole module's APIs and can cause undefined behavior without using the unsafe keyword, leading to a misleading sense of safety and unsound issues in Rust. We present the first systematic study of mufs, defining five root cause categories from empirical analysis. We develop Coin, a detection system using fine-tuned large language models for vulnerability identification and proof-of-concept generation. Coin achieves 63.7% precision and 80.4% recall on labeled evaluation set, outperforming existing tools. On evaluation of 10,000 randomly sampled Rust crates, Coin identified 26 unknown mufs with 14 developer confirmations and 10 CVE assignments.
evidence_items.title: The Illusion of Rust Safety: Detecting Modular Unsafe Functions with LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Large language models increasingly serve as extraction layers in financial decision pipelines, but their quality is typically evaluated with field-level accuracy metrics that treat all errors as equally consequential. We distinguish two questions: which extraction errors are most damaging when they occur, and which matter most at their observed prevalence. We develop a decision-aware stress-testing framework that combines opportunity-set-normalised error injection with human calibration and measures downstream degradation through changes in cross-sectional RankIC. Applied to 28,857 earnings 8-K events from 2016–2025, the framework shows that sign reversals are the most damaging tested corruption conditional on occurrence. Yet in a representative probability sample of 380 human-labelled releases, direction disagreements are common (\(29.8\%\)) but consist overwhelmingly of lower-severity one-step moves. No sign reversals are observed (95% upper bound \(0.8\%\)). An exact decomposition shows that downstream loss is governed by return-aligned rank movement, explaining why frequent extraction errors need not be the most decision-critical. Financial LLM validation should therefore prioritise errors by both downstream severity and observed prevalence, not by aggregate error frequency alone.
evidence_items.title: From Extraction Error to Decision Cost: Stress-Testing Financial LLM Extraction Pipelines

evidence_items.summary: The Internet hosts billions of publicly accessible services, many of which inadvertently expose sensitive data or allow device manipulation. Historically, understanding the security implications of exposed Internet services required manual analysis or a priori knowledge, neither of which scales to the diversity of devices and services in the wild. In this paper, we show that Large Language Models (LLMs) change this dynamic and can identify security-relevant exposure without predefined rules or fingerprints. After evaluating their efficacy, we leverage LLMs to conduct the first large-scale measurement of HTTP(S)-based exposure and RTSP camera feeds. We use LLMs to build a hierarchical taxonomy of services and develop a multi-stage pipeline that combines lightweight ML classifiers with targeted LLM analysis to identify and triage security-critical exposure. We examine five types of security-critical exposure: directory listings, business applications and dashboards, IoT device interfaces, pages showing stack traces, and camera feeds. Our approach identifies thousands of dangerously exposed services, including healthcare management systems, financial documents, API keys, and private cameras.
evidence_items.title: Exposure is All You Need: Using LLMs to Identify Critical Endpoints at Internet Scale

evidence_items.summary: Large language models can generate programs that compile and pass functional tests, but these outcomes are insufficient for evaluating code in secure multi-party computation (MPC). MPC programs must also follow the target interface's programming constraints, implement the requested algorithm, and satisfy the stated secure-operation efficiency criteria. Using NLMPC, a staged code-generation framework, we conduct an empirical study of 3,600 C++ programs generated by three LLMs for three algorithms under four generation settings that vary API instructions, explicit programming constraints, and iterative repair. We evaluate each program along four dimensions: functional correctness, MPC conformance, algorithmic adherence, and MPC efficiency. Although 59.2% of the generated programs passed the functional correctness tests, only 31.0% satisfied all four criteria. Functional testing alone did not establish conformance, adherence to the requested algorithm, or compliance with the stated efficiency criteria. Adding MPC-specific constraints revealed trade-offs: aggregate functional correctness and MPC conformance increased, while algorithmic adherence decreased. Validation-guided repair had a higher observed overall pass rate than single-pass generation, but this improvement was not statistically significant after correction. Its recorded token use, including LLM-validator calls, was 1.77×-3.19× that of single-pass generation. These findings show that passing functional tests does not establish the overall quality of LLM-generated MPC code, and that additional constraints and repair do not necessarily improve all evaluation dimensions. They motivate separate checks for functional behavior, MPC programming constraints, algorithmic invariants, and source-level efficiency, rather than relying on compilation or functional testing alone.
evidence_items.title: Multidimensional Evaluation of LLM-Generated MPC Programs

evidence_items.summary: Almost ten years after the publication of CryptoNets, the field of Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning based on Homomorphic Encryption (HE) has advanced considerably. While the trend moves towards deeper networks and even Large Language Models (LLMs), a thorough understanding of the fundamentals remains essential. Every network relies on matrix-vector multiplications and activation functions, making it crucial to understand the strengths and weaknesses of each implementation. We therefore study these building blocks in detail on small networks, providing insights that can be transferred to larger architectures. To this end, we conduct a performance evaluation of three binary classification neural networks on consumer hardware, demonstrating the impact of selecting the appropriate matrix-vector multiplication algorithm: runtimes differ by up to a factor of three, and memory usage by up to a factor of two. Our results show that high speed and low memory footprint cannot be achieved simultaneously, requiring this trade-off to be weighed carefully. In addition, we propose a novel method for deriving a network's final classification using the binary step function.
evidence_items.title: Classification in the Dark: Performance Insights and Novel Methods for Homomorphic Binary Networks

organizations: Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology
The University of Texas at Austin
evidence_items.summary: Forecasting real-world events requires reasoning under uncertainty from information available at a fixed cutoff. Recent work has improved how large language models (LLMs) retrieve evidence and produce probabilistic forecasts, but each question is treated independently even when similar events recur. Resolved occurrences carry experience for later forecasts, yet past outcomes and case summaries do not preserve the relationships that made an earlier occurrence informative. We develop ReFoRM (Recurrent-event Forecasting with Reasoning Memory), which organizes reasoning from resolved events into predictive paths, retrieves relevant paths for a later occurrence, and reconstructs their relations using evidence at the new forecast cutoff. We evaluate ReFoRM on the Recurring Financial Events Set, which contains 300 questions across 40 recurring financial event families and uses earlier occurrences as hindsight for 100 forecast targets. Across five LLMs and six baselines, ReFoRM improves categorical and probabilistic forecasting performance. Further analyses show that validating historical relations with current evidence and reconstructing them enhances forecasting. Reasoning evaluation also demonstrates stronger evidence grounding, logical validity, and mechanism specificity.
evidence_items.title: From Hindsight to Foresight: Adapting Reusable Reasoning Structures from Recurring Financial Events

evidence_items.summary: Static analysis has been widely used to analyze web applications, yet its effectiveness largely relies on the quality of vulnerability patterns. In this work, we present MoCQ, which leverages large language models (LLMs) to automatically generate executable detection queries that capture these vulnerability patterns. To address challenges like LLM hallucinations and the complexity of industrial static analysis tools, MoCQ introduces a DSL-based harness. This harness extracts and models a core subset of domain-specific languages (DSLs) to provide the formal structure and guidance needed to generate valid queries. MoCQ employs an iterative refinement loop with trace-driven symbolic validation that provides precise feedback for query correction and optimization. Such a neuro-symbolic approach thus combines the scalability of pattern-based static analysis with the semantic understanding and automation capabilities of LLMs. We evaluated MoCQ on multiple vulnerability types across web programming languages, including Java, PHP, and JavaScript. MoCQ achieves detection performance comparable to expert-developed patterns while requiring only hours of query generation versus weeks of manual effort. Notably, MoCQ uncovered 45 new vulnerability patterns that security experts had missed and discovered 25 previously unknown vulnerabilities in real-world applications. MoCQ also outperforms prior approaches with stronger analysis capabilities.
evidence_items.title: Automatically Learning Vulnerability Patterns for Scalable Static Analysis of Web Applications

evidence_items.summary: Nginx serves as the authentication enforcement point for millions of web applications, yet its configuration language can silently disable authentication through cross-directive interactions among location ordering, map variable resolution, URI normalization, and per-block access controls. We identify seven classes of configuration-semantic authentication bypasses that arise from these interactions and present NginxBuster, a detection framework combining static configuration analysis with targeted active validation. NginxBuster's static analyzer models nginx's four-phase location matching algorithm to detect cross-location routing conflicts, while a configuration-aware mutation engine derives all test payloads from the target configuration's structure. A dual-baseline detection model confirms bypasses only when unauthenticated requests achieve authenticated-equivalent responses. On 20 synthetic benchmarks containing 55 planted vulnerability instances, the static analyzer detected 54 true positives with 3 false positives (precision 0.95, recall 0.98); an active scanner issuing 1.1 million mutated requests independently confirmed 44 of these as working bypasses against live nginx deployments. Five widely-used security tools tested under identical conditions detected at most one vulnerability class. On 1,344 real-world nginx configurations drawn from 10,434 configuration files collected from public GitHub repositories, NginxBuster flagged 11.8% as vulnerable; manual verification confirmed 144 of 195 vulnerability-class flags as genuine bypasses. These results demonstrate that authentication correctness is a property of the entire routing configuration, not of any individual directive, and that detecting configuration-semantic bypasses requires routing-aware analysis that no existing tool provides.
evidence_items.title: Breaking the Gate: Detecting Invisible Authentication Slip-Through in NGINX Reverse Proxy

evidence_items.summary: As generative AI models gain widespread adoption, an urgent question arises: are they being exploited to produce hateful content in online communities? We present the first large-scale, multi-modal measurement study to investigate this question, drawing on 465M text posts spanning 2016-2026 and 16.9M images spanning 2021-2025 from 4chan's /pol/ board. Specifically, we focused on two hate targets with long-established phenomena in parallel: anti-Indian hate and anti-Semitic hate. By benchmarking five text and five image AI detectors on hateful content, we deploy the best-performing detectors on over 31K long-form hateful posts and approximately 50K hateful images to measure AI-generated content prevalence. We find that the two targets exhibit different growth patterns: anti-Indian hate is substantially self-sustaining, with 46.15% of detected peaks driven by organized community campaigns rather than external events, against only 5.88% for anti-Semitic hate, which is instead largely reactive, with 94.12% of peaks triggered by real-world events such as the October 7 Hamas attack. AI-generated hateful posts have grown steadily since late 2022, reaching 1.42% of long-form posts by 2025. More importantly, AI adoption diverges across the two targets. For anti-Indian hate, AI content prevalence correlates significantly with slur frequency, nearly doubles during hate peaks, and AI-generated posts are 55.72% more toxic than human-written ones. Anti-Semitic hate, by contrast, shows no significant AI-hate correlation, indicating that AI tools are more widely adopted in campaign-driven hate than in established hate discourse. Lead-lag analysis reveals that hate campaigns precede AI adoption by approximately three months, suggesting that generative AI serves as an accelerator for existing hate movements rather than an independent driver.
evidence_items.title: Does AI Amplify Online Hate- A Multi-Modal Measurement Study on 4chan's /pol/

evidence_items.summary: Every few years a new downside- or tail-risk metric promises to improve on plain return volatility. The premise is always the same. The shape of the loss distribution, whether its asymmetry, tail heaviness, or co-crash structure, is supposed to carry information that symmetric volatility misses. We test that premise as adversarially as the data allow, on an evaluation that is survivorship-free where survivorship can be fixed (crypto), multi-regime, and multiple-testing-corrected, with survivorship-biased equity beds as a cross-asset check. The two properties trade off. The survivorship-free crypto beds are thin (seven to nine formation dates each), so their significance is suggestive, while the well-powered beds are the survivorship-biased equity ones. Across ten metrics and five test beds, no metric reliably beats volatility at forecasting an asset’s forward maximum drawdown, whether drawn from the published literature or found by an automated own-asset search. The failure has a clean anatomy, which we call magnitude, not shape. The only increments that survive Benjamini–Hochberg correction come from metrics that embed the size of downside losses (Value-at-Risk on all five beds, reaching 0.19 at its largest; downside deviation; and, weakly, negative semibeta). Every magnitude-free shape metric adds nothing or subtracts. Yet the shape metrics are not broken. On genuinely shape-sensitive targets they beat volatility. Drawdown is simply a magnitude phenomenon that shape does not drive. Volatility is hard to beat because it is persistent, though a predictive mediation test indicates it is not a sufficient statistic. The tiny magnitude edge does not pay its way either. A cost-aware backtest and a pre-registered composite add nothing over volatility outside fat-tailed crypto. Finally, an autonomous large-language-model discovery loop inflates validation sharply, yet its selections, scored once on a locked holdout, beat volatility out-of-sample by only about + 0.02. That residual is statistically detectable but economically negligible, and it tracks the same tail-magnitude increment rather than new signal, a data-snooping caution now that agentic search makes signal-hunting nearly free. On a level field, plain volatility is very hard to displace.
evidence_items.title: Magnitude, Not Shape: Volatility Beats Downside- and Tail-Risk Metrics at Forecasting Drawdown

evidence_items.summary: Speech eavesdropping has become a significant security concern. While non-acoustic side channels (e.g., mmWave and RFID) offer eavesdropping pathways, they invariably rely on external hardware deployed in proximity to victims. This limits their stealth and practicality. Earphones, by contrast, pose a more insidious threat. Their embedded inertial measurement units (IMUs), accessible without user permissions, create a hardware-free stealthy side channel. In this paper, we propose a novel side-channel attack that achieves the first open-vocabulary, full-duplex speech eavesdropping on commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) earphones. This attack uniquely accomplishes full-duplex recognition of both 'what you say' (user speech) and 'what you hear'(audio played through the earphones), even when overlapping (e.g., talking while listening to music or multi-person conversing). We resolve the severe mutual interference inherent to this underdetermined signal separation problem. Constrained by COTS earphones' fixed IMU sampling rates of merely 25~Hz, we propose a multi-axial data fusion strategy to extract speech features from this limited bandwidth. A dual-stream attention network, along with a phoneme-based pixel-reorganization strategy (to support open-vocabulary recognition) and large language model (LLM)-assisted refinement, is employed to accurately recognize sensitive speech. Extensive evaluations on COTS earphones demonstrate the attack's practicality and urgent threat to speech privacy.
evidence_items.title: Turning Everyday Earphones into a Full-Duplex Speech Eavesdropping Platform via Zero-permission IMU
Design and Evaluation of Energy Efficient Spiking Neural Architectures for Edge AI: A Neuromorphic Computing Approach

evidence_items.summary: Human oversight is widely prescribed for high-impact artificial intelligence, but “human in the loop” is not an operational policy when review capacity is finite and agent activity varies over time. We formulate oversight for financial AI agents as a capacity-constrained allocation problem: for each proposed action, a controller decides whether to permit automated execution or consume scarce human review. Unlike a preliminary version of this study, risk scores are not drawn conditional on the realized outcome: observable features are generated first, harm is a hidden logistic function of those features, and a logistic-regression risk model is fit on a separate 60-day, 14,264-action calibration stream, then frozen and evaluated out-of-sample on a held-out 120-day, 28,174-action test stream across five financial domains. The frozen model is well calibrated out of sample (test Brier score 0.091; predicted/observed decile harm rates agree within 1–2 points). We compare no review, random review, a calibration-frozen threshold (uncapped and capacity-truncated), daily risk ranking, a convex risk-severity heuristic, and a genuine expected-loss policy selecting marginal-benefit-maximizing cases under the model’s own optimality argument. The uncapped threshold captures 40.9% of harm value but breaches the 33-action daily capacity on 49 of 120 days; truncating it recovers feasibility at a coverage cost (36.9%). Under the hard constraint, risk ranking captures 38.9% of harm value; the expected-loss policy raises this to 45.5% (a 17% relative gain) and achieves the lowest total expected cost among all evaluated policies, 10.2% below risk ranking at the same 14.1% review rate, while random allocation captures only 13.2%. A 27-cell factorial sensitivity analysis over reviewer effectiveness, review cost, and score discrimination, plus a sweep over harm prevalence and severity dispersion, shows this advantage is stable throughout. Results are computed outputs of the stated synthetic simulation; harm prevention is evaluated in expectation via the assumed reviewer-effectiveness parameter, not observed human-review outcomes. These results show that effective human oversight is jointly a prediction, allocation, and workforce-capacity problem: calibrated risk scores alone are insufficient, and unconstrained cost optimization can redistribute review away from low-severity domains.
evidence_items.title: When Should Humans Intervene? Capacity-Aware Oversight for Financial AI Agents

evidence_items.summary: Recent advances in generative AI (artificial intelligence) have enabled the creation of highly realistic visual content, posing significant challenges to image authenticity verification. Existing detection methods predominantly rely on supervised learning of generator-specific artifacts, potentially limiting their ability to generalize to unseen generation models and image manipulation scenarios. In this work, we propose a training-free framework for AI-generated image detection based on perturbation-induced representation coherence. Instead of measuring the response to a single perturbation, we construct multiple complementary residual-guided perturbation families and analyze the internal coherence of their feature representations extracted by a frozen DINOv3 model. Furthermore, we extend the proposed coherence analysis across network depth by introducing a layer-wise coherence trajectory, capturing the evolution of representation consistency throughout the hierarchical feature space. Extensive experiments on both fully AI-generated images and images locally modified using AI models demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves the highest mean AUROC among the evaluated training-free methods, while remaining competitive with training-based approaches.
evidence_items.title: Training-Free Detection of AI-Generated Images Based on Coherence Analysis of Image Representations

evidence_items.summary: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) has democratised content creation while scaling systemic threats in Deepfakes, Deception, and Disinformation (D3). As traditional content detection and watermarking are increasingly bypassed, this paper presents a position and baseline synthesis of Reverse Prompt Engineering (RPE) as a defensive capability. RPE inverts the generative pipeline to infer plausible instruction prompts and support, rather than definitively proving source-model attribution. Grounded in threat telemetry, we synthesise representative RPE frameworks while explicitly delineating the evidentiary limits of prompt recovery, attribution, and content provenance. We further evaluate RPE across public information, legal, and policy/governance viewpoints, analyse key technical limitations such as cross-modal generalisation, and outline a research roadmap to establish RPE as a cornerstone of digital provenance and AI accountability.
evidence_items.title: Reverse Prompt Engineering in Generative AI: A Baseline for Deepfake, Deception and Disinformation Mitigation

evidence_items.summary: Institutions that each hold part of the equity market’s history cannot pool it. FAP-Bench measures what they give up by training a return-prediction model together instead, exchanging model updates and, to standardize inputs, monthly aggregate histograms. It is a controlled laboratory for horizontal federation rather than a model of any particular consortium. It prices the coordination cost of that restriction, not the privacy it buys: clients are stylized industry splits of one licensed panel, and privacy is priced at a single differential-privacy setting. The benchmark builds a 3.27M firm-month panel from CRSP and Compustat over 1964–2023, splits it into twelve industry clients, and runs centralized, local-only and three federated rules at a matched compute budget. Every configuration publishes the smallest gap it can resolve before any method is ranked, and every heterogeneity treatment is paired with a control that imposes the same aggregate burden evenly, so the difference isolates cross-client structure. Two findings. First, a coordination cost appears in the one configuration where the model resolves more signal. On seven characteristics, where the network resolves little signal, no rule separates from pooling economically. On twenty, where the model resolves substantially more signal, the two averaging rules give up accuracy that the cell does resolve (Rank IC, q < 0.02). They also show a net Sharpe shortfall that it does not resolve, which we report as a bound. An adaptive server optimizer stays level with pooling on both, but its server step size was searched and the pooled model’s optimizer was not, so this does not show that it matches an equally tuned pooled model. Both configurations resolve gaps of comparable size, so this is a difference in effect, not in power. Two configurations cannot establish a trend, and they differ in panel width, network size and client learning rate at once, so the cost cannot be attributed to any one of these. Swapping the network for ridge also changes which rule pays, so no ranking among the rules holds across model classes. Second, heterogeneity in what a client holds clears the benchmark’s noise floor, while heterogeneity in how it participates almost never does. The participation side is measured mostly on 60 test months, where our intervals are somewhat too narrow, and only one of its three treatments is rechecked on 408. Most economic differences sit below what this data can resolve, so we report magnitudes as bounds rather than estimates.
evidence_items.title: FAP-Bench: A Matched-Control Benchmark for Horizontal Federated Cross-Sectional Equity-Return Prediction

evidence_items.summary: Groundwater, an essential natural resource, comprises approximately 34% of the planet’s total freshwater supply. Since the last century, factors such as over-exploitation, rapid urbanization, industrial contamination, agricultural activities, and residential pressures on groundwater reserves have escalated the global demand for freshwater. In Bangladesh, a densely populated developing country, water pollution, scarcity, and safety concerns are particularly severe, with Dhaka and its surrounding urban fringes undergoing rapid groundwater depletion. Recently, machine learning models have gained prominence in groundwater potential zone (GWPZ) mapping due to their ability to model complex hydrogeological relationships. This study develops a GWPZ map for Gazipur, a major industrial district neighboring Dhaka, by applying geospatial techniques and ensemble machine learning algorithms to integrate groundwater level data with twenty selected topographical, hydrological, meteorological, soil, geological, and land surface factors. Models employed include Logistic Regression, K-Nearest Neighbor, Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, Multilayer Perceptron, and a Voting Classifier. Model performance was evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, ROC–AUC, and McNemar’s test. Random Forest achieved the highest predictive performance (Test AUC = 0.911), followed by the Voting Classifier (Test AUC = 0.909). Results indicate that nearly half of Gazipur falls within low groundwater potential zones concentrated in Kapasia and Kaliakoir upazilas, while moderate to very high potential zones are predominantly situated in the southern part of the district. The comparative evaluation demonstrates the effectiveness of ensemble machine learning for groundwater potential mapping and provides practical guidance for sustainable groundwater management and informed decision-making.
evidence_items.title: Delineation of groundwater potential zone mapping using machine learning algorithms in industrial zone

evidence_items.summary: This paper studies how structural sensitivity in supply chain networks can improve prediction of financial downside cascades. We develop an origin-specific measure of shock transmission in a production network whose link weights are motivated by Cobb–Douglas input shares. In the absence of output constraints, sectoral responses are characterized by the Leontief inverse, and under the standard competitive benchmark the derivative of a fixed-weight aggregate output index with respect to a sectoral productivity shock equals the corresponding Domar weight. We impose a sector-level output equality jointly with the reduced equilibrium equations and solve for sectoral log outputs and the associated signed implementation wedge. Under the spectral-radius condition, the constrained equilibrium exists uniquely for every shock and admits a closed-form solution: its response equals the unconstrained Leontief response minus a rank-one adjustment induced by the maintained sector. This yields a shock-specific cross-sector transmission statistic that separates origin importance from transmission bottlenecks. We also derive sensitivity measures for individual changes in input–output coefficients and row-sum-preserving reallocations of input shares while holding the baseline normalization and aggregate-output weights fixed. Applying the framework to BEA input–output data shows that transmission rankings can differ from conventional sector-importance rankings. In a recursive pseudo-out-of-sample financial validation, a downside-weighted cross-origin response-reduction score improves forecasts of cross-industry downside cascades beyond own-industry risk, aggregate risk, and conventional Leontief exposure.
evidence_items.title: Structural Sensitivity in Supply Chain Networks for Financial Downside Cascade Prediction

evidence_items.summary: Many bandit problems exhibit recurring reward structure whose phase, amplitude, and frequency drift over time. We study this setting under partial feedback and propose Latent Oscillator Thompson Sampling (LOTS), in which each arm carries a drifting baseline and latent oscillator states that evolve online. LOTS uses a lightweight particle filter to maintain an approximate posterior over these states. On the theory side, we isolate a stable linear-Gaussian specialization and prove an explicit dynamic-regret bound under exact Gaussian inference; for the broader model, we reduce regret to one-step latent-score prediction error. Empirically, LOTS attains the lowest cumulative dynamic regret in five of six synthetic environment families. Across the recurring regimes, it consistently outperforms fixed harmonic, seasonality-aware finite-state, and strong generic baselines, whereas RW-KalmanTS and D-UCB remain better matched to the purely nonperiodic control. Complementary real-data replay benchmarks built from MTA subway hourly ridership, UCI ElectricityLoadDiagrams traces, and daily and 15-minute trading volume across ten liquid ETFs expose the same division of labor, with LOTS best on the two panels with time-varying reward dynamics and runner-up when recurrence is either exactly captured by a fixed dictionary or rigid but common across arms. A controlled common-mode intervention shows why: recurrence helps a bandit when it differentiates arms, whereas a cycle shared across arms cancels under arm comparison. Overall, explicitly modeling drifting recurrent structure improves decision making under partial feedback where that structure distinguishes the arms.
evidence_items.title: Latent Oscillator Thompson Sampling for Recurrent Nonstationary Bandits

evidence_items.summary: Deploying Secure Multiparty Computation (MPC) to operate on data from real world sources requires many connective elements that have not received much attention in the literature. One prominent example is that MPC protocols typically assume conveniently structured data, whereas data in the real world comes in formats that are meant to be handled by string parsing engines. In this work, we give a new constant round protocol for securely parsing secret shared strings into an MPC-friendly format, built upon secure shuffle as a key primitive. Secure shuffle applies a permutation to a list while keeping both the permutation and the underlying data secret-shared at all times. While highly efficient protocols exist in the semi-honest setting, achieving malicious security has incurred significant overhead in both rounds and communication. We present Truffle, a new three-party shuffle protocol that is secure against one active corruption to bridge this gap. Truffle achieves an amortised round complexity that for the first time matches the state-of-the-art semi-honest protocol, while incurring only sublinear communication overhead. The core technique that underlies Truffle is a novel distributed verifier zero-knowledge proof that checks the correctness of a putative shuffle. We implement Truffle and show via benchmarks that it is performant enough to handle real application data. Beyond parsing secret shared data, secure shuffle finds applications in graph analytics, anonymous communication, Distributed Oblivious RAM, aggregate statistics, and secure sorting, each of which stand to benefit from the improvement that Truffle provides.
evidence_items.title: Truffle: Maliciously Secure Three-Party Shuffles with Applications to Parsing

evidence_items.summary: Distilling a tabular foundation model (TFM) into a CPU-deployable tree is established practice on IID benchmarks, where retention of the teacher’s absolute accuracy exceeds 95%, but financial risk breaks that setting twice over: the data are temporally ordered, and a gradient-boosted baseline is strong enough that the teacher’s edge is only an increment, so absolute retention stays high even when nothing useful transfers. We therefore report gain retention, Rgain, the fraction of the teacher’s advantage over a matched labels-only student that survives compression, and we factorially vary the one choice a practitioner must make: how the teacher’s soft targets are built. On frozen test windows of five temporal fraud streams (Bank Account Fraud with two bias variants, IEEE-CIS and Elliptic), a student scoring a row in 0.52 ms on one CPU core (107 × the teacher’s batched throughput) retains 96% of the teacher’s incremental advantage at a 16K-label budget (+ 8.7 pp PR-AUC). The decisive design choice is target coverage, not chronology: on BAF’s development window, labelling every available row is worth + 3.03 pp against + 0.50 pp for the construction protocol, and forward chaining, the temporally cautious scheme most practitioners reach for, is unnecessary and costs up to 3.5 pp; on frozen test windows the coverage advantage holds in all four replication streams (median + 0.97 pp over 12 cells). That advantage is conditional, and we quantify the condition: across 12 frozen-test stream–budget cells it grows with the teacher’s margin over a matched labels-only tree (r = 0.79), and where a tree already matches the foundation model the selector discards the teacher in 10 of 12 runs, making the choice moot by construction. The calibration cost that appears to accompany distillation is an artifact of temperature-scaled targets, not a property of the teacher, and inverts at no cost to ranking.
evidence_items.title: Coverage Beats Chronology: Distilling Tabular Foundation Models for Drifting, Rare-Event Financial Risk

evidence_items.summary: Property finance depends on a deceptively simple operation: deciding whether two textual addresses denote the same physical property. Errors in this identity layer can silently propagate into loan books, securitisation data tapes, and regulatory reporting. Lexical matchers struggle to commit safely under the UK’s heterogeneous address conventions, whilst neural matchers fail in the opposite direction, by conflating adjacent properties that are semantically near-identical but legally distinct—an unacceptable error when the match decides which asset should secure a loan. We present PropertyLM-UK, a hybrid system over an 18.2-million-property national index composing (i) postcode-hierarchy blocked dense retrieval over a Qdrant vector store, (ii) cross-encoder reranking, and (iii) a deterministic adjudication layer that extracts postcode, house-number, and unit identifiers from both sides (i.e., any candidate contradicting the query on an identity key is forced to no_match, however high its neural similarity). Every decision carries a log of named, testable reasons, giving a regulator-legible audit trail, and the pipeline can run locally in containers with no external API calls. On a 10,000-query UPRN-labelled benchmark from Ordnance Survey AddressBase Premium spanning nine corruption families, PropertyLM-UK resolves 94.6% of present-property queries at rank one with 99.6% precision on confident matches, and correctly abstains on 92.6% of absent-property queries, at 352 ms median latency on commodity CPU hardware, using two unmodified 22M-parameter open models with no task-specific training. Ablations show the deterministic layer both vetoes and licenses: removing it costs 22 accuracy points and escalates 99% of decisions into human review. Against blocked BM25, fuzzy, and neural-only baselines, it is the only matcher that commits on over 80% of present queries at ≥ 99% precision without a single commitment across an identity contradiction; its precision and zero-contradiction property are stable under perturbation of every hand-set weight. We conclude that the architecture—not model capacity—determines the primary safety property of a regulated AI system. We release the system under Apache-2.0 with the corresponding benchmark methodology at https://github.com/anon0404/propertylm-uk.
evidence_items.title: PropertyLM-UK: Deterministically Adjudicated Neural Address Resolution for the Identity Layer of Property Finance

evidence_items.summary:
BACKGROUND
The medical-education literature on ChatGPT has grown rapidly since 2023, but bibliometric patterns vary with database coverage, indexing fields, and the boundary used to define educational relevance. We examined publication growth, collaboration, and thematic development and assessed whether the leading patterns were stable under a stricter topic definition.


METHODS
Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC) and PubMed were searched on September 5, 2026; the PubMed publication-date filter extended through September 4, 2026. WoSCC supported citation- and Author Keyword-based science mapping, whereas PubMed provided a complementary Medical Subject Headings-based view. The expanded corpora contained 665 WoSCC and 1106 PubMed records, with strict topic-specific subsets of 532 and 898 records, respectively. Bibliometrix/R, VOSviewer, CiteSpace, and Microsoft Excel were used for descriptive bibliometrics, collaboration networks, thematic mapping, multiple correspondence analysis, keyword co-occurrence, Trend Topics, burst detection, and journal mapping. Data from 2026 were treated as partial-year observations.


RESULTS
WoSCC publication output increased from 66 records in 2023 to 169 in 2024 and 242 in 2025; 188 records were indexed during the partial 2026 period. The United States had the largest corresponding-author output, and Sichuan University was the leading displayed affiliation. The keyword structure centered on medical education, ChatGPT, artificial intelligence, and large language models. CiteSpace identified 9 keyword clusters, including medical education, large language models, medical students, generative artificial intelligence, prompt engineering, clinical decision-making, and patient education. Recently emerging terms included DeepSeek, clinical reasoning, and anatomy education. Author Keyword rankings were highly concordant between the expanded and strict WoSCC datasets (Spearman ρ = 0.973, P < .001).


CONCLUSION
ChatGPT-related medical-education research expanded substantially after 2023 and diversified across assessment, clinical reasoning, educational applications, and broader LLM-related themes. The leading WoSCC keyword structure remained stable under the stricter topic definition. WoSCC and PubMed captured different bibliographic features and are best interpreted as complementary sources.
evidence_items.title: ChatGPT-related research in medical education: A dual-database bibliometric review and science-mapping analysis, 2023 to 2026.

evidence_items.summary:
This study aims to examine where generative artificial intelligence (AI) may add value in mental health care, where its clinical limits remain and how human oversight should change as AI assumes greater responsibility.
 
 
 
 This opinion piece draws on recent randomized trials, systematic reviews, safety evaluations and international guidance on conversational AI in mental health. The evidence is interpreted through a three-level framework: supportive self-management, clinician-augmented care and autonomous clinical care.
 
 
 
 AI-supported interventions can improve symptoms of depression and anxiety in some settings and may widen access to low-intensity support. However, evidence remains heterogeneous and important concerns persist around suicide-risk responses, privacy, bias, over-reliance and accountability. Current evidence supports AI more strongly as an adjunct than as an autonomous therapist.
 
 
 
 Access alone should not be mistaken for inclusion. Safe mental health AI also requires attention to digital access, language, culture, affordability and routes to human care.
 
 
 
 The paper proposes a practical clinical hierarchy in which the evidence threshold, regulatory scrutiny and human oversight increase with the clinical responsibility assumed by AI.
evidence_items.title: AI as therapist or assistant? Opportunities and boundaries of artificial intelligence in mental health care

evidence_items.summary: The development of foundation models that learn a general grammar of DNA (DNA language models) has accelerated in recent years. The vast majority of DNA large language models (LLMs), such as DNABERT-2 and Nucleotide Transformer, are pretrained almost exclusively on reference genomes. They therefore cannot represent the two sources of variation most directly tied to regulatory differences between people: genetic variants and DNA methylation. Long-read sequencing (Nanopore and PacBio) now measures both from the same native DNA molecules, but no model is designed to use this joint readout. With this in mind, we developed ModBERT, a DNA language model built on a five-letter probabilistic genome representation in which each position is a distribution over A, C, G, T, 5mC (represented with M). In pretraining, these distributions encode population allele frequencies and CpG methylation levels from 242 individuals in the 1000 Genomes Long-Read Sequencing Consortium, learned with a soft-target masked language modeling objective. We further propose probabilistic fine-tuning, in which the same representation encodes one individual's genotype and methylation. A fine-tuned model can then make person-specific predictions from a single assay. Under this novel fine-tuning framework, we show that ModBERT effectively utilizes methylation information to classify peaks from functional genomic assays, including histone mark (n=11 different marks) and transcription factor binding (n=69 TFs) ChIP-seq data, outperforming ab initio trained models and ModBERT pretrained on sequences without methylation. In silico methylation perturbations yield TF sensitivities that correlate with independent methylation-aware motif models. Using an evaluation design that separates generalization to new loci from generalization to new individuals, ModBERT predicts chromatin accessibility at held-out loci in held-out individuals (AUROC 0.88).
evidence_items.title: ModBERT: a DNA modification and genetic variant-aware DNA large language model
