evidence_items.summary: Abstract The Evo2 Variant Effect Database (Evo2VED; https://dnallmved.org/) is a publicly accessible resource cataloging precomputed Evo2-derived variant effect scores, defined as allelic score differences, for 6.48 million human variants common in the gnomAD non-Finnish European population. Evo2VED includes scores from the 7B and 40B models under three scoring schemes, alongside annotations of variant function, evolutionary constraint, allele age, and disease associations. It integrates genome-wide association study (GWAS) data from UK Biobank, FinnGen, and the Million Veteran Program. Three complementary modules support variant-level interpretation, regional and region-set exploration, and trait-level analysis through flexible queries, interactive visualizations, and downloadable results. Evo2VED also catalogs associations between Evo2 annotations and per-SNP heritability across thousands of traits from these biobanks. A guided workflow connects GWAS with associated regions and individual variant evidence. Case studies of hypertension and depression illustrate how regional comparisons of Evo2 scores and GWAS signals can guide candidate variant prioritization. Evaluations using massively parallel reporter assays, molecular QTLs, fine-mapping probabilities, and clinical annotations assess associations with Evo2 scores alone and their added value beyond conservation and regulatory annotations. By providing accessible scores, contextual annotations, and comparative analyses, Evo2VED facilitates exploration and application of genomic language model predictions in human genetics research.
evidence_items.title: Evo2VED: a database of DNA large language model-derived scores for variant interpretation

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Discharge instructions are an important component of the transition from hospital to home for patients with diabetic kidney disease (DKD), whose care often involves multiple comorbidities, medications, and stage-specific management needs. However, producing complete, accurate, clear, and personalized instructions can be challenging for junior physicians. Objective This study aimed to evaluate whether large language model (LLM) assistance improves the quality of DKD discharge instructions produced by junior physicians and whether its benefits vary according to chronic kidney disease (CKD) stage. Methods The study included 101 hospitalized patients with DKD. Discharge instructions for each patient were initially drafted by a group of junior residents (resident group); subsequently, another group of residents at the same level, with the assistance of DeepSeek-V3.2 (AI-assisted group), generated a separate set of discharge instructions for the same 101 patients, resulting in a total of 202 documents. Four clinical experts, including 2 nephrologists and 2 endocrinologists, independently scored both versions of the discharge instructions using a 5-point Likert scale across 5 dimensions: completeness, accuracy, safety, clarity, and personalization. Interrater reliability was assessed using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). Results Interrater reliability was excellent in both the resident group (ICC=0.817, 95% CI 0.763‐0.864; P <.001) and the AI-assisted group (ICC=0.860, 95% CI 0.816‐0.897; P <.001). Compared with resident-only instructions, AI-assisted instructions received significantly higher scores across 5 evaluation dimensions and the overall evaluation (all Bonferroni-adjusted P <.001), with large effect sizes ( r =0.741‐0.927).
evidence_items.title: Large Language Model–Assisted Discharge Instructions for Diabetic Kidney Disease: Comparative Evaluation Study

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Vision-language-action (VLA) models offer a promising approach to robotic manipulation, yet reliable long-horizon execution in dynamic environments remains challenging. OpenVLA supports strong task generalization and parameter-efficient adaptation, but its single-image input limits temporal modeling, while its standard framework lacks explicit use of failure experience and runtime recovery mechanisms. To address these limitations, we propose TPRVLA, which integrates temporal memory, preference learning, and closed-loop recovery. A lightweight temporal memory adapter incorporates consecutive observations into the frozen OpenVLA backbone to capture short-term dynamics. Weighted preference pairs are constructed from successful and failed trajectories under similar visual observations and identical instructions. The policy is then adapted through a joint direct preference optimization (DPO) and behavior cloning (BC) objective to favor preferred actions. During execution, a rule-based state monitor combines end-effector motion, action repetition, and visual changes to trigger checkpoint-guided recovery when anomalies persist. Evaluations across 900 rollouts on ten LIBERO Spatial tasks with three random seeds show improved task performance, particularly on tasks requiring extended execution and closed-loop adjustment, while increasing peak GPU memory usage by less than 1%.
evidence_items.title: TPRVLA:Temporal-Preference-Recovery Vision-Language-Action Model

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Autoscalers for large language model (LLM) inference clusters that add capacity when a predicted overload probability crosses a threshold depend on the probability scale, not only on the ranking. This simulation study evaluates five such predictors under sparse telemetry and runtime anomalies on two latent-state generators and a request-level serving simulator with queueing, service-level objectives (SLOs), startup delay, and modeled power. With 3-period instead of 50-period histories, models trained on long histories became overconfident (expected calibration error up to 0.099) or conservative, whereas a Markov filter stayed calibrated and retraining on short histories removed most of the error. Temperature scaling fitted on long histories did not transfer; refitted for short histories, it cut this error by up to 68.7%, removed all 290 wrong high-confidence predictions of one model by lowering their confidence, and cut the overconfident models' idealized unmitigated overload by 59.8–82.8% at the cost of more idle capacity. With a 20-s startup delay in the request-level simulator, learned predictors used 24.0–25.3% less modeled energy than always-on scale-out, with a 1.0–1.2 percentage-point increase in the SLO-violation rate, and 95.3% of scale-out-induced violations occurred on slow new replicas. Calibration should therefore be validated per telemetry regime and checked against request-level outcomes.
evidence_items.title: Predictive Reliability and Calibration of Workload Autoscaling Models for Large Language Model Inference Clusters Under Sparse Telemetry and Runtime Anomalies

evidence_items.summary: BACKGROUND Large administrative health databases are often underused because the people who need answers depend on technical staff to translate operational questions into code. Dashboards expose predefined indicators but cannot answer new questions. Large language models (LLMs) can generate executable code from natural language and may offer a complementary interface, provided their outputs are checked and remain auditable. OBJECTIVE To test whether a natural language–only ("no-code") workflow, in which the operator never writes or edits code, can convert operational public health questions into reproducible analytical outputs from a real-world prison telehealth dataset; to document the errors that arise and how they were detected; and to make the process publicly inspectable. METHODS We applied a no-code workflow to 52,181 anonymized consultation records (293 variables) from TeleSAP, the prison telehealth program of São Paulo State, Brazil (June 2024–July 2025). One operator interacted with Gemini (Google) through its web interface in March 2026, in a single thread of 360 prompts, to obtain Python scripts for 17 management questions, executed in Google Colab. Execution errors and implausible numbers were returned to the model as corrective prompts; code was never edited by hand. Gemini then generated a public portal and reconstructed, from each final script, the prompt that reproduces it. RESULTS Of 17 scripts, 15 ran and answered their question; 1 was excluded because the model silently substituted simulated values for the absenteeism field; 6 were curated into public case studies (chronic disease burden by age, teleconsultation duration, first-contact resolution, gender identity and clinical complexity, respiratory seasonality, cardiovascular risk). Illustrative outputs: hypertension in 39.9% of consultations at age ≥45 years vs 11.3% under 45 (P<.001); 64.8% of consultations resolved at first contact; respiratory peak in August (7.9%; P=.008).
evidence_items.title: No-Code Analysis of 52,181 Prison Telehealth Records With a Large Language Model: Formative Case Study of a Natural Language–Only Workflow and Its Failure Modes in Brazil (Preprint)

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Objectives Information overload in electronic health records hampers clinicians’ ability to efficiently extract and synthesize critical information from a patient’s longitudinal health record, leading to increased cognitive burden and delays in care. This study explores the potential of large language models (LLMs) to address this challenge by generating problem-based admission summaries for patients admitted with heart failure, a leading cause of hospitalization worldwide. Materials and Methods We developed an extract-then-abstract approach guided by disease-specific “summary bundles” to generate summaries of longitudinal clinical notes that prioritize clinically relevant information. Through a mixed-methods evaluation using real-world clinical notes, we compared physicians’ ability to answer patient-specific clinical questions with the LLM-generated summaries vs standard chart review. Results While summary access did not significantly reduce overall questionnaire completion time, frequent summary use significantly contributed to faster questionnaire completion (P = .002). Individual physicians varied in how effectively they leveraged the summaries. Importantly, summary use maintained accuracy in answering clinical questions (88.0% with summaries vs 86.4% without). All physicians indicated they were “likely” or “very likely” to use the summaries in clinical practice, and 87.5% reported that the summaries would save them time. Preferences for summary format varied, highlighting the need for customizable summaries aligned with individual clinician workflows. Discussion This exploratory, mixed-methods pilot study provides one of the first extrinsic evaluations of LLMs for longitudinal summarization, demonstrating their potential to enhance clinician efficiency, alleviate workload, and support informed decision-making in time-sensitive care environments.
evidence_items.title: Verifiable summarization of electronic health records using large language models to support chart review

evidence_items.summary: Grid energy storage systems are a trending technology, attracting researchers due to their significant market and need. An update is essential for this technology, as it has several drawbacks, such as improper charging, high cost, resource limitations, and weak grid stability. To overcome these drawbacks, this study presents a Solar PV system with grid stability (SPGSEV) model. This model integrates core modules, such as mobility and charging systems, charging stations, and a solar-powered photovoltaic system with battery storage and PV modules. The grid stability management system is developed to achieve effective resource utilization and, with the Multi-Objective Remora Optimization Algorithm (MOROA), to support proper decision-making and charge scheduling. The overall framework is implemented in MATLAB, and the parameters measured for result analysis include Electricity Price, Voltage, PVs Capacity, PVs Output Power, Power Loss, Voltage Magnitude, and Stay Time. The results are also compared with earlier models such as EMEVC, OEPSM, and EVESS. The outcome proves the stability of the proposed model by attaining lower loss and high PV output power, which leads to maximum energy utilization and grid stability for the energy storage systems.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Energy Management in Grid Energy Storage Systems: Design and Performance Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Widely accessible generative artificial intelligence has unsettled long held assumptions about how learning can be measured and trusted. Tools capable of producing fluent essays, functional code, and plausible solutions on demand have exposed the fragility of evaluation models that reward the unsupervised production of polished artifacts. This paper argues that the appropriate institutional response is not an escalating contest between detection software and evasion techniques, but a deliberate redesign of evaluation around authentic human competency. Drawing on established scholarship in authentic assessment, constructive alignment, and formative feedback, the paper develops a five-principle framework for evaluation that remains meaningful when capable AI is freely available. The framework shifts emphasis from the finished product toward the reasoning process, foregrounds contextual judgment that machines cannot convincingly simulate, distributes evidence of competency across a program rather than isolated high stakes events, treats AI as a declared and scrutinized instrument rather than prohibited contraband, and grounds security in thoughtful design rather than pervasive surveillance. Common assessment formats are appraised for their resilience, and implementation challenges relating to staff workload, equity of access, and institutional policy are examined. The paper concludes that the disruption introduced by generative AI, although genuinely destabilizing, presents an overdue opportunity to align evaluation with the competencies that human learners must actually develop, and to recover the formative purpose of assessment that narrow integrity policing has long obscured.
evidence_items.title: Assessment Integrity in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Redesigning Learning Evaluation for Authentic Human Competency

evidence_items.summary: Emergency radiology operates at the intersection of high imaging volumes, time-critical diagnoses, and persistent workforce shortages, making it one of the most promising yet demanding environments for artificial intelligence (AI) deployment. This narrative review critically appraises the evidence on AI in emergency radiology, emphasizing diagnostic accuracy, workflow efficiency, and the strength of the underlying evidence. We searched PubMed for peer-reviewed literature published between January 2015 and August 2026 using a structured, reproducible strategy, and we classified key studies by design and outcome level. Deep learning algorithms approach expert-level performance in retrospective and reader-study settings for several high-stakes conditions, including intracranial hemorrhage (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve up to 0.991), acute pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, and skeletal fractures, for which a multicenter multireader diagnostic accuracy study found that AI assistance increased reader sensitivity by 10.4 percentage points and specificity from 90.6% to 95.6%. However, real-world evaluations report substantially lower sensitivity than development studies, and workflow evidence is mixed: in one prospective implementation, head CT studies flagged by AI for intracranial hemorrhage were interpreted sooner than routine studies (median 19 vs. 512 min), whereas a pulmonary embolism notification system produced no measurable turnaround benefit. Deep learning reconstruction can reduce radiation dose, and large language models show early promise for report error detection and communication. Prospective, multisite, patient-outcome evidence remains scarce. AI should be viewed as an augmenting technology whose value in emergency radiology depends on local validation, deliberate workflow integration, and continuous post-deployment monitoring.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence in emergency radiology: opportunities, evidence, and limitations

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Background A proportion of Australians encounter substantial unmet oral health needs despite eligibility for government‐subsidised care. Yet, government dental services operate within a fragmented, mixed public‐private system with limited capacity to support priority populations. The National Oral Health Plan (2015–2024) responds to this visible and measured need for priority. As the next National Oral Health Plan is developed, these priorities provide a timely basis to consider whether emerging technologies can support access and system performance without reproducing existing inequities. Methods This narrative review aims to examine the potential uses, evidence for, challenges and implementation considerations of the use of Artificial Intelligence including machine learning, in Australian public‐funded dental services, and to examine the implications for access, equity, governance, community co‐design and workforce capability. The evidence is interpreted through a multidimensional framework for access to care, while retaining the National Oral Health Plan (2015–2024) as the policy context. Conclusions Limited research conducted in Australian‐based healthcare settings shows evidence for public dental system‐level improvements for triage, risk stratification, service planning and workflow, but also identifies material concerns about opportunity cost, human oversight, non‐representative data, algorithmic bias, cultural safety, Indigenous Data Sovereignty and clinician education. Artificial Intelligence and machine learning technologies may support more responsive public‐funded dental services, but technical performance alone is not evidence of improved access or equitable care. Intentional, values‐led implementation requires representative data, Indigenous‐led governance, community co‐design, transparent evaluation, human accountability and a digitally capable workforce.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Australian Public‐Funded Dental Services

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) sovereignty is often associated with domestically controlled infrastructure, data localisation and nationally developed models. Such measures may be valuable, but they cannot by themselves preserve public authority when consequential functions rely on AI systems that institutions cannot adequately inspect, constrain, challenge, evaluate or replace. This Perspective distinguishes ordinary technological interdependence from algorithmic dependence and proposes governed interdependence as a more practicable sovereignty objective for resource-constrained states. Drawing on scholarship on technological sovereignty and public-sector AI governance, together with documented policy developments in Somalia, we identify five tests of meaningful public control: legibility, enforceability, contestability, reversibility and independent evaluative capability. For Somalia, these tests suggest three priorities: a risk-tiered register of consequential public-sector AI systems, procurement safeguards that secure oversight and exit rights, and independent Somali-language evaluation connected to accessible human redress. These priorities are prospective policy proposals rather than findings from an empirical assessment of existing government AI deployments. The framework reframes AI sovereignty as the demonstrated capacity to govern dependence, providing a basis for comparative policy analysis and future empirical evaluation in low-resource settings.
evidence_items.title: Governed Interdependence as a Framework for Artificial Intelligence Sovereignty in Somalia

evidence_items.summary: This study combines artificial intelligence forecasts with a digital twin updated from operational data to support adaptive logistics management. The model compares feasible decisions in terms of time, cost and risk, then feeds the observed outcomes into the next decision cycle. A numerical example illustrates how the model responds to a reduction in terminal capacity. A comparative pilot study is proposed to evaluate its performance.
evidence_items.title: ADAPTIVE MANAGEMENT OF LOGISTICS SYSTEMS USING ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND DIGITAL TWINS

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background and Aims A major challenge in dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) care is the identification and management of individuals at risk before disease manifestation. An artificial intelligence (AI) model applied to electrocardiography (ECG) was developed to detect and predict the echocardiographic DCM phenotype (left ventricular dilatation with systolic dysfunction) and was evaluated for its ability to stratify the risk of incident DCM in familial cohorts. Methods A deep learning model was trained to detect the echocardiographic DCM phenotype and to predict its future onset, using more than 330 000 ECG-echocardiogram pairs from the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston. Model performance was validated in cohorts from the UK Biobank, Zhongshan Hospital, and Antwerp University Hospital, and compared with models based on traditional ECG features and echocardiographic traits. To assess performance in familial DCM, genetically predisposed individuals identified through cascade screening at the cardiogenetics clinics of Antwerp University Hospital (n = 166, 18% DCM positive) and Maastricht University Medical Center (n = 177, 18% DCM positive) were evaluated. Results The AI-ECG model achieved areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve of .87–.97 for diagnosing the prevalent DCM phenotype, outperforming traditional ECG parameters. AI-ECG was comparable to echocardiography for predicting future DCM (C-index .80–.87 and .80–.90, respectively). In familial cohorts, 5-year negative predictive values were 95.5% (Antwerp) and 91.5% (Maastricht), with corresponding positive predictive values of 42.4% and 39.4%, while high-risk scores were associated with a 5.1–6.4-fold increased risk of incident DCM. Conclusions The explainable AI-ECG model detects the echocardiographic DCM phenotype and predicts future disease, and supports the exclusion of short- to mid-term disease in genetically at-risk individuals.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence-enhanced electrocardiography for detection and prediction of dilated cardiomyopathy

evidence_items.summary: Purpose: This article examines the legal and governance implications of AI-assisted employee performance evaluation in Czech local government. It focuses on how such systems interact with labour law, administrative law principles, data protection requirements, anti-discrimination norms, and the emerging EU framework for high-risk AI systems.Design/Methodology/Approach: The article combines a structured literature review with doctrinal legal analysis and a limited comparative approach. Although interdisciplinary, its primary analytical focus remains legal and regulatory. It examines AI-assisted evaluation tools that process employee-related data to generate classifications, scores, recommendations, or summaries that may support managerial assessments of employee performance.Findings: The analysis shows that Czech law does not expressly regulate AI-assisted employee performance evaluation in local government, which creates uncertainty regarding transparency, accountability, lawful data use, human oversight, and remedies. It further shows that some employee-evaluation systems may fall within the high-risk employment category under the AI Act, in which case enhanced obligations concerning governance, documentation, transparency, and oversight would apply.Practical Implications: Local authorities considering the use of AI-assisted evaluation tools should adopt clear internal rules on permissible data sources, purpose limitation, documentation, explainability, human review, and complaint handling. The article identifies practical safeguards that may reduce legal and organisational risk while preserving AI’s role in supporting, rather than replacing, human judgement in personnel assessment.Academic Contribution to the Field: The article contributes to the literatureby connecting debates on algorithmic management, public administration, and AI regulation to the specific setting of employee evaluation in local government.
evidence_items.title: Using Artificial Intelligence in the Performance Evaluation of Local Government Employees

evidence_items.summary: Background Intracardiac echocardiography (ICE) has becoming indispensable for ensuring safety and efficacy during atrial fibrillation (AF) ablation. However, ICE interpretation remains highly observer-dependent, presenting a steep learning curve in rapidly distinguishing complex, dynamic cardiac structures. Objectives This study aimed to develop and validate a multi-task deep learning system (AI-ICE) for real-time, automated interpretation of cardiac structures and ultrasound views during AF ablation. Methods The interpretation task is defined as two sub-tasks, one for detecting 12 anatomical structures and the other for classifying 5 standard views. A total of 373,091 ICE images from 350 patients undergoing AF ablation across three centers were collected. The dataset was split into training/internal validation cohorts (two centers) and an independent external testing cohort (one center, 35,335 frames). The AI-ICE model combined a ResUnet backbone with an LSTM module to capture spatiotemporal dependencies across consecutive frames, reflecting the streaming nature of real-time clinical ICE imaging. The two tasks were formulated as a multi-task coupled framework with shared representations, exploiting the intrinsic interdependence between the imaging view and the visible anatomy. Results For the internal validation, the average AUC for classifying ultrasound views and detecting structures reached 0.971 (95% CI: 0.947–0.992) and 0.974 (95% CI: 0.968–0.980). For the external validation, the AI-ICE system achieved an AUC of 0.984 (95% CI: 0.974–0.993) for ultrasound view classification and 0.955 (95% CI: 0.948–0.962) for anatomical structure objection. Compared with three cardiologist experts, it achieved higher accuracy (AUC: 0.941 vs. 0.916) and superior inter-rater agreement (Kappa coefficient: 0.791 vs. 0.716). Additionally, the system demonstrated high efficiency, with an inference time of 12 milliseconds per ICE image.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence for intracardiac echocardiography interpretation and guidance during atrial fibrillation ablation

evidence_items.summary: Backpropagation has been the dominant credit-assignment mechanism behind the deep-learning revolution, yet it is global, memory-hungry, biologically implausible, and costly on hardware dominated by data movement. In parallel, predictive coding, equilibrium propagation, contrastive Hebbian learning and forward-only schemes have shown that useful credit assignment can also arise from local variables and the relaxation of an energy function. This manuscript is a review with a reproducible benchmark, not a proposal of a new learning rule. We organise existing backpropagation-free methods and continual-learning strategies under a common Local Equilibrium Learning (LEL) formulation, re-validate the core theoretical links numerically, and use a controlled continual-learning benchmark as an auditable case study within the review. The theoretical contribution is unification and verification, not priority over predictive coding, equilibrium propagation or replay. The empirical contribution is diagnostic rather than exhaustive: a benchmark of catastrophic forgetting with local networks that makes the review reproducible. We compare regularisation (EWC, SI), noise replay and generative “dreaming” across MNIST, Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10 in two independent implementations. Generative replay with local generators turns class-incremental Split-MNIST forgetting (chance level, the same as EWC and SI) into 86.8±0.2%, which is 96% of the joint-training ceiling and 97.4% in the task-incremental setting; the same mechanism reaches 82.0% on Fashion-MNIST and 37.0% on CIFAR-10. evidence_items.summary: When using the in situ nylon bag technique to evaluate rumen degradation characteristics, if the microbial contamination in the nylon bag residue is not corrected, the degradation rate of roughage nitrogen in rumen will be underestimated. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to determine the bacterial contamination of roughages during in situ rumen culture, and to establish an equation for predicting microbial contamination of rumen culture residue. Using the nylon bag technique, a total of 30 roughages was incubated in the rumen of four Zhaowuda meat sheep. (15NH4)2SO4 was continuously infused into the rumen, and then pellets of labeled rumen solids-associated bacteria (SAB) and rumen liquid-associated bacteria (LAB) were isolated by differential centrifugation of samples of ruminal contents. The rumen degradation rate of 24 kinds of roughage nitrogen was significantly increased after microbial correction (p < 0.05), six kinds of roughage nitrogen species were increased in numerical value although there was no significant difference (p > 0.05), and there was no difference between the two labeling methods of SAB and LAB. Except for imported alfalfa hay (AH), the course of bacterial contamination of 29 roughages was described by an exponential function of the general type Ncont. = Nmax [1 − exp(−C·t)], where Nmax varied with the feed’s nutritional composition. Separate prediction models were established for straw roughages, hay roughages, and all 29 roughages combined, incorporating crude protein (CP), neutral detergent fiber (NDF), acid detergent fiber (ADF), dry matter (DM), and organic matter (OM) to estimate Nmax. The results confirm that microbial contamination systematically biases nylon bag measurements, causing a consistent underestimation of true ruminal nitrogen degradability, especially for high-fiber, low-protein feeds.
evidence_items.title: Development of Equations to Estimate Microbial Nitrogen Contamination of In Situ Roughage Residues

evidence_items.summary: This work develops and benchmarks a numerical framework for computing decaying traveling-wave solutions of the Degasperis–Procesi equation. The approach provides a unified treatment of smooth solitary waves and peaked wave solutions across the relevant parameter regimes. Cusped and anticusped profiles are excluded, as their stronger singular behavior is not compatible with the regularity assumptions underlying the numerical formulation. The method addresses the challenges associated with the asymptotic behavior of the solutions and the non-smoothness of peaked profiles. Its performance is systematically assessed through convergence studies and comparisons with exact solutions. For smooth traveling waves, the numerical results exhibit the expected second-order convergence, while the computations for peaked waves demonstrate the method’s ability to resolve the non-smooth profile. The results also illustrate the dependence of wave profiles and amplitudes on wave speed and other model parameters, providing a benchmark for numerical computation of these solutions.
evidence_items.title: Numerical Computation of Smooth and Peaked Decaying Traveling-Wave Solutions of the Degasperis–Procesi Equation: A Benchmark Study

evidence_items.summary: Agentic healthcare platforms that combine large language models with physician oversight are growing quickly, but little is known about who uses them. We characterized 3,223 enrollees of Lotus AI, a free, physician-supervised agentic platform, who completed onboarding, messaged the agent, and had a linked health record between February and July 2026, and compared them with national benchmarks. Median age was 51 years and 62% were male. Chronic condition prevalence exceeded 2024 National Health Interview Survey estimates in every age band by 4 to 7 percentage points; 18% had a functional or symptom-defined disorder; among the 30% with four or more ambulatory visits in the prior year, care was spread across nearly five providers, with 44% meeting a threshold for high fragmentation. Users with functional disorders generated 1.8 times as many physician escalations and 2.6 times as many laboratory orders as other users, but no more prescriptions. This profile differs from the younger, predominantly female populations reported for direct-to-consumer telemedicine. It moves chronic disease management, functional disorder pathways, and care coordination from aspirations to design requirements, and we argue that deployed AI care platforms should characterize their populations against national benchmarks early.
evidence_items.title: Enrollees and Early Lessons from an Agentic Healthcare Platform with Physicians in the Loop

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Kernel-level rootkits subvert the operating system to conceal the network ports through which they maintain covert channels, and cloud tenants who cannot access the hypervisor have few reliable defences. Existing detectors stop at a verdict, leaving investigation and response to human analysts and admitting a window during which an active rootkit persists. This paper presents an agentic AI framework that both detects and autonomously responds to kernel rootkits through port-level behavioural analysis. On cloud guests hosted on Google Cloud Platform, a kernel-mode Port Enumerator and a user-mode Port Monitor produce cross-view port lists whose discrepancy, formalized here as a temporal behavioural signal, is classified by a deep ensemble of CNN-LSTM, Bi-LSTM, Autoencoder and GAN. The resulting Rootkit/Benign verdict is handed to an LLM Agent Orchestrator that executes an autonomous perceive-plan-act-reflect loop, invoking security tools under human-in-the-loop oversight for high-impact actions. A second evidence channel is released with the paper as a labelled concealment matrix of 87 kernel rootkit samples described by a binary vector over a 968-entry dictionary of concealed objects, each carrying the technique it uses to hide. We give a mathematical model of the cross-view signal, the fused decision, and the agent’s utility-driven action selection. Evaluated on a Windows Server 2025 guest, the framework detects rootkits with a mean detection latency of 1.2 s while autonomously triaging confirmed threats; on the released concealment matrix the technique of a confirmed rootkit is recovered from its hook vector at 0.846 accuracy against a 0.713 majority-class rate, with the three-way distinction among inline, SSDT and IAT concealment still limited by class imbalance. The response layer is specified and instantiated but not yet measured; Section 5.6 states the protocol by which it will be tested.
evidence_items.title: An Agentic AI Framework for Autonomous Cross-View Kernel Rootkit Detection and Response in Cloud Environments

evidence_items.summary:
Background
DeepSeek, an open-source large language model (LLM) extensively adopted in hospitals across China, presents a locally deployable alternative to proprietary models such as GPT. However, its real-world clinical performance and safeguards remain underexplored.


Objective
The aim of this study is to evaluate the performance of the general-purpose and reasoning versions of DeepSeek (DeepSeek AI) and GPT models in diagnosis, medical record analysis, and safeguards against adversarial vulnerabilities.


Methods
This cross-sectional study included 50 real-world medical records from 10 hospitals spanning 14 specialties. A total of 7 LLMs were evaluated, including DeepSeek-V3, DeepSeek-R1, GPT-4o (via ChatGPT; OpenAI), o3-mini (via ChatGPT), o3-mini-high (via ChatGPT), GPT-4o (via Copilot; Microsoft), and GPT-4o-reasoning (via Copilot). Models were tasked with generating diagnoses based on admission notes, answering 12 questions related to extraction, summarization, and inference using discharge summaries, and undergoing 4 rounds of simulated adversarial prompt attacks designed to elicit misinformation. The diagnostic evaluation was performed on 47 records after the exclusion of 3 flawed admission notes, while the other tasks used the full set of 50 records. Diagnostic performance was evaluated based on accuracy, with the causes of misdiagnosis further categorized. Medical record analysis was assessed by scores in extraction, summarization, and inference tasks. Safeguard evaluation included identifying the earliest round of successful prompt attack and verifying reference authenticity and accuracy.


Results
Among the 7 models included in this study, DeepSeek-R1 and GPT-4o-reasoning (via Copilot) achieved the highest diagnostic accuracy at 64% (30/47). In medical record analysis, both models also excelled across the 3 subdimensions. GPT-4o-reasoning (via Copilot) achieved accuracies of 97.7% (293/300) in extraction, 87.5% (175/200) in summarization, and 87% in inference, while DeepSeek-R1 reached 97.7% (293/300), 83.5% (167/200), and 85% (85/100), respectively. In simulated adversarial safeguard evaluation involving 4 rounds of prompt attacks, all evaluated models showed high vulnerability. DeepSeek-R1 generated medical disinformation in 98% (49/50) of cases, with only a 2% refusal rate. GPT-4o-reasoning (via Copilot) showed the highest refusal rate at 30%, but it still generated disinformation in 70% (35/50) of cases. True hallucination rates ranged from 38.6% (27/70; GPT-4o-reasoning via Copilot) to 73% (73/100; DeepSeek-V3).


Conclusions
These findings underscore the clinical application potential of DeepSeek models, while also emphasizing the critical need to strengthen safeguards against adversarial vulnerabilities prior to their clinical deployment.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating DeepSeek in Real-World Clinical Scenarios on Performance and Safeguards: Multicenter Comparative Study.

evidence_items.summary:
MOTIVATION
Accurate prediction of translation efficiency from mRNA sequences is an important step toward mRNA sequence design. In recent years, the widespread adoption of high-resolution ribosome profiling techniques, such as Ribo-seq, has led to rapid accumulation of large-scale datasets that capture the relationship between mRNA sequences and translation efficiency. This progress has facilitated the development of machine-learning-based models for translation efficiency prediction. However, most existing approaches rely primarily on mRNA-derived features, such as codon usage frequency and 5' untranslated regions (5'UTRs), and do not directly utilize the amino-acid-level information.


RESULTS
In this study, we show that incorporating distributed representations (embeddings) of amino acid sequences translated from mRNA as model features can improve translation efficiency prediction. By combining fixed amino acid embeddings derived from a pretrained protein language model with mRNA-derived features, the proposed model integrates complementary protein-level and nucleotide-level information for more accurate prediction of translation efficiency.


AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION
Codes are available at GitHub (https://github.com/gterai/AA_emb) and Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23968476).
evidence_items.title: Leveraging amino acid embeddings for accurate translation efficiency prediction.

Results are compared with tensile strength predictions from previous studies, and both Tsai-Hill and Tsai-Wu failure criteria are applied and benchmarked against literature values. The results revealed that for the [0°/90°/0°] layup, all compressive loading cases are governed by transverse matrix crushing in the 90° ply. The uniaxial compressive strength (136–144 MPa) is only 22–23% of the tensile strength (617 MPa). This large tension–compression asymmetry arises from the low transverse compressive strength (140 MPa) combined with stress concentration in the 90° layer. Further, under biaxial compression, failure occurs at just 28–33 MPa — a 77–80% reduction from uniaxial compressive strength and a 95% reduction from the tensile benchmark. Tsai-Wu predicts 5–14% lower failure loads than Tsai-Hill under compressive loading. The [0°/90°/0°] stacking is poorly optimized for compressive or biaxial loading; incorporating ±45° plies is recommended to improve biaxial compressive performance.
evidence_items.title: Compressive Strength Behaviour of Plain Weave Fabric Composites under Uniaxial and Biaxial Loading

evidence_items.summary: Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion (OTEC) is a marine energy technology that utilizes the temperature difference between surface seawater and deep seawater to generate electricity. One of the main components in this system is the Cold Water Pipe (CWP), which functions to transport cold seawater from deep ocean layers to the power generation system. The long pipe structure with a large diameter-to-thickness ratio makes it susceptible to bending deformation. This study aims to analyze the effect of geometric imperfections on the bending capacity of CWP pipes using the Finite Element Method (FEM). The numerical model was validated through a benchmarking process against a bending formulation, with a deviation of 2.64%. A parametric study was conducted on circumferential imperfections in the form of sinusoidal waves with variations in amplitude and number of waves. The results show that increasing imperfection amplitude reduces the bending capacity, while increasing the number of waves tends to increase the ultimate moment value. This behavior is likely related to the denser wave distribution along the longitudinal direction of the pipe, which may create a local stiffness effect similar to a stiffener element, thereby improving the structural resistance against bending deformation. Variations in imperfection configuration result in changes in the UM value of up to 24.1%, indicating that imperfection characteristics have a significant influence on the bending response of the CWP structure.
evidence_items.title: Numerical Study on the Bending Behavior of OTEC Cold Water Pipes Considering Geometric Imperfections

evidence_items.summary:
Circumstellar debris disks are sustained by ongoing collisional processes that provide information about the formation and evolution of planetary systems. HD 170773, a nearby F5V star at 37 pc, hosts a large and narrow debris belt resolved at millimeter wavelengths by ALMA.
We targeted HD 170773 with HST/STIS to obtain high-contrast coronagraphic images of the system in the optical with the aim of detecting the debris disk in scattered light to better characterize its properties at 3.7 au resolution.
We observed HD 170773 and a point-spread function (PSF) reference star in order to achieve high contrast, revealing the faint scattered light from micron-sized grains.We modeled the disk geometry through iterative illumination correction, ellipse fitting, and deprojection. We then examined the azimuthal and radial flux-density profiles to characterize the disk morphology and search for asymmetries.
The disk brightness is approximately axisymmetric, with a radius of 194.6 ± 0.8 au, a position angle of 112.6^ +2.2 _ - 2.3 degr, and an inclination of 25.5 ^ +1.0 _ - 1.1 degr, with its geometric center matching the stellar position. A narrow region to the southwest has decreased flux density, which suggests a local deficit of scattering material. Radially, the belt exhibits a plateau of surface brightness between 175 and 200 au and both the inner and outer edges have very steep profiles.
Our results provide a detailed characterization of HD 170773’s disk morphology and offer a benchmark for studies of large, narrow debris rings and their connections to exoplanetary systems. HD 170773 is unusual because the dust scattering phase function appears isotropic in the 65degr--115degr scattering angle range and the surface brightness plateau indicates a dust surface density in the birth ring that increases as the square of the radius, which is predicted from models of collisional erosion and local stirring.
evidence_items.title: First scattered-light imaging of HD 170773: HST/STIS observations and disk morphology
Causal Machine Learning for Treatment Effect Heterogeneity: Interpretation, Benchmarking, Validation.

evidence_items.summary: The widespread terminological asymmetry in China–Uzbekistan agricultural cooperation raises the costs of qualification verification, technical training, and contract negotiation. This paper explains the construction pathway for a Chinese–English–Uzbek agricultural terminology database: using a Chinese–English agricultural dictionary as the base text, 15,158 trilingual entries were empirically annotated, and 275 newly added terms were supplemented, forming a dual-source corpus of “stock resources plus incremental resources.” The terminology database uses entry numbers as the primary key and contains eight fields: Chinese headword, Pinyin annotation, English equivalent, Uzbek translation, subject classification, original page number, status marker, and cross-reference entry. It supports three-way retrieval in Chinese, English, and Uzbek. The database construction process is divided into six stages: layout parsing, column-by-column transcription, main-table alignment, discrepancy checking, translation-name generation, and output release. Artificial intelligence significantly reduces manual costs in transcription, batch comparison, and preliminary translation drafting. Quality control relies on a four-stage process of “machine drafting—rule constraints—expert review—version consolidation,” with emphasis on preventing four types of risks: misrecognition of visually similar characters, coexistence of multiple translations, semantic drift, and instability in the translation of policy terminology. This paper summarizes four roles and six practices of artificial intelligence in terminology construction and compares the applicable boundaries of general large language models, execution-oriented agents, and terminology-specific systems.
evidence_items.title: Research on the Construction of a Chinese–English–Uzbek Agricultural Terminology Database

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI)-based computer-aided detection (CAD) of tuberculosis (TB) on chest X-ray (CXR) may standardize screening and triage in settings with few radiologists but its accuracy in clinical cohorts remains uncertain. We searched five databases (PubMed, ScienceDirect, IEEE Xplore, OpenAlex, Lens.org) on 15 March 2026 for studies published between January 2020 and March 2026, and we appraised these studies using QUADAS-2. Evaluations from clinical cohorts with complete 2 x 2 data and a microbiological or composite reference standard for all participants were pooled using a bivariate random-effects model, with 95% prediction intervals. We accounted for overlapping participants by performing a post hoc analysis with one evaluation per cohort and used GRADE to assess the certainty of the evidence. No protocol was prepared or registered. We included 21 studies (26 evaluations of AI models). Nine evaluations from three independent cohorts were pooled. Pooled sensitivity was 0.896 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.874 to 0.915, prediction interval 0.798 to 0.950) and pooled specificity was 0.689 (95% CI 0.642 to 0.732; prediction interval 0.499 to 0.831). Both confidence intervals include the World Health Organization (WHO) triage thresholds (sensitivity 90%, specificity 70%). When a screening study with partial verification was added, pooled specificity increased to 0.735. Eighteen of 24 assessed evaluations were at high risk of bias and only 1 of 21 studies was prospective, fully verified, externally validated and met the WHO thresholds. Certainty of evidence was low for sensitivity and very low for specificity. A subsequent PubMed search found additional eligible clinical evaluations that were not screened, so the review is incomplete for those studies. In clinical cohorts, AI-CXR sensitivity is close to the WHO triage target, and specificity is close to, but not clearly above, its target. The evidence is pooled across only three cohorts, and specificity varies by product and setting. Thresholds need to be calibrated locally, and prospective, externally validated evaluations are needed before widespread deployment.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence for pulmonary tuberculosis detection on chest X-ray images: A systematic review and diagnostic accuracy meta-analysis

evidence_items.summary: This analysis evaluated whether a pre-referral artificial intelligence-supported pathway could reduce urgent suspected skin cancer referrals from primary to secondary care. Using synthetic control methods to compare six pilot GP practices with a matched control based on 30 non-pilot practices, the analysis found no statistically significant reduction in referral rates during the 11-month pilot.
evidence_items.title: Suspected skin cancer referral rates after implementation of a pre-referral artificial intelligence-supported pathway: a synthetic control analysis.

evidence_items.summary:
INTRODUCTION/OBJECTIVES
The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into healthcare offers significant potential for enhancing diagnostic accuracy and personalised medicine, yet carries inherent risks including algorithmic bias, opacity, and threats to patient safety and fundamental rights. These concerns demand robust governance frameworks that transcend aspirational recommendations. This article examines the role of ex ante evaluation in ensuring compliance with ethical and regulatory standards for AI systems in healthcare, using the PIO Model (Principles, Indicators, and Observables) as an illustrative case study.


METHODS
The PIO Model on Health provides a structured self-assessment methodology grounded in the European Commission's ethical principles for trustworthy AI while aligning with binding legal obligations under the EU Artificial Intelligence Act, the Medical Devices Regulation, and the General Data Protection Regulation. Built around the operational question "Have we done it?", the Model enables stakeholders to critically evaluate AI systems through a comprehensive checklist organised according to seven ethical principles: transparency; justice and fairness; security and non-maleficence; responsibility; privacy; autonomy; and sustainability. The paper frames AI in healthcare within the human rights framework, examining risks including algorithmic bias, automation bias, erosion of the patient-physician relationship, and challenges posed by generative AI such as hallucinations and data protection concerns.


RESULTS
The PIO Model performs an essential ex ante evaluation function, enabling identification of ethical and legislative deficiencies prior to formal conformity assessment or market placement. It facilitates continuous monitoring through medical algorithmic audit, generating metrics including conformity percentages, risk matrices, and improvement catalogues that serve as actionable guides for implementing corrective measures.


CONCLUSIONS
Designed for collective administration incorporating technical, clinical, legal, and ethics experts alongside patient representatives, the Model synthesises proliferating ethical guidelines and complex regulatory requirements into an operational instrument that transcends minimum legal standards, contributing to developing trustworthy AI systems that safeguard patient welfare and fundamental rights.
evidence_items.title: The role of ex ante evaluation for compliance with ethical and regulatory standards applicable to AI systems in healthcare: The example of the PIO Model.

evidence_items.summary: Precision oncology still faces low clinical translation rates. This is largely because two-dimensional (2D) culture systems cannot reproduce tumor heterogeneity and microenvironmental stress. Here, we review the applications of 3D cancer models, including scaffold-free spheroids, patient-derived organoids (PDOs) biobanks, and microphysiological systems (MPSs), in drug resistance modeling and personalized therapy. These platforms effectively model metabolic gradients, lineage plasticity, and immunological features within the tumor microenvironment (TME), thereby bridging the genotype-phenotype gap. They also capture physical immune exclusion, T cell exhaustion, and antigen presentation to facilitate the evaluation of immunotherapies. Last, we discuss key translational bottlenecks such as standardization and throughput, proposing the integration of advanced biomanufacturing, artificial intelligence (AI)-driven phenomics, and computational modeling to develop 3D cancer platforms into clinical predictive systems for optimizing precision treatment strategies.
evidence_items.title: Decoding cancer therapy resistance through advanced 3D organoid systems.

evidence_items.summary: Generative artificial intelligence tutors produce detailed records of how learners question, reason, and revise, and these interaction traces are increasingly available to teachers and institutions. This commentary examines what happens to the evidential value of interaction traces when they are used to assess learning in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) education. I describe an Observability–Authenticity Paradox: the features that make interaction traces informative, such as exploration, expressed uncertainty, and error, are the features that learners have most reason to suppress or manage once they expect the traces to be evaluated. In terms of argument-based validity, such reactivity to evaluation weakens the extrapolation from interaction observed under evaluative conditions to learning activity that takes place without evaluation; it can also reduce the exploration on which learning depends. The threat is greatest when traces generated during learning are used for grading or credentialing without learners knowing when and how, and when inferences rest on behaviors that learners can choose to display or withhold. I distinguish this situation from teachers’ ongoing formative monitoring, consider whether assessment could instead reward productive failure, and explain why differential reactivity is a fairness issue in the measurement sense. I conclude by proposing three design principles (declared, episodic, and learner-owned assessment) and illustrating them with STEM tasks, drawing examples mainly from science education.
evidence_items.title: Learning on the record: the observability–authenticity paradox in AI-era STEM assessment

evidence_items.summary: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly influencing language education by providing opportunities for personalized practice, immediate feedback, and flexible access to learning resources. However, effective use of GenAI in Maritime English requires competencies beyond general language proficiency and basic technological skills. Maritime English involves specialized terminology, standardized communication, operational contexts, and professional requirements in which inaccurate or inappropriate AI-generated content may have practical consequences. This conceptual study develops an AI literacy framework for Maritime English education through a conceptual literature synthesis. The synthesis draws on literature published between 2020 and 2026, supplemented by earlier foundational works on AI literacy and English for Specific Purposes (ESP), as well as authoritative Maritime references, including IMO Standard Marine Communication Phrases and IMO Model Course 3.17. Sources were selected based on their relevance to AI literacy, generative AI in language education, ESP, learner autonomy, and Maritime English, with particular attention to their conceptual contributions and applicability to Maritime communication. The synthesis identifies digital-AI competence as the core AI literacy capability, supported by two contextual knowledge bases: language competence and professional Maritime competence. Language competence enables learners to evaluate AI-generated language, while professional Maritime competence supports the verification of terminology, operational relevance, and contextual appropriateness. Digital-AI competence enables critical and responsible interaction with AI systems, including prompt formulation, output evaluation, and information verification. The proposed framework provides a conceptual basis for integrating AI literacy into Maritime English education while maintaining linguistic and professional standards. Future empirical research is needed to operationalize and validate the framework among Maritime English learners, lecturers, and Maritime professionals.
evidence_items.title: Towards an AI Literacy Framework for Maritime English Education: Integrating Language, Professional, and Digital Competencies

evidence_items.summary:
Drawing on Expectancy Violation Theory, this study examines how product image creator identity (AI vs. human) influences purchase intentions and the underlying psychological mechanisms.
 
 
 
 Three online experiments examined consumers' attitudes toward AI-generated product images and purchase intentions toward the featured products, assessed how these evaluations deviated from expectations associated with human-created images, and identified conditions under which artificial intelligence (AI) imagery was more or less effective in shaping consumer responses. Data were analyzed in Statistical Package for the Social Sciences using Multivariate Analysis of Variance and Multivariate Analysis of Covariance, with serial and moderated mediation analyses conducted using the PROCESS macro.
 
 
 
 Consumers consistently prefer human-created product images and perceive them as more novel, whereas AI-generated images evoke greater eeriness. Perceived novelty, eeriness, positive and negative expectancy violations, and attitudes mediate the relationship between image creator identity and purchase intention. Product type serves as a boundary condition, with AI-generated images evaluated more favorably for search products than for experience products.
 
 
 
 This research identifies positive and negative expectancy violations as central psychological mechanisms shaping consumer responses to AI-generated product images. By highlighting product type as a boundary condition, it helps reconcile mixed findings in the AI-generated marketing literature and provides actionable guidance for the strategic use of AI-generated product imagery.
evidence_items.title: Novelty or eeriness? Investigating consumer responses to AI-generated product images through expectancy violation theory

evidence_items.summary: Precision oncology based on the identification of actionable genomic alterations (AGAs) has been transformative in the care of solid tumors, yet optimal treatment selection is often hindered by tissue exhaustion and slow turnaround times. Artificial intelligence (AI) addresses these barriers by predicting AGAs directly from routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained slides. Recent landmark studies, including the prospective EAGLE and ANNAR trials, have demonstrated that deep learning models can identify alterations such as EGFR in non-small cell lung cancer and FGFR in urothelial cancer across diverse global cohorts. By providing near-instant, non-destructive results, AI-based prediction can triage patients for molecular testing or clinical trials at the time of initial diagnosis. This perspective evaluates the maturing evidence base and outlines a pragmatic pathway for integrating these tools into clinical practice. Ultimately, these models offer the opportunity to extract critical molecular information from slides generated in every laboratory worldwide and to significantly improve timely access to the rapidly evolving therapeutic landscape of solid tumors.
evidence_items.title: AI-based prediction of actionable genomic alterations from H&E-stained slides

evidence_items.summary: Contact dermatitis (CD) plays a significant role in occupational health due to its frequent occurrence and environmental triggers and is among the most common occupational diseases in Western countries. Despite its prevalence, occupational contact dermatitis (OCD) is often overlooked by occupational physicians, largely due to limited knowledge and a lack of validated detection tools. Advances in digital technologies and artificial intelligence (AI) offer promising opportunities for improving early detection, yet an overview of available digital tools and their effectiveness in dermatitis detection is lacking. A systematic review was conducted in PubMed, Embase, Cinahl, and Scopus. The search focused on original studies published in peer-reviewed journals between 2014 and 2024. Forty-three studies evaluating digital tools for dermatitis detection were included, categorized as models (n = 31) or devices (n = 12). Models represent AI algorithms not yet in practical use, while devices are tools already implemented. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) were the most commonly used computational technique. Median sensitivity and specificity were 0.84 and 0.97 for all tools, 0.85 and 0.97 for models, and 0.78 and 0.97 for devices. The results provided in this review will serve as valuable input for the development of new tools to enhance early OCD detection.
evidence_items.title: Digital Tools for the Detection of Dermatitis: A Systematic Review.

evidence_items.summary: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used to support English as a Foreign Language (EFL) writing through automated comments, language correction, and rubric-based scoring. Yet the usefulness of these applications depends on whether their outputs are consistent, aligned with intended assessment criteria, and pedagogically appropriate. This critical narrative review examines selected research on large language models in writing assessment and considers implications for CEFR-aligned assessment in Uzbek higher education. The discussion is organized around three issues: rating reliability, validity of score interpretations, and the quality and use of AI-generated feedback. Existing evidence indicates that large language models can produce consistent rubric-based ratings under particular conditions, but consistency alone does not establish that a score validly represents writing proficiency or a CEFR level. Feedback may support revision, particularly when it addresses language form and textual organization, but learners and teachers still need to evaluate the relevance and accuracy of suggestions. The review identifies a context-specific research priority: comparing AI-generated judgments with trained human ratings using transparent CEFR-informed criteria and investigating how learners use the resulting feedback. Because this article is a critical narrative review rather than a systematic review or an original empirical study, its conclusions are provisional and should be followed by a documented literature search and local validation study.
evidence_items.title: FROM CEFR DESCRIPTORS TO AI-GENERATED FEEDBACK: RELIABILITY, VALIDITY, AND RESEARCH PRIORITIES FOR EFL WRITING ASSESSMENT IN UZBEKISTAN

evidence_items.summary:
This paper benchmarks Vietnamese banks’ technical efficiency and tests whether the benchmarks, and their association with intellectual capital, are robust to the choice of data envelopment analysis (DEA) specification.
 
 
 
 Using an unbalanced panel of 624 bank-years from 42 banks (2002–2022), efficiency is estimated under the intermediation and production approaches on an identical common sample. The scores are related to the Modified Value Added Intellectual Coefficient (MVAIC) through fractional probit regression, with system GMM and Simar–Wilson estimation as robustness checks.
 
 
 
 MVAIC is positively and significantly associated with efficiency under the intermediation approach but only marginally under the production approach. Specification choice changes which banks are identified as benchmarks: most bank-years efficient under one approach are not efficient under the other. State-owned banks are far more consistently robust benchmarks than joint-stock banks. We find no evidence that the association differs by ownership or across systemic shock periods.
 
 
 
 Banks efficient under both specifications are the safest benchmarks; single-specification benchmarks suit only the activity that specification measures, and disagreement between specifications indicates which activity warrants closer examination.
 
 
 
 This is among the first studies to show directly, through rank correlations, frontier transitions and bank-level benchmark identification that a bank’s benchmark status depends on which of two standard DEA specifications is used, with implications for benchmarking institutions with heterogeneous business models.
evidence_items.title: Benchmarking bank efficiency under alternative measurement specifications: intellectual capital and ownership structure in Vietnam

evidence_items.summary: Despite decades of attention to port performance measurement, prevailing benchmarking frameworks rely almost exclusively on mean turnaround time, systematically suppressing information about variance, the dimension most consequential for supply chain schedule reliability. This study addresses that gap by proposing Port Time Variability (PTV) as a standardised reliability metric, operationalised as the coefficient of variation of port time derived from high-frequency Automatic Identification System (AIS) data. Key factors are innovatively extracted from Automatic Identification System (AIS) data and country-level port data, capturing port dynamics and complex vessel flow network metrics. Structural equation modelling (SEM) is employed to assess their influence on port time variability, measured as the statistical dispersion of port call durations across 401 ports in 119 countries. The findings reveal that high-quality port infrastructure and geographically favourable locations enhance port logistics efficiency, leading to reduced port time variability. Additionally, port infrastructure quality, location conditions, and network connectivity positively influence port dynamic flow. Port network connectivity and dynamic flow partially mediate the relationship between location conditions and port time variability. Crucially, the analysis demonstrates that ports trapped in a vicious cycle of low investment, poor service responsiveness, and reduced vessel calls exhibit systematically higher PTV, a pattern consistent with rent-seeking dynamics identified in institutional port economics. These insights contribute to developing strategic port management approaches aimed at improving operational efficiency, reducing congestion and delays, and guiding long-term infrastructure investments to strengthen inter-port connectivity.
evidence_items.title: Modelling the factors affecting port time variability

evidence_items.summary:
OBJECTIVE
Sinonasal inverted papilloma (IP) is a benign epithelial neoplasm with a propensity for malignant transformation. Reported rates of synchronous or metachronous carcinoma vary widely. Our aim was to determine the rates of both synchronous and metachronous malignancy in patients with IP.


DATA SOURCES
Embase, MEDLINE, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library were searched from 2005 until June 2026.


REVIEW METHODS
We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. Prevalences were pooled using a random-effects model.


RESULTS
A total of 68 studies (n = 7412 patients) were identified. The pooled prevalence of overall malignancy was 5.6% (95% CI: 4.5-6.8), comprising synchronous malignancy in 4.3% (95% CI: 3.4-5.3), and metachronous malignancy in 1.3% (95% CI: 0.8-2.0). The pooled recurrence rate was 17.5% (95% CI: 15.0-20.2).


CONCLUSIONS
These weighted, IP-specific estimates place the prevalence of malignancy in inverted papilloma below the figures most often cited in the literature. These findings provide a methodologically robust benchmark for patient counseling and postoperative surveillance.
evidence_items.title: Prevalence of Synchronous and Metachronous Malignancy in Sinonasal Inverted Papilloma: Meta-Analysis.

evidence_items.summary:
This study aims to critically examine the management effectiveness of structural health governance in Queensland multi-storey community title scheme (CTS) residential buildings above three storeys, focusing on the statutory role and competency of Bodies Corporate and their service providers. It seeks to identify systemic weaknesses in current legal frameworks, documentation practices and decision-making processes and to develop evidence-based recommendations for legislative and institutional reforms to strengthen preventative maintenance, regulatory oversight and structural health outcomes.
 
 
 
 This study adopted a qualitative methodology using semi-structured online interviews, surveys and a strategic records search to examine structural health management within CTS. Structured responses were analysed verbatim, while open-ended data and records were coded and thematically analysed following grounded theory principles. Data were collected from 270 stakeholders across diverse CTS typologies in Queensland. Cross-analysis of interviews, surveys, records and literature enabled triangulation, identification of convergent themes and validation of findings, supporting an exploratory assessment of stakeholder relationships and maintenance practices.
 
 
 
 The study finds that structural health governance in Queensland CTS buildings is undermined by under-qualified Bodies Corporate, poor documentation and reactive, delayed defect remediation. Systemic gaps in legislation, mandatory inspections, record-keeping and enforcement allow serious defects to escalate, heightening safety and financial risks.
 
 
 
 The study is limited by its non-legal analytical approach, relying on the author's interpretation of complex regulatory frameworks rather than formal legal analysis. It is further constrained by scarce, fragmented data on structural defects and maintenance performance across Queensland CTS buildings, restricting the ability to generalise findings sector-wide.
 
 
 
 The study urges legislative reforms like mandatory periodic structural inspections, time-bound repair timelines for defects and a centralised SH databank for CTS buildings. Bodies Corporate can enhance governance via technical training, better documentation handover from developers and proactive maintenance planning. Regulators should establish a dedicated Structural Health Division in Queensland building and construction commission (QBCC) for enforcement, inspections and penalties, mitigating risks like those in Mascot Towers and improving safety, accountability and resident confidence in CTS buildings above three storeys.
 
 
 
 The study highlights profound social implications from poor structural health governance in Queensland CTS buildings. Unremedied defects like waterproofing failures and concrete degradation cause resident displacement, health risks, psychological distress and economic burdens on vulnerable owners and tenants. Neglect exacerbates inequality, erodes community cohesion, strains public services and risks catastrophic failures akin to Mascot Towers, underscoring the urgent need for reforms to safeguard occupant safety, wellbeing and housing stability.
 
 
 
 The study is the first focused analysis of structural health governance deficiencies in Queensland's multi-storey CTS buildings, benchmarking against Mascot Towers and Champlain Towers failures. It uniquely identifies gaps in Bodies Corporate competency, regulatory frameworks and documentation practices specific to Queensland's coastal context. The novel proposals namely a centralised SH databank, mandatory inspections with timed repairs, a dedicated QBCC Structural Health Division and an advance policy reform discourse lays a foundation for proactive, evidence-based strategies to enhance building safety and resilience.
evidence_items.title: Strengthening structural health governance in Queensland multi-storey residential buildings
